- **Timing:** In period one the firms simultaneously set uniform prices and consumers choose a brand, generating observed customer segments. In period two the firms first simultaneously select uniform or segment-specific quality-disclosure thresholds, then set old- and new-customer prices, after which consumers observe available disclosures and prices, update quality beliefs, and stay with the prior firm or switch.
- **Actions:** firms set first-period uniform prices; consumers choose an initial brand; firms select disclosure format and quality thresholds by segment; firms set second-period prices for own and rival customers; consumers update beliefs and choose whether to stay or switch
- **Information:** New-product quality is privately observed by its firm and initially unknown to consumers.; Consumers infer nondisclosed quality from the announced equilibrium cutoff.; First-period purchases reveal persistent horizontal brand preference and are observed by both firms.; Disclosure cost, prior quality distribution, prices, and model primitives are common knowledge.; Firms and consumers rationally anticipate continuation pricing, disclosure, and switching.
- **Objective:** Each firm maximizes the sum of first-period revenue and expected second-period profit, anticipating how the first-period marginal customer determines future retention and poaching opportunities.
- **Representative equation:** `$Π_a(p_{a1},p_{b1}) = p_{a1}x_1 + E[π_{a2}];  Π_b(p_{a1},p_{b1}) = p_{b1}(1-x_1) + E[π_{b2}]$ (Section 3.3, Equation (8), paper p. 8517 (PDF p. 8))
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric two-period rational-expectations equilibrium solved by backward induction
- **Solution:** In equilibrium firms set lower disclosure thresholds, hence disclose more often, to their own customers while charging lower prices to rival customers. Relative to uniform disclosure, BBD improves second-period profit through more efficient targeting and greater perceived quality differentiation. Its first-period effect changes sign with disclosure cost; total firm profit falls at low cost but rises at higher cost, while social welfare increases through lower disclosure waste. Both firms nevertheless choose BBD endogenously, creating a prisoner's dilemma when cost is low and a win-win outcome when cost is high.
- **Evidence:** First-period prices determine customer histories and the old/new segments available for second-period discrimination.; In period two firms simultaneously select disclosure thresholds, then segment-specific prices, and consumers update quality beliefs before staying or switching.; Proposition 1 proves firms disclose more to existing customers but price more aggressively to rivals' customers.; Proposition 4 shows both firms endogenously adopt behavior-based disclosure even when low disclosure cost makes that mutual adoption a prisoner's dilemma.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses two periods, full market coverage, zero marginal production cost, independent uniform qualities, no discounting, persistent one-dimensional tastes, and simultaneous product launches. Disclosure is represented by a public cutoff with linear per-recipient cost. The conclusion notes that paid trials, continuing sales of the old product, repeated switching, and sequential launches remain outside the model.

### Strategic Inattention in Product Search

Adrian Hillenbrand; Svenja Hippel (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.03413](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.03413). First published online: 2025-02-14.

- **Question:** When online sellers infer willingness to pay from product-search behavior, how much should consumers deliberately limit search, and can personalized pricing improve seller profit without destroying consumer and total surplus?
- **Players:** single buyer choosing product-search filters and the final purchase; monopolistic seller observing search intensity and setting price
- **Timing:** The value distribution is common knowledge. The buyer first chooses filter intensity a, which truncates the possible valuation distribution from below. The seller observes a and sets a take-it-or-leave-it price p(a). Nature then draws the buyer's value from the filtered distribution, and the buyer buys if value is at least price. The laboratory and online implementations repeat a discrete version for 15 rounds.
- **Actions:** buyer chooses search or filter intensity; seller observes filters and sets a conditional price; buyer accepts or rejects the realized product offer; human sellers choose an entire price vector in the strategy-method experiment
- **Information:** The prior value distribution and filter technology are common knowledge.; The seller observes the buyer's filter choice and the induced distribution but not the realized valuation when pricing.; The buyer observes realized value and price before accepting or rejecting.; Experimental buyers know that filters may affect prices but do not initially know the seller's pricing rule.; Algorithmic sellers do not use earlier-round behavior, and buyer beliefs about all conditional prices are elicited each round.
- **Objective:** After observing filter intensity a, the seller chooses price to maximize expected revenue, while the buyer chooses a ex ante to maximize expected net surplus anticipating the seller's best-response price and later buys only when value covers price.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi_S(p|a) = p Pr(v >= p | a); U_B(a) = E[(v-p_star(a))_+ | v >= a]$ (Section 2.2, Equation (2), and Section 2.3, printed p. 696 (PDF p. 4), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium in search, pricing, and purchase
- **Solution:** The seller's equilibrium price is flat up to the unrestricted monopoly price and then rises with the filter; anticipating this, the buyer chooses exactly that cutoff and remains strategically inattentive. Human sellers and buyers respond in the predicted directions, while algorithmic treatments show that buyers restrict search specifically when pricing makes it strategically useful. Personalized pricing that induces strategic inattention substantially reduces welfare and buyer surplus, and aggressive extraction can also lower seller profit because buyers search less and reject more offers.
- **Evidence:** Proposition 1 proves that the seller's optimal price is weakly increasing in the buyer's filter choice.; Proposition 2 derives strategic inattention: in subgame-perfect equilibrium the buyer chooses the unrestricted monopoly price as the search cutoff, strictly below full search.; In the HUMAN treatment, endogenous prices increase with filters and buyers restrict search in roughly three quarters of interactions.; In the THEORY treatment, buyers' average filter choice is close to the predicted value and is substantially below the uniform-price benchmark.; The HUMAN, THEORY, and REDUCED schemes that induce strategic inattention lower welfare and buyer surplus relative to the UNIFORM and EQUAL benchmarks; only REDUCED raises seller profit relative to uniform pricing by leaving positive surplus for buyers.
- **Caveat:** The core theory has one monopolistic seller, one buyer, a single filter dimension, perfect observability of search intensity, direct conditional pricing, regular valuations, and purchase under indifference. The experiment makes the information channel unusually transparent, so it may upper-bound consumer sophistication in real markets. Competition, heterogeneous search methods, indirect product steering, persistent data use, and field-market identification are left for future work.

### Economics of Social Media Fake Accounts

Zihong Huang; De Liu (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.02616](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.02616). First published online: 2025-02-19.

- **Question:** How do platform antifake effort, consumer literacy and the price of fake accounts reshape strategic fake-follower purchases, advertising revenue and consumer welfare?
- **Players:** a social-media platform; a high- or low-quality influencer; informed and uninformed consumers; an informed or uninformed representative advertiser whose payment is mechanically determined in the model
- **Timing:** At time 1 the platform chooses antifake effort. Nature then draws the influencer's type, consumers' quality valuations, and the advertiser's information type. At time 2 informed consumers choose whether to follow while the influencer simultaneously chooses fake-account purchases. At time 3 uninformed consumers observe apparent early followers and choose whether to follow. At time 4 the advertiser observes total followers, advertises, and makes the formula-determined payments.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses costly fake-account detection effort; the influencer chooses how many fake accounts to buy; consumers choose whether to follow
- **Information:** The influencer privately knows whether content quality is high or low.; Some consumers and advertisers observe quality while others infer it from apparent follower counts.; Fake accounts inflate observable followers; platform effort raises their unit price according to p_f=p_0+d/(1-tau) while also increasing legitimate consumers' nuisance cost.; Bayesian beliefs after observed follower counts support pooling or separating equilibria.
- **Objective:** The influencer chooses fake accounts to maximize advertising revenue net of fake-account cost. The platform chooses antifake effort to maximize a weighted sum of its own profit and consumer welfare, rather than profit alone.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi_p=(1-w)pi_p+wU; pi_p=lambda_p mu E[n_r]-(gamma/2)d^2; pi_i=lambda_i mu E[n_r]-p_f x$ (Sections 3.1 and 3.5, Equations (3), (5), and (6), printed pp. 8869-8870 / PDF pp. 5-6)
- **Equilibrium:** Undefeated perfect Bayesian signaling equilibrium
- **Solution:** As antifake effort rises, equilibrium can move from pooling to costly separation and then natural separation. More enforcement or social-media literacy can perversely increase equilibrium fake-account purchases because high-quality influencers buy defensively. A purely profit-driven platform chooses zero antifake effort and pooling, whereas a platform placing weight on consumer welfare may induce separation; better detection technology can align platform and consumer interests.
- **Evidence:** A low-quality influencer may buy fake followers to mimic a high type.; A high-quality influencer may buy fake followers defensively to make imitation too expensive.; The platform chooses costly detection anticipating influencer signaling and the response of followers and an advertiser.; The paper maps parameter regions into pooling, costly-separating and natural-separating outcomes.
- **Caveat:** The baseline studies influence-boosting fake accounts with one representative influencer, advertiser and platform, two influencer types, a stylized consumer-value distribution, exogenous revenue shares, and no direct harm from fake accounts beyond distorted beliefs and nuisance cost. Repeated and multi-type extensions broaden the mechanism, but influencer competition, scams or political manipulation, direct user harms, and field validation remain outside the model.

### Platform Competition and Interoperability: The Net Fee Model

Mehmet Ekmekci; Alexander White; Lingxuan Wu (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.02810](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02810). First published online: 2025-02-19.

- **Question:** Will adding rivals reduce a dominant platform's power, or can interoperability and a stronger challenger be more effective than fragmented entry?
- **Players:** J competing platforms choosing side-specific net fees; unit masses of users on one or more sides choosing a platform or outside option
- **Timing:** Platforms simultaneously announce a vector of net membership fees across market sides. Users observe all fees and choose at most one platform or the outside option on their side. Joining demand is determined by standalone tastes and net fees. After joining, platform-specific interaction benefits arise; the net-fee conduct assumption lets each platform extract those benefits through subsequent interaction charges, so realized demand and network values determine platform profit.
- **Actions:** each platform sets a net fee for every side it serves; each user selects one platform or the outside option; under interoperability policy, users obtain a specified fraction of cross-platform interaction benefits
- **Information:** User taste vectors are heterogeneous and distributed according to commonly known smooth distributions.; Platforms know demand systems, costs, and within- and cross-side interaction-value parameters.; Net fees are publicly observed before users join.; The baseline equilibrium is in pure strategies; user demand follows optimal discrete choice for the announced fee profile.
- **Objective:** Each platform chooses its vector of net fees to maximize membership-margin revenue plus the value it captures from within- and cross-side interactions, taking rivals' fees and induced demands as given.
- **Representative equation:** `$max_{t^j} pi^j(t^j,t^{-j}) = sum_s (t_s^j-c_s^j)n_s^j(t_s) + sum_{s,s_hat} gamma_{s,s_hat}^j n_s^j(t_s)n_{s_hat}^j(t_{s_hat}).$ (Equations (7)-(8) and the Nash definition, printed p. 8845 / PDF p. 4, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in platform net fees
- **Solution:** Equilibrium net fees equal marginal cost plus a standard demand-markup term minus a network discount. Under the stated curvature assumptions a pure equilibrium exists, and in the one-sided logit case it is unique when the network coefficient is below 2.610. For stronger but still existence-compatible effects, triopoly can contain a platform more dominant than any platform in the associated duopoly. A merger between two smaller platforms needs less cost synergy to reduce dominance as network effects grow. Raising interoperability compresses asymmetric shares and, in the symmetric benchmark, generally lowers net fees and raises consumer surplus, with the paper identifying a no-outside-option duopoly exception in which net fees do not change.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 defines demand, platform profit, consumer surplus, and simultaneous net-fee choices for arbitrary numbers of platforms and market sides.; Proposition 1 decomposes every equilibrium net fee into marginal cost, a standard market-power term, and a network discount reflecting the platform's marginal interaction benefits.; Propositions 2 and 2-prime give general and logit existence conditions; Proposition 3 establishes uniqueness in the one-sided logit model when network effects are below the stated bound.; Proposition 4 constructs triopoly equilibria in which adding a platform increases the largest firm's share; Proposition 5 shows that the cost synergy needed for a merger of two smaller rivals to reduce dominance falls as network effects strengthen.; Propositions 6-8 show how interoperability can compress an asymmetric market-share gap, generally lower net fees and raise consumer surplus under symmetry, and extend the pricing logic to competitive bottlenecks.
- **Caveat:** The net-fee conduct assumption requires post-joining captivity or another mechanism through which platforms extract all interaction surplus; it is microfounded but will not fit every platform. Several headline dominance and interoperability results rely on one-sided logit demand, symmetry, a fixed network coefficient, selected pure equilibria, and sometimes no outside option. Multiplicity remains possible at stronger network effects, so comparative statements must be read with their equilibrium-selection and parameter conditions. The model abstracts from dynamic investment, multi-homing in the main setup, and endogenous interoperability costs.

### Adaptive Pricing in Combinatorial Auctions

Sébastien Lahaie; Benjamin Lubin (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.4993](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.4993). First published online: 2025-02-26.

- **Question:** Can an iterative combinatorial auction start with simple prices and add just enough expressiveness to clear heterogeneous markets quickly and efficiently?
- **Players:** a seller or auctioneer allocating multiple indivisible items; multiple bidders with private valuations over bundles
- **Timing:** In each round, the seller posts possibly personalized polynomial prices and a provisional allocation. Bidders report utility-maximizing demanded bundles; the seller tests market-clearing and LP integrality, updates prices, and expands the polynomial or personalized price structure when needed. The process stops when an epsilon-competitive equilibrium is reached.
- **Actions:** the seller posts and updates prices; each bidder selects a demanded bundle at current prices; the seller selects a revenue-maximizing feasible allocation; the mechanism expands the set of polynomial price terms or personalizes prices when clearing fails
- **Information:** Each bidder knows its valuation over bundles and observes posted prices.; The auctioneer observes submitted demand responses rather than the complete valuation function.; The feasible allocation set and price-update rules are common knowledge.; The main analysis treats bidders as answering demand queries straightforwardly.
- **Objective:** The efficient-allocation benchmark maximizes bidders' total valuation over feasible assignments, and competitive prices decentralize that allocation through bidder demand and seller supply; the iterative mechanism elicits demand rather than full valuation reports.
- **Representative equation:** `$Y in argmax_{Y' in F} sum_i v_i(Y'_i)$ (Section 2.1, Equation (1), printed p. 8971 / PDF p. 5)
- **Equilibrium:** Epsilon-competitive equilibrium with conditional ex post Nash support for straightforward bidding
- **Solution:** Adaptive polynomial pricing clears at least 97% of tested instances and retains at least 93.2% efficiency in the reported simulation suite, while fixed benchmark price languages perform substantially worse in mismatched valuation domains. Integrality tests identify when the current price structure is insufficient, and targeted expansion guarantees progress without immediately resorting to fully expressive bundle prices.
- **Evidence:** Bidders respond to posted bundle prices with utility-maximizing demand and the seller chooses revenue-maximizing feasible supply.; The mechanism detects when a price language cannot support an integral allocation and adds price terms or personalization.; The algorithm terminates at an epsilon-competitive equilibrium under its bidding assumptions.; Simulations compare adaptive prices with linear- and bundle-price auction benchmarks.
- **Caveat:** The principal performance analysis assumes straightforward bidding. Without consistency-enforcing activity rules and either VCG payments or an appropriate second phase, strategic bidders need not reveal demand straightforwardly; broader incentive analysis and laboratory validation remain future work. Prices can be nonmonotone and increasingly personalized, and the design is core-selecting but does not guarantee a bidder-optimal core outcome.

### Position Auctions with Endogenous Product Information: Why Live-Streaming Advertising Is Thriving

Ying-Ju Chen; Guillermo Gallego; Pin Gao; Yang Li (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2021.01299](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.01299). First published online: 2025-03-11.

- **Question:** How should a live-streaming commerce platform jointly allocate product positions and design product information to maximize advertising revenue from privately informed sellers?
- **Players:** a platform or auctioneer; multiple sellers with private types; consumers with heterogeneous product preferences who inspect ads sequentially
- **Timing:** The platform commits to a direct mechanism specifying position allocation, seller payments and information provision. Each seller observes its type and reports it. The mechanism chooses the ordered ad allocation and information signals; a consumer then inspects ads in cascade order, decides whether to purchase or continue, and seller payments are realized.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses a mechanism mapping reports to positions, information and payments; each seller reports its private type; consumers sequentially decide whether to purchase an advertised product or continue browsing
- **Information:** Each seller privately observes its revenue type before reporting.; The platform knows the independent type distributions and consumer-preference distribution.; The mechanism can disclose endogenous product information to consumers.; Consumers observe the information attached to each displayed product as they move through the cascade.
- **Objective:** The platform chooses a position-allocation, payment and information mechanism to maximize expected seller payments subject to dominant-strategy incentive compatibility and individual rationality.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi*=max_M E_theta[sum_{m=1}^M P_m(theta_m)], subject to (IC) and (IR)$ (Section 2.4.2, Equation (4), printed p. 9296 / PDF p. 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Truthful dominant-strategy implementation of the revenue-optimal direct mechanism
- **Solution:** Joint position and information optimization is NP-hard. Heuristics using product-information provision can guarantee as much as 66.9% of optimal revenue in the worst case, whereas reliance on position allocation alone can incur arbitrarily large loss. The mechanism therefore explains why information-rich live-streaming formats can outperform conventional position-focused sponsored search; the insight survives multiproduct purchases and random attention spans.
- **Evidence:** Sellers have private revenue types and report them to the platform.; The platform controls both position allocation and the information a consumer receives about each product.; Truthful reporting is enforced through incentive compatibility and nonnegative interim utility.; The transformed mechanism links revenue maximization to an order-selection problem and supports approximation algorithms.
- **Caveat:** The mechanism assumes commitment, independent seller types, a regular virtual-value environment, costless platform information and a stylized cascade. The finite information set and lack of consumer personalization simplify implementation, and the approximation guarantees are not field estimates of live-streaming revenue gains.

### Retailer-Led Marketplaces

Andres Hervas-Drane; Sandro Shelegia (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.00315](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00315). First published online: 2025-03-28.

- **Question:** How should a capacity-constrained retailer set marketplace fees, allocate its own assortment, and steer consumers when third-party sellers compete on the retailer's storefront?
- **Players:** monopolist retailer and marketplace operator M; one potential third-party seller T for each product; attentive and inattentive consumers
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the retailer announces an ad valorem marketplace fee f. Stage 2: for every product value v, its third-party seller decides whether to enter; after observing all seller entries, the retailer chooses which products to supply subject to assortment capacity k. Stage 3: in a product supplied by both firms, the third party posts price first and the retailer then posts its price and chooses which offer to show inattentive consumers; consumers purchase. The game is solved backward for Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium.
- **Actions:** the retailer sets the uniform marketplace fee; each third-party seller enters or stays out; the retailer allocates limited capacity across products after seller entry; the third party posts its product price; the retailer posts its price and steers inattentive demand; consumers buy from the displayed or preferred offer
- **Information:** Product valuations v, common marginal cost c, the product-value distribution, retailer capacity k, fee f, and steering parameter lambda are common knowledge.; The retailer observes third-party entry choices before allocating its own capacity.; Consumers are attentive with probability 1-lambda and compare offers, or inattentive with probability lambda and follow the retailer's steering choice.; Products are strategically independent in pricing conditional on the common fee and the retailer's aggregate capacity allocation.
- **Objective:** Choose the marketplace fee and capacity allocation to maximize the retailer's integrated direct-sales and fee profit, anticipating seller entry and product-level pricing equilibria.
- **Representative equation:** `$max_f Pi_M(k,f), where Pi_M(k,f) = integral_{v_L}^{v_T} pi_M^SBM(v)g(v)dv + integral_{v_T}^{v_H} pi_M^SBT(f,v)g(v)dv + integral_{v_H}^{infinity} pi_M^SBMT(f,v)g(v)dv, with cutoffs induced by equilibrium entry and capacity allocation.$ (Equation (4), printed p. 9656 / PDF p. 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium of fee choice, sequential entry, and pricing
- **Solution:** In a jointly supplied product, the retailer charges v and steers inattentive consumers to itself, while the third party charges [lambda v+c(1-lambda)]/[1-f(1-lambda)] and serves attentive consumers. Third parties enter at v at least c/(1-f). With low retailer capacity, Mode I concentrates direct entry in the highest-value marketplace products; with high capacity, Mode II also includes retailer-only and third-party-only segments. The optimal fee is strictly positive and can become marketplace deterring when capacity is high. A ban on the retailer's hybrid seller-platform role generally reduces consumer surplus and can reduce welfare. Reduced steering can trigger fee increases or marketplace closure. A binding fee cap improves consumer surplus and usually welfare if accepted, but an excessively low cap induces closure and makes both fall.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 defines a continuum of independent product markets, a capacity-k retailer, ad valorem fee f, steering effectiveness lambda, and the three-stage order of play.; Proposition 1 solves the pricing subgame for retailer-only, third-party-only, and retailer-plus-third-party supply configurations.; Lemma 1 and Proposition 2 derive the third-party entry threshold and characterize low-capacity Mode I versus high-capacity Mode II retailer allocation.; Lemma 2 and Proposition 3 establish a strictly positive optimal fee and show how capacity and steering determine a marketplace-accommodating or marketplace-deterring regime.; Propositions 4-6 compare a hybrid-model prohibition, reduced steering, and a binding fee cap, including the retailer's endogenous decision to keep or close the marketplace.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses independent products, unit inelastic demand, common constant cost, no seller entry cost, an exogenous retailer capacity, and an exogenous fraction of inattentive consumers. Sequential third-party-then-retailer pricing and the retailer's steering authority soften competition. A single uniform fee spans the product space, and the retailer has no rival retail channel. Because quantity is fixed in active product markets, welfare effects operate mainly through product availability and cannot capture every demand-expansion benefit of lower prices.

### The Adoption of Central Bank Digital Currency

Emilio Barucci; Matteo Brachetta; Daniele Marazzina (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.01504](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01504). First published online: 2025-04-03.

- **Question:** How do remuneration, subsidies, interoperability and public-private platform architecture determine whether a CBDC reaches its adoption target?
- **Players:** a continuum of heterogeneous potential CBDC users; the central bank; private platform developers in the two-layer architecture; competing payment technologies represented in extensions
- **Timing:** Over a finite horizon, users make myopic adoption and quantity choices from the current platform state and aggregate adoption. The central bank dynamically chooses subsidy and development effort. Under a two-layer design, private developers concurrently choose complementary effort; platform productivity, adoption and transaction volume evolve until a terminal scrap value is realized.
- **Actions:** users choose whether to adopt and how much CBDC to use; the central bank chooses monetary subsidy and platform-development effort; private developers choose development effort in the two-layer architecture
- **Information:** Users observe the current productivity, remuneration, subsidy, costs and aggregate adoption when making myopic choices.; Users differ in an idiosyncratic taste for CBDC and are represented by a known distribution.; The central bank and developers observe the state variables used in their dynamic control problems.; Policy and technology primitives are common knowledge within the partial-equilibrium model.
- **Objective:** The central bank chooses development effort and adoption subsidy to balance deviation from a target volume, subsidy and effort costs, transaction revenue and terminal platform value.
- **Representative equation:** `$J_CB^I(a;H,v)=E[int_0^T e^{-rho t}(-omega_1(V_t-V_bar)^2-omega_2 N_t v_t-omega_3(H_t+theta_1 H_t^2)+kV_t)dt+G(V_T)]$ (Section 2, one-layer central-bank program, printed p. 3688 / PDF p. 5)
- **Equilibrium:** Dynamic partial-equilibrium control solution with an endogenous adoption fixed point and concurrent public-private controls
- **Solution:** Remuneration and monetary incentives materially change both adoption and transaction volume. The calibrated 60% adoption target can be reached in a one-layer design if productivity improves substantially, but complementary effort and coordination make it much harder in a two-layer design. The simulations predict CBDC is more likely to outperform stablecoins than debit cards in the adoption contest.
- **Evidence:** Users choose whether and how much CBDC to hold as current utility depends on platform productivity, remuneration, subsidy, interoperability and aggregate adoption.; The central bank controls subsidy and development effort to balance adoption targets, costs and terminal value.; In the two-layer architecture, central-bank and private-developer efforts are complementary and are solved concurrently through coupled HJB controls.; Calibration evaluates a 60% digital-euro adoption target and competition with stablecoins and debit cards.
- **Caveat:** The framework is partial equilibrium with myopic users, a finite horizon, continuum symmetry and exogenous fees, interest rates and several technology parameters. It does not model inflation, bank disintermediation or a complete welfare system, and the digital-euro results depend on stylized proxies and calibration choices rather than causal estimation.

### “Sherlocking” and Platform Information Policy

Jay Pil Choi; Kyungmin Kim; Arijit Mukherjee (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.05215](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05215). First published online: 2025-04-07.

- **Question:** How should a marketplace platform combine referral fees and internal data-sharing rules when copying successful third-party products is profitable later but deters seller entry today?
- **Players:** marketplace platform P that sets a fee and may imitate; privately informed third-party seller S deciding whether to enter; platform product division receiving an information-policy signal
- **Timing:** Before seller entry, the platform posts a uniform ad valorem referral fee r and, in the information-policy regime, commits to a signal structure governing what its product division will observe. The seller privately observes profitability theta and decides whether to pay fixed cost K and enter. During period 1 of length 1-delta, an entrant sells and pays the fee. At the start of period 2, the platform or its product division observes theta or the committed signal and decides whether to imitate at cost K_P. If it imitates, self-preferencing directs all second-period consumers to the platform product; otherwise the seller continues.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses a referral fee; the platform may commit to an entry rule or information structure; the seller enters or stays out after observing its type; the platform product division enters by imitating or stays out after its observation
- **Information:** The seller privately knows theta, its normalized flow monopoly profit, before entering.; Under no commitment the platform learns theta after first-period marketplace operation.; Under information design, the product division observes only the realization of a platform-chosen signal and forms a posterior about theta.; The prior theta is uniform on [0,1], and fees, costs, period lengths, and signal rules are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** Choose the referral fee and, when available, a type-contingent entry commitment or information policy to maximize platform referral and imitation profit while preserving seller entry incentives.
- **Representative equation:** `$max_{r,alpha(.)} integral_{Theta_E} [(1-alpha(theta,r))r theta + alpha(theta,r)((1-delta)r theta + delta theta-K_P)]dtheta, subject to seller entry: [(1-delta)+delta(1-alpha(theta,r))](1-r)theta >= K.$ (Section 4 full-commitment problem, printed p. 9818 / PDF p. 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Weak Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium of seller entry and platform imitation
- **Solution:** Without commitment, the platform sets a fee at least as high as under a commitment never to copy; the higher fee reduces its own imitation incentive but deters some low types. Full contingent commitment weakly lowers the fee below the no-entry benchmark and induces maximal seller entry, maximizing platform payoff and consumer surplus among the studied regimes. A binary signal is sufficient to implement any attainable information-policy outcome. It implements full commitment exactly when the loss from mistakenly entering on pooled lower types can discipline the gain from pooled higher types after a no-entry recommendation. Otherwise the optimal binary policy selectively pools types to satisfy obedience. An outright ban on platform entry or internal data sharing need not help consumers, because the platform may respond with a higher referral fee that suppresses seller entry.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 defines the seller's private profitability type, the platform's uniform ad valorem fee, two-period payoffs, the entry-and-imitation timeline, and weak Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium.; Proposition 1 shows that the no-commitment fee is at least the fee under a commitment never to enter, because a higher fee reduces the platform's ex post incentive to copy and can attract lucrative seller types.; Proposition 2 shows that full contingent entry commitment produces a weakly lower fee than the no-entry commitment benchmark, induces maximal seller entry, and improves both platform profit and consumer surplus relative to the two benchmarks.; Lemma 1 and Proposition 3 show that binary entry/no-entry recommendations suffice and give the obedience condition under which an information policy implements the full-commitment outcome.; Proposition 4 characterizes the constrained-optimal binary signal when full commitment is not implementable; Proposition 5 compares entry and data-sharing bans while accounting for the platform's endogenous referral-fee response.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses one representative seller, a uniform one-dimensional type, zero marginal costs, no alternative marketplace, a two-period horizon, and extreme self-preferencing that gives the platform all consumers after imitation. The platform's fee is uniform and consumers pay the same monopoly price regardless of supplier, so consumer surplus varies only through seller entry. Information design assumes commitment to a signal structure even when commitment to entry itself is unavailable. Some ban regimes permit multiple equilibria, and the regulatory ranking depends on equilibrium selection and the endogenous fee response.

### Nonparametric Estimation of Sponsored Search Auctions and Impact of Ad Quality on Search Revenue

Dongwoo Kim; Pallavi Pal (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.02052](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02052). First published online: 2025-04-15.

- **Question:** How can a search platform recover advertisers' private values from quality-weighted GSP bids and choose ad-quality scoring rules to improve revenue?
- **Players:** a sponsored-search platform running a weighted GSP auction; advertisers with private per-click values and ad-quality scores; search users generating position-dependent clicks
- **Timing:** For a search opportunity, advertisers observe their private values and ad qualities and simultaneously submit bids. The platform ranks weighted bids, assigns ordered positions and charges each winner the minimum per-click price needed to retain its rank. Clicks and profits are then realized.
- **Actions:** each advertiser chooses a bid per click; the platform applies a known ad-quality scoring rule and ranks weighted bids; the counterfactual analysis varies that rule; users click according to position and ad relevance
- **Information:** Each advertiser privately observes its value and quality component.; Advertiser types are independently drawn from a common distribution in the baseline.; The number of competitors, position click rates, scoring rule and type distribution are common knowledge.; The platform observes auction bids, scores, positions and clicks but not values directly.
- **Objective:** An advertiser chooses its bid to maximize expected profit summed over possible positions, where each position payoff equals click probability times per-click surplus.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi(b_j;v_j,s_j)=sum_{k=1}^K Pr(b_{j,w}=b^{[k]}_w)(c_k s_j)(v_j-E[p_{j,k}|b_{j,w}=b^{[k]}_w])$ (Section 3.1.4, Equation (3), printed p. 10051 / PDF p. 5)
- **Equilibrium:** Unique symmetric Bayesian Nash equilibrium of the weighted generalized-second-price auction
- **Solution:** The equilibrium and monotonicity structure nonparametrically identify advertiser values despite quality-weighted ranks. In the Yahoo counterfactuals, product-specific scoring rules can raise platform revenue by as much as 24.3%, but the best rule depends on competition and can reduce advertiser profit by 28.3% and consumer welfare by 30.2%, exposing a sharp distributional tradeoff.
- **Evidence:** Advertisers rank by bid times ad-quality score and pay a quality-adjusted next-bid price.; The equilibrium weighted bid is a function of weighted value, enabling inversion despite the two-dimensional type.; The estimators recover valuation distributions from bids, positions, clicks and quality scores.; Counterfactuals vary the quality-scoring rule and trace platform revenue, advertiser profit and consumer welfare.
- **Caveat:** Identification relies on symmetric independent private types, monotone weighted bids and separable click rates. The aggregate Yahoo data do not identify which ads appeared together; the analysis infers the potential bidder count from observed markets, and the reserve price was unreported. The static model also abstracts from budgets, endogenous entry, repeated learning and cross-auction dynamics, so current-platform external validity is uncertain.

### Internal Capital Allocation, Voluntary Disclosure, and Investment Efficiency

Hyun Hwang (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.01295](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.01295). First published online: 2025-04-16.

- **Question:** Should an owner place two projects inside one multidivisional firm or separate firms when managers privately learn profitability and disclosure is costly?
- **Players:** founder choosing organizational structure; one multidivisional manager or two stand-alone managers; competitive outside investors
- **Timing:** At date 0 the founder chooses a multidivisional firm or two stand-alone firms. At date 1 the relevant manager or managers observe binary project profitability and choose whether to make truthful costly disclosures. At date 2 competitive investors observe disclosures and choose capital and break-even ownership shares. At date 3, if a multidivisional firm receives only one unit, its manager allocates that unit across projects. At date 4 project cash flows and payoffs are realized.
- **Actions:** choose multidivisional or stand-alone organization; disclose or withhold each observed project type; supply zero, one, or two units of external capital; set competitive equity shares; allocate scarce capital within the multidivisional firm
- **Information:** Each project's profitability is binary and privately observed by its manager before disclosure.; Disclosure is verifiable and truthful but withholding is permitted.; Investors observe organizational form and disclosure decisions but not withheld project types.; Investor beliefs after every disclosure history are updated by Bayes' rule wherever possible.; A multidivisional manager observes both project types and controls internal allocation after financing.
- **Objective:** Choose organizational form to maximize expected project cash flows net of disclosure costs, anticipating equilibrium disclosure, financing, and internal allocation.
- **Representative equation:** `$o* in argmax_{o in {s,m}} E[sum_i net cash flow_i(o)], where s denotes two stand-alone firms and m a multidivisional firm, subject to the Perfect Bayesian equilibrium of the continuation game.$ (Founder objective and timing in Section 2, printed p. 10090 / PDF p. 3; equilibrium definition in Section 2.6, printed p. 10091 / PDF p. 4, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Perfect Bayesian equilibrium with investment-efficiency selection
- **Solution:** When disclosure costs are sufficiently high relative to project payoffs, a multidivisional firm can finance one project without disclosure and use private information to allocate capital, so centralization is strictly more efficient. When project payoffs are high relative to disclosure costs, the multidivisional manager's cross-subsidization incentive makes separate stand-alone firms strictly better. When disclosure and payoff combinations make equilibrium investment identical across forms, the founder is indifferent. The qualitative trade-off survives the paper's distributional and disclosure-friction extensions.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 lays out a five-date game in which the founder chooses organizational form, managers learn project types and choose truthful disclosure, investors competitively finance projects, and a multidivisional manager may reallocate a single unit of capital.; Section 2.6 defines Perfect Bayesian equilibrium using sequential optimality and Bayes-consistent investor beliefs and selects, when multiple equilibria exist, the equilibrium with the greatest investment efficiency.; Proposition 1 partitions disclosure and financing behavior for stand-alone firms according to disclosure cost and project payoff.; Proposition 2 characterizes multidivisional disclosure, financing, and internal allocation, including the region where the manager can raise one unit without disclosure and allocate it to a profitable division.; Proposition 3 compares organizational forms: multidivisional organization is strictly preferred when costly disclosure makes internal allocation valuable, stand-alone organization is strictly preferred when avoiding cross-subsidization dominates, and the forms are equivalent in the remaining regions.; Extensions allow heterogeneous project success probabilities, correlated project cash flows, additional cash-flow uncertainty, and alternative disclosure frictions.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses two independent, binary, ex ante identical projects, truthful disclosure with a reduced-form implementation cost, competitive risk-neutral investors, and a specific empire-building managerial payoff. Organizational form is chosen once, and the equilibrium-selection rule favors investment efficiency. The model abstracts from noisy or deceptive reports, investor market power, managerial contracting, and a richer internal hierarchy; robustness results relax only selected assumptions.

### Demographic Diversity and Collusion in Teams

Jonathan Glover; Eunhee Kim (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.00855](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.00855). First published online: 2025-04-23.

- **Question:** Can a firm use demographic or horizon diversity and asymmetric performance pay to preserve peer-enforced effort without making employee collusion too attractive?
- **Players:** principal choosing workforce composition and performance contracts; more-patient type-h agent; less-patient type-l agent
- **Timing:** At the outset, the principal permanently selects two agents and commits to short-term wages contingent only on the current task outcome. In every period, both agents privately choose work or shirk, observe each other's effort, and receive success-contingent wages if the stochastic team task succeeds. Their actions and continuation play can follow history-dependent punishments; a correlation device may coordinate collusive alternating-effort profiles. The same strategic interaction repeats over an infinite horizon.
- **Actions:** the principal selects a homogeneous or diverse workforce; the principal sets agent-specific success and failure wages; each agent privately chooses work or shirk each period; agents condition future effort on observed teammate behavior; agents may coordinate correlated alternating work and shirk patterns
- **Information:** Agent discount-factor types h and l are publicly observable to the principal and teammates.; Each agent observes the teammate's effort, but the principal observes only public task success or failure.; The production technology, wages, discount factors, and correlation device are common knowledge.; The principal cannot receive direct reports about within-team effort observations.
- **Objective:** Choose workforce types and limited-liability success-contingent wages to maximize the principal's per-period expected production net of compensation while inducing work-work as a Pareto-undominated subgame-perfect team equilibrium.
- **Representative equation:** `$min_{workforce k, wages w_k} f(2)(w_k^i+w_k^j), subject to Cooperation, Pareto (collusion-deterrence), individual-rationality, and limited-liability constraints; production is fixed at f(2)S once work-work is induced.$ (Section 3, printed pp. 10185-10186 / PDF pp. 4-5; the formal program is referenced at the beginning of the appendix)
- **Equilibrium:** Pareto-undominated subgame-perfect team equilibrium with collusion-proof contracting
- **Solution:** When agents are relatively impatient, minimum cooperative wages suffice. When both are patient enough for collusion to bind, the principal pays the less-patient prospective bribee a higher-powered collusion-proof wage and the more-patient agent a lower-powered cooperative wage. If discount factors can be selected, the optimal workforce combines the most patient feasible agent with a second agent just impatient enough that the diverse-team collusion constraint does not become costly. With two high- and two low-discount-factor agents, diverse assignment costs no more than homogeneous assignment and costs strictly less whenever collusion binds. The core diversity benefit persists in the team-horizon and continuous-effort extensions under the stated conditions.
- **Evidence:** Section 3 defines an infinite-horizon hidden-action team in which a principal commits to a short-term success-contingent contract and permanently selects the two agents.; Lemma 1 derives the minimum cooperative wage under the relevant stage-game punishment; cooperation is supported by grim-trigger strategies in a subgame-perfect team equilibrium.; Lemmas 2-3 characterize correlation-device-supported collusion and the minimum asymmetric contract that makes every feasible regret-free collusion unattractive.; Lemma 4 and Proposition 1 compare homogeneous and diverse workforces and show that, when discount factors are selectable, the optimal workforce pairs the most patient agent with one just impatient enough to avoid a costly collusion constraint.; Proposition 2 shows that diverse assignment weakly lowers total wages for a four-agent workforce and lowers them strictly whenever collusion binds; Propositions 3-4 establish related results with finite team horizons and continuous effort.
- **Caveat:** The interpretation of demographic diversity is reduced to publicly observed discount factors or continuation horizons rather than modeled demographic mechanisms. The baseline has two agents, binary effort, risk neutrality, limited liability, symmetric contributions, productive substitutability, short-term outcome-only contracts, and a stationary equilibrium path. Agents can observe one another perfectly and can use a correlation device, while the principal cannot communicate with them about effort. Some proofs and robustness results rely on parameter restrictions, and the downloadable main PDF refers to a separate online appendix.

### Lemon Ads: Adverse Selection in Multichannel Display Advertising Markets

Francesco Balocco; Yixin Lu; Ting Li; Alok Gupta (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.03407](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.03407). First published online: 2025-04-23.

- **Question:** Does allowing publishers to use both private marketplaces and real-time bidding create adverse selection that harms RTB-only publishers and advertisers?
- **Players:** a dual-channel publisher using PMP and RTB; a single-channel publisher using only RTB; multiple advertisers active across channels
- **Timing:** The dual-channel publisher first commits to a quality threshold for PMP. When an impression arrives, each publisher observes its quality, chooses a channel when relevant and sets a floor price. Advertisers receive a bid request, form rational channel-level quality expectations and simultaneously bid in a second-price auction; the winner's ad is displayed and pays the applicable second-highest bid or floor.
- **Actions:** the dual-channel publisher chooses the PMP quality threshold; publishers choose channel allocation and RTB floor prices; advertisers submit bids based on value and expected impression quality
- **Information:** Each publisher privately observes the realized quality of its impression.; Advertisers know equilibrium channel-allocation rules and form rational expectations of quality by publisher type and channel.; Advertisers know their private per-unit value before bidding.; The dual-channel publisher can selectively route impressions after observing quality, whereas the RTB-only publisher cannot.
- **Objective:** An advertiser chooses a bid against expected channel quality, while a publisher chooses its floor, channel allocation and—if dual-channel—quality threshold to maximize auction revenue.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi_a(beta)=v q_hat-max{r,beta_(2)} if beta>=max{r,beta_(2)}, and 0 otherwise; Pi_p(r)=max{r,beta_(2)} if beta_(1)>=r, and 0 otherwise$ (Sections 3.4-3.5, Equations (3)-(4), printed p. 10248 / PDF p. 5)
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium of the three-stage channel-allocation and second-price auction game
- **Solution:** The dual-channel publisher sends high-quality impressions to PMP and lower-quality impressions to RTB, yet RTB pricing pools quality expectations and can let those lower-quality impressions sell at relatively high prices. This adverse selection reduces the RTB-only publisher's payoff, while advertisers prefer multichannel access. The empirical analysis finds significantly lower viewability for RTB impressions from dual-channel publishers, consistent with the model.
- **Evidence:** The dual-channel publisher observes impression quality before assigning high-quality impressions to PMP and low-quality impressions to RTB.; Advertisers bid from channel-level expected quality rather than the publisher's privately observed realization.; The model derives equilibrium bidding, floor pricing and channel allocation.; The empirical test compares viewability of RTB impressions from dual- and single-channel publishers while correcting sequential selection.
- **Caveat:** The baseline assumes uniform quality and values, zero publisher reservation payoffs, exogenous channel adoption, second-price auctions and rational channel-level quality beliefs, while omitting strategic SSPs, DSPs and ad exchanges. The one-week proprietary sample uses viewability as only one quality proxy and lacks competitor bids, so it cannot identify economic losses or alternative-market counterfactuals and is not a randomized causal test.

### Robustly Optimal Contracts for Agricultural Supply Chains

Zhaolin Li; Guitian Liang (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.01673](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.01673). First published online: 2025-04-30.

- **Question:** How should a landowner and farmer share crop yield and risk when effort is hidden and neither party knows the full yield distribution?
- **Players:** a landowner contributing farmland; a skilled farmer choosing costly cultivation effort
- **Timing:** The party with bargaining power offers a yield-contingent take-it-or-leave-it contract. The other party accepts or rejects; after acceptance, the farmer privately chooses effort. Crop yield is realized and verified, and the contract allocates the harvest or its value between farmer and landowner.
- **Actions:** the contract proposer selects a yield-contingent payment schedule and target effort; the receiving party accepts or rejects; the farmer chooses unobservable cultivation effort
- **Information:** Effort is privately chosen by the farmer and is not contractible.; Realized crop yield is verifiable and can determine payment.; Both parties know only the effort-contingent yield mean and variance, not the full distribution.; The ambiguity set and reservation payoffs are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** In the landowner-offer model, the landowner chooses effort and a yield-contingent transfer to maximize worst-case expected retained yield subject to the farmer's robust participation and effort incentive constraints and the landowner's own reservation value.
- **Representative equation:** `$U_l=max_{a,w(theta)>=0} inf_{G in Omega_a} E_G[theta_tilde-w(theta_tilde)], subject to Z_l(w,a)>=0, a in argmax_e Z_l(w,e), liability constraints, and U_l>=I$ (Section 2.3, Equations (2.2)-(2.6), printed p. 10400 / PDF p. 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Robust incentive-compatible take-it-or-leave-it contracting outcome
- **Solution:** When the landowner offers the contract, a debt-equity hybrid is robustly optimal. When the farmer offers, the optimum is either a linear equity contract or a nonlinear quadratic debt contract depending on yield variation and the landowner's reservation profit. USDA-calibrated cases show that the party with bargaining power shares more risk as the coefficient of variation rises, and bargaining power can reverse which arrangement induces greater effort.
- **Evidence:** The contracting party offers a yield-contingent transfer before the farmer chooses hidden effort.; Both parties optimize against the worst distribution in a mean-variance ambiguity set induced by effort.; The contract must satisfy robust participation and make the requested effort optimal for the farmer.; Separate landowner-offer and farmer-offer models isolate bargaining-power effects on form, effort and risk sharing.
- **Caveat:** The baseline assumes common mean-variance ambiguity beliefs, risk neutrality, a fixed crop price, one crop, verifiable yield and a max-min criterion; country-level yields can understate farm-level variation. The USDA exercise illustrates calibrated implications rather than estimating causal contract effects, and the authors identify multiple crops, effort-dependent hedging, and laboratory validation as future work.

### Bank Compensation for the Penalty-Free Loan Prepayment Option: Theory and Evidence

B. Espen Eckbo; Xunhua Su; Karin S. Thorburn (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.00159](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00159). First published online: 2025-05-02.

- **Question:** How should a bank charge for a penalty-free prepayment option without intensifying the borrower's incentive to refinance or rationing otherwise valuable projects?
- **Players:** a competitive risk-neutral bank; a risk-neutral borrowing firm with an investment project; a potential refinancing lender represented by the competitive outside loan rate
- **Timing:** At date 0, the bank offers a rate and possibly an upfront fee, and the firm borrows one unit and invests. At interim date theta, a public but noncontractible project-quality signal arrives; a good-news borrower may pay a refinancing cost and prepay, whereas a bad-news borrower continues. At date 1, the project payoff is realized and the loan is repaid if successful.
- **Actions:** the bank sets the loan rate and fee to break even; the firm accepts and invests if its ex ante NPV is positive; after the signal, the firm chooses prepayment/refinancing or continuation; in the relationship-lending extension, bank and good borrower may bargain over a cancellation fee
- **Information:** Project success probability and signal structure are common knowledge at origination.; The interim signal is public but noncontractible.; A high signal makes the project risk free; a low signal leaves a positive but loss-making repayment probability for the bank.; Contract terms cannot be conditioned directly on the signal.
- **Objective:** Without an upfront fee, the competitive bank selects the rate so that expected repayment from good-news prepayment and bad-news continuation equals its initial one-unit loan.
- **Representative equation:** `$p(1+\theta r)+(1-p)q(1+r)=1$ (Equation (2), printed p. 10418 (PDF p. 5), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Competitive two-part loan-pricing equilibrium with endogenous prepayment
- **Solution:** A higher interest rate alone can amplify prepayment selection until positive-NPV, high-prepayment-risk borrowers are rationed. A minimum upfront fee combined with a capped rate restores break-even lending because the fee compensates the bank without increasing the refinancing incentive. A larger fee can alternatively sustain a rate low enough to eliminate prepayment. The data support the central prediction that upfront fees rise with prepayment risk and fall when credit-line or performance-pricing features already reduce that risk.
- **Evidence:** Proposition 1 shows that relying only on the interest rate can ration positive-NPV borrowers with sufficiently high prepayment risk.; Proposition 2 derives a minimum upfront fee and rate that restore competitive break-even lending while allowing good-news prepayment.; Proposition 3 gives an alternative two-part schedule that removes the prepayment incentive with a larger fee.; Extensions distinguish standard term loans, performance-sensitive debt, credit lines, and ex post cancellation-fee bargaining.; Empirical tests first correct selective public fee reporting with a probit/inverse-Mills two-step procedure, construct a prepayment-risk index, and use industry M&A activity as an instrument; upfront fees rise with predicted prepayment risk and are lower for credit lines and performance-sensitive loans.
- **Caveat:** The theory uses a competitive risk-neutral bank, a single borrower and project, binary public learning, noncontractibility, and no borrower moral hazard. Empirical identification relies on proxies for upside potential and renegotiation cost, the fee-reporting selection model and its distance-to-NYC exclusion restriction, and the validity of industry M&A activity as an instrument; observed fees may also compensate origination services outside the model.

### Competing for Cookies: Platforms’ Business Models in Data Markets with Network Effects

Sarit Markovich; Yaron Yehezkel (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.07744](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07744). First published online: 2025-05-20.

- **Question:** When competition threatens a platform, should it monetize user data, sell privacy through subscriptions, or offer both—and when does banning pay-or-consent plans help users or welfare?
- **Players:** incumbent platform I with a focality advantage; entrant platform E; unit mass of heterogeneous users choosing a platform, plan, or nonparticipation
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the incumbent chooses data-based D, subscription S, or hybrid H. Stage 2: after observing that choice, the entrant selects its business model. Stage 3: platforms choose any subscription prices implied by their models and compete for users. Users choose a platform and, under H, either the free data-commercialized plan or paid private plan. When network effects create multiple user-adoption outcomes, users coordinate on the incumbent whenever that outcome is feasible.
- **Actions:** the incumbent selects D, S, or H; the entrant selects D, S, or H after observing the incumbent; subscription or hybrid platforms set participation prices; each user joins a platform and chooses a data or private plan, or opts out
- **Information:** Users know their own privacy or ad-disutility cost k, which is uniformly distributed on [0,1].; Platforms and users know base value v, network-effect strength beta, commercial value alpha, business models, and prices.; Each user's payoff depends on how many other users join the same platform, creating rational-expectations coordination.; The incumbent is focal: where multiple feasible adoption equilibria exist, users expect others to join it.
- **Objective:** The incumbent chooses the business model that maximizes its equilibrium profit after the entrant's best response and the price-and-user-adoption continuation game; a hybrid platform earns both data-commercialization revenue and subscription revenue.
- **Representative equation:** `$B_I^* in arg max_{B_I in {D,S,H}} pi_I(B_I,B_E^*(B_I)); for H, pi_i(H,B_j)=alpha n_i^D(H,B_j)+p_i n_i^S(H,B_j).$ (Section 2 profit definitions and Section 4.4 / Proposition 2, printed pp. 918 and 923 / PDF pp. 4 and 9)
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction platform business-model equilibrium with incumbent-focal user adoption
- **Solution:** In the baseline weak-network-effects region, a monopolist uses hybrid only when the commercial value of data is high and otherwise uses subscription. Under competition, the incumbent uses hybrid and dominates above the competitive threshold; below it, the incumbent chooses subscription and the entrant chooses data-based, so they split the market. Competition can therefore shift a monopolist from hybrid to subscription when network effects are weak, reducing commercialization, but can shift subscription to hybrid at stronger intermediate effects, increasing it. A hybrid ban has no commercialization effect below the hybrid-choice threshold; above it, the ban reduces commercialization when beta exceeds one-quarter and increases it otherwise. In the stated regulatory comparison, hybrid availability always raises consumer surplus, and raises total welfare for beta above one-quarter; below one-quarter it raises welfare only on the paper's commercial-value side of the cutoff. The model also notes that hybrid can deter efficient quality-improving entry, a long-run cost outside the main welfare formula.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 defines heterogeneous user privacy costs, network benefits, three platform business models, platform profit functions, the three-stage timing, and the incumbent-focality selection rule.; Proposition 1 compares subscription, data, and hybrid choices for a monopolist and gives the commercial-value threshold above which hybrid is optimal in the baseline weak-network-effects region.; Lemmas 2-6 solve the entrant's response and platform-price/user-participation continuation outcome for every incumbent business model.; Proposition 2 characterizes the competitive equilibrium: above a network-dependent commercial-value threshold the incumbent uses hybrid and dominates; below it the incumbent uses subscription while a data-based entrant shares the market.; Corollaries 1-3 and Propositions 3-4 compare monopoly with competition, quantify how a hybrid-model ban changes data commercialization, and state when hybrid availability raises welfare; Corollaries 4-6 extend the business-model ranking to stronger network effects.
- **Caveat:** Headline results depend on homogeneous platforms, zero marginal cost, uniform one-dimensional privacy costs, linear within-platform network effects, and an incumbent-focal equilibrium-selection rule. The baseline weak-network-effects restriction excludes full data-plan coverage, with stronger effects treated separately. The main welfare comparison assumes an equal-quality entrant and does not include the long-run loss if a hybrid incumbent deters superior-quality entry. Users single-home, business-model commitments are credible, and the model abstracts from endogenous data quality, advertising demand, security risks, and privacy regulation other than hybrid availability.

### Credible Cheap-Talk Communication of Private Demand Information on Both the Forecast Average and Accuracy

Tao Lu; Brian Tomlin (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.02726](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02726). First published online: 2025-05-21.

- **Question:** Can a retailer credibly communicate both expected demand and forecast accuracy without a contingent contract, and how should a manufacturer respond through its capacity portfolio?
- **Players:** a retailer privately informed about demand mean and forecast accuracy; a manufacturer procuring and executing capacity from multiple sources
- **Timing:** The retailer observes type (a,b) and sends a costless unverifiable message. The manufacturer updates her belief and reserves capacities. Demand is realized, the manufacturer chooses source-specific execution quantities up to capacity, and both parties receive profits under a predetermined wholesale price.
- **Actions:** the retailer chooses a cheap-talk message; the manufacturer chooses capacity reservations after updating beliefs; after demand realizes, the manufacturer chooses execution quantities
- **Information:** Demand mean a and accuracy b are privately observed by the retailer.; The manufacturer knows their prior distribution and all cost and price parameters.; Messages are costless, nonbinding, and unverifiable.; Posterior beliefs satisfy Bayes' rule on the equilibrium path.
- **Objective:** After message m, the manufacturer reserves two capacity types to maximize expected execution profit under her posterior belief net of reservation costs.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_m(K_1,K_2\mid m)=\mathbb E[R(K_1,K_2,D)\mid m]-\sum_{i=1}^{2}r_iK_i$ (Equation (1), printed p. 992 (PDF p. 4), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Informative and influential perfect Bayesian cheap-talk equilibrium
- **Solution:** Communicating both mean and accuracy supports credible informative equilibria even though a point forecast alone would babble under a fixed wholesale price. With sufficiently different capacity sources, messages change capacity, strictly raise manufacturer expected profit, leave the retailer no worse off, and Pareto-improve supply-chain profit. Improving or adding capacity can paradoxically hurt the manufacturer when it compresses message-contingent responses and reduces information revelation.
- **Evidence:** Equations (1)-(3) define manufacturer capacity profit, ex post execution, and retailer payoff.; Section 3.4 defines reporting, belief, and capacity strategies in perfect Bayesian equilibrium.; Proposition 1 proves existence of an informative partition equilibrium under broad conditions.; Propositions 2 and 3 characterize when communication changes capacity and Pareto-improves the supply chain.; Later propositions show that improving or expanding the capacity portfolio can reduce manufacturer profit by weakening information revelation and extend the result beyond two discrete accuracy types.
- **Caveat:** The baseline is a single-season, risk-neutral, price-only supply chain with predetermined wholesale price, a particular two-source flexibility ordering, and a two-point accuracy type. Informative partitions need not fully reveal either dimension, babbling equilibria continue to exist, and the preferred informative equilibrium relies on equilibrium selection by Pareto dominance.

### Last-Iterate Convergence in No-Regret Learning: Games with Reference Effects Under Logit Demand

Mengzi Amy Guo; Donghao Ying; Javad Lavaei; Zuo-Jun Max Shen (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.03464](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03464). First published online: 2025-05-21.

- **Question:** Can competing firms using only their own revenue gradients learn prices that are both Nash optimal and dynamically stable when consumer reference prices evolve over time?
- **Players:** n competing firms, each selling one substitutable product; consumers choosing among products and an outside option under MNL demand
- **Timing:** At each discrete period, firms simultaneously post prices without observing current rivals' prices. Consumers choose under MNL utility with current and reference prices. Revenues and own first-order feedback are observed, reference prices update by exponential smoothing, and firms apply OPGA or its conservative loss-averse variant for the next period.
- **Actions:** each firm chooses its price each period; each firm updates price using own log-revenue gradient or subgradient information; consumers choose one product or the outside option
- **Information:** A firm need not observe rivals' prices, reference prices, market shares, or demand functions.; Each firm observes enough own-price, sensitivity, and own-share or revenue information to compute first-order feedback.; Reference prices are deterministic functions of own past posted prices.; Consumer utility shocks are i.i.d. standard Gumbel.
- **Objective:** For a fixed reference-price vector, each firm chooses its price as a best response to rivals to maximize price times MNL market share; a stationary Nash equilibrium is a fixed point where equilibrium prices equal reference prices.
- **Representative equation:** `$p_i^E(r)=\arg\max_{p_i\in P}\{p_i d_i((p_i,p_{-i}^E(r)),r)\}$ (Equation (5), printed p. 1012 (PDF p. 6), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Stationary Nash equilibrium with decentralized no-regret learning
- **Solution:** Under loss-neutral reference effects, OPGA drives both prices and references to the unique SNE in the last iterate, achieves a near inverse-square squared-distance rate under suitable steps, and has constant dynamic regret. Under loss aversion, nonsmooth payoffs require C-OPGA, which converges to the SNE set at a slower square-root rate. Firm-differentiated step sizes retain convergence under the stated conditions, but uniformly bounded gradient error delta yields only an O(delta) neighborhood under OPGA or an O(delta+epsilon)-SNE under C-OPGA rather than exact convergence. Gain-seeking behavior can destroy SNE existence.
- **Evidence:** Equation (5) defines the single-period pure-strategy equilibrium pricing policy and Definition 2 defines its stationary fixed point.; Propositions 1 and 2 establish SNE existence, structure, and uniqueness conditions.; Theorems 1-3 prove last-iterate convergence, rates, and dynamic-regret properties for OPGA in the loss-neutral case.; Theorems 4 and 5 establish approximate-set convergence and rates for C-OPGA under nonsmooth loss aversion.; Theorem 6 allows firm-specific step sizes; Theorem 7 shows that uniformly bounded first-order errors yield only an O(delta) neighborhood of the unique SNE under OPGA or an O(delta+epsilon)-SNE under C-OPGA.
- **Caveat:** The guarantees rely on MNL demand, compact prices, a specific memory update, sign restrictions on reference sensitivities, and prescribed step-size conditions. Exact SNE convergence uses exact first-order feedback; uniformly bounded nonzero errors support only neighborhood guarantees. Firms are modeled as following the proposed algorithms, and the paper proves mathematical learning performance rather than empirically observed adoption or welfare optimality.

### Price Informativeness and Corporate Investment: A Model of Costly Manipulation and Share Repurchases

Murillo Campello; Rafael Matta; Pedro A. C. Saffi (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.05452](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05452). First published online: 2025-05-21.

- **Question:** How should a firm use funding commitments and share repurchases when short sellers can manipulate prices that guide corporate investment?
- **Players:** outside capital provider; firm manager; privately informed speculator; competitive market maker
- **Timing:** At date 0 the manager and capital provider sign an observable financing contract. At date 1 the state and a possibly informative common signal arrive; the manager and speculator choose orders, a nonstrategic noise trader submits a random order, and the market maker sets a competitive price from aggregate flow. Trading repeats at date 2. At date 3 the capital provider observes prices and implements the contract's funding and reinvestment decision; final cash flows and trading payoffs follow.
- **Actions:** design and accept a financing contract; buy, sell, or abstain in each trading round; repurchase shares subject to the manager's trading constraint; set Bayesian zero-profit stock prices; fund or withhold corporate investment
- **Information:** The project's state is high or low and the manager and speculator observe the same signal, which is informative with probability alpha and uninformative otherwise.; The competitive market maker observes aggregate order flow rather than each trader's identity or signal.; The capital provider observes the price history and any contractible variables before funding investment.; Noise orders conceal informed and manipulative trades.; Contracts and equilibrium strategies are common knowledge, and off-path beliefs complete the Bayesian equilibrium.
- **Objective:** Choose an ex ante contract and price-contingent funding rule to maximize firm value subject to the manager's and speculator's trading incentives, competitive Bayesian prices, and the capital provider's break-even condition.
- **Representative equation:** `$C* is a contract that maximizes firm value subject to a nonnegative expected return for the capital provider; competitive prices satisfy p_1(Q_1,C)=E[V(k,omega)-k|Q_1,C] and p_2(Q_1,Q_2,C)=E[V(k,omega)-k|Q_1,Q_2,C], with manager and speculator orders as mutual best responses.$ (Model and equilibrium conditions in Section 2, printed pp. 1028-1029 / PDF pp. 4-5; ex ante contracting problem in Section 2.3, beginning printed p. 1032 / PDF p. 8)
- **Equilibrium:** Pure-strategy Bayesian trading and investment equilibrium with competitive pricing
- **Solution:** At very low shorting costs, informed trade coexists with downward manipulation; as costs rise, manipulation becomes less profitable but early informed trading may also disappear. Moderate costs eliminate manipulation while retaining useful information, whereas sufficiently high costs suppress informed shorting. Without contracting, these forces can make investment nonmonotone in shorting costs. With an optimal ex ante contract, funding commitments and price-contingent reinvestment induce informative manager repurchases and neutralize manipulation in the relevant low-cost regions; investment and repurchases then weakly decrease as shorting becomes costlier, and the welfare effect of a short-sale ban depends on signal informativeness and the initial shorting-cost region.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 defines a four-period game in which a capital provider and manager first contract, the manager and speculator trade after observing a common signal, a market maker sets Bayesian zero-profit prices, and the provider makes the real-investment decision.; Section 2.2 defines equilibrium by optimal manager and speculator strategies, competitive pricing consistent with aggregate order flow and Bayes' rule, and optimal investment; the paper restricts attention to pure strategies and uses an efficiency criterion where needed.; Proposition 1 partitions equilibrium by the per-unit shorting cost: low costs permit manipulation together with informed trade, an intermediate region can crowd early informed trading out, moderate costs eliminate manipulation, and high costs also impede informed shorting.; Proposition 2 and Corollary 1 show that, without ex ante contracting, investment capacity can be nonmonotone in shorting costs because reducing manipulation and suppressing information have opposing effects.; Propositions 3-5 characterize the optimal direct mechanism and an implementable contract that precommits funding and conditions reinvestment on prices; manager repurchases can signal information and offset uninformed manipulation.; Corollary 4 gives the exact short-sale-ban comparison: a ban lowers investment capacity when alpha is below the lower threshold; at intermediate alpha it lowers capacity for c<c' but raises it for c>c'; above the upper alpha threshold it raises capacity. Figure 1 is descriptive rather than causal evidence.
- **Caveat:** The baseline has discrete states, fixed-size orders, a common perfectly correlated signal for the manager and speculator, an exogenous fixed shorting cost, competitive risk-neutral pricing, and pure strategies with an efficiency selection. The manager can repurchase but not short; under the maintained assumptions the paper rules buy-side manipulation out as unprofitable rather than developing a general analysis of it. Richer institutional constraints are omitted, and Figure 1 is correlational rather than causal validation of the mechanism.

### Privacy and Polarization: An Inference-Based Framework

Tommaso Bondi; Omid Rafieian; Yunfei (Jesse) Yao (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.06054](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06054). First published online: 2025-06-09.

- **Question:** Will banning behavioral tracking make ad-funded media choose more extreme content, and how does competition change that response?
- **Players:** one monopolist or two competing media firms; ideologically heterogeneous consumers
- **Timing:** At stage 1 each consumer's ideological type theta is realized; firms observe it under behavioral targeting but not under contextual targeting. At stage 2 media firms choose ideological positions x. At stage 3 consumers observe positions and idiosyncratic tastes and choose one firm's content or the outside option. At stage 4 each chosen firm selects an ad a using the information allowed by the targeting regime and earns the ad-consumer match value.
- **Actions:** choose mainstream or one of two niche ideological positions; choose a media firm's content or an outside option; choose an impression-level ad location or type
- **Information:** Consumer type theta is one of 0, 1/2, or 1 and is observed by firms under behavioral tracking but remains private under contextual targeting.; Each consumer observes the relevant firm positions and a firm-specific idiosyncratic utility shock before choosing content.; Under behavioral targeting the firm's information is {x,theta}; under contextual targeting it is only the chosen content x.; A contextual firm uses Bayes' rule to infer the posterior distribution of types among its audience.; Firm positions and the targeting regime are common knowledge.
