- **Evidence:** Random latency creates an uncertain ordering of market makers submitting at the same price.; The liquidity-demanding investor optimally chooses a market-order size after observing depth and private valuation information.; Because early queue units have greater execution probability, simultaneous quantity competition can make aggregate depth exceed the ex post profitable amount.; Queue resolution induces tail cancellations, generating testable cancel-to-add count and size ratios.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses a static one-tick empty-book environment, risk-neutral makers, no explicit fees, time priority, no queue jumping or rationing, and tractable distributional assumptions. The main top-of-queue and overshooting analysis maintains the threshold conditions a>a* and tau_U>tau_U* (or an alternative sufficiently large private-signal precision). It omits multi-level books, repeated order flow, inventory, cross-venue routing, strategic latency investment, and many exchange-specific priority and fee rules.

### To Each Their Own: Personalized Product Offerings in Competition

Jinzhao Du; Z. Eddie Ning (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.02540](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02540). First published online: 2025-09-17.

- **Question:** How does prediction accuracy change firms' personalized product and price choices, profits, consumer welfare, and incentives to invest in customer data?
- **Players:** two competing firms with private prediction signals; a consumer choosing between the firms' personalized offers
- **Timing:** Nature draws the consumer's ideal location and an idiosyncratic relative preference shock. Each firm privately observes its own imperfect signal. The firms simultaneously choose the product position and price offered to that consumer without observing the rival's signal or offer. The consumer observes both offers and buys from the higher-utility firm. In the investment extension, firms choose signal accuracy before this product-market game.
- **Actions:** choose prediction accuracy in the investment extension; choose a signal-contingent personalized product position; choose a signal-contingent price; select one of the two offers
- **Information:** Each firm privately observes only its own noisy signal of the consumer's ideal location.; Signal accuracies and the signal-generating process are common knowledge.; A firm does not observe its competitor's signal, personalized offer, or price before acting.; The consumer observes both offers, knows the realized ideal location and preference shock, and then chooses.
- **Objective:** Conditional on its signal, each firm chooses a personalized position and price to maximize expected demand times price.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi_i(y_i,p_i | s_i,y_j(s_j),p_j(s_j)) = D_i(y_i,p_i | s_i,y_j(s_j),p_j(s_j)) p_i$ (Section 3, Equation (10), printed p. 4742 / PDF p. 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in signal-contingent personalized positions and product-line prices
- **Solution:** Equilibrium personalization equals each firm's posterior expectation of the consumer's ideal point. A firm charges more for niche products unless its prediction accuracy is sufficiently below its rival's; when both firms improve equally, differentiation and profit are inverse-U-shaped in accuracy. Analytically, ex ante social surplus rises with symmetric accuracy. Numerically, aggregate consumer welfare also rises, although sufficiently mainstream consumers can lose when accuracy increases from a modest level. In the investment extension, equilibrium accuracy exceeds the joint-profit-maximizing level because of business stealing. An accuracy cap near that collusive benchmark can therefore raise firms' profits and lower consumer welfare, although the consumer-data-choice extension shows that this conclusion is moderated by privacy disutility. The core mechanisms survive the paper's search, uniform-pricing, Salop, and correlated-signal extensions.
- **Evidence:** Each firm receives a private signal that is correct with a firm-specific accuracy and otherwise independently noisy.; Firms simultaneously select a personalized product location and price without seeing the rival's offer.; The equilibrium personalization rule equals the firm's posterior mean of the consumer's ideal point.; A separate first-stage game lets both firms choose prediction accuracy before competing for consumers.
- **Caveat:** The baseline has two firms, full market coverage, nonbinding price bounds, a sufficiently wide taste-shock range for interior solutions, costless and unlimited product lines, one product shown per consumer, a uniform one-dimensional location, simultaneous price and position choices, public signal accuracies, and no capacity or production costs. The displayed equilibrium is not proved unique in the original strategy space. Signals are modeled as a reduced-form black box, and menus, multidimensional tastes, endogenous data generation, and price discrimination based directly on willingness to pay are outside the core model.

### Anticompetitive Effects of a Dominant Retailer’s Guaranteed Profit Margin and Low-Price Contracts

Leela Nageswaran; Aditya Jain; Haresh Gurnani (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.06332](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06332). First published online: 2025-09-22.

- **Question:** When do guaranteed-margin and low-price contracts imposed by a dominant retailer raise market prices, induce supplier exclusivity, and reduce consumer access?
- **Players:** a dominant focal retailer; a competing retailer; an upstream supplier
- **Timing:** In Models M and ML, focal retailer 1 first chooses its guaranteed margin alpha. The supplier then chooses whether to partner with both retailers or exclusively and sets wholesale price w; served retailers next set retail prices, after which demand and profits are realized. Model ML adds the supplier-funded low-price-guarantee rule. In benchmark Model W there is no retailer contract stage: the supplier first selects coverage and w, followed by retail pricing.
- **Actions:** choose guaranteed profit margin alpha under Models M and ML; choose inclusive or exclusive retailer coverage; set uniform or retailer-specific wholesale prices; set retail prices subject to the applicable low-price guarantee
- **Information:** Contract terms and prices are publicly observed in the complete-information baseline.; Consumer demand and cost primitives are common knowledge.; An extension allows retailer 2 not to observe the focal retailer's guaranteed margin and uses rational expectations.; The supplier anticipates downstream price responses when choosing coverage and wholesale terms.
- **Objective:** The supplier maximizes wholesale margin over served retailers and each active retailer maximizes its retail margin times demand, subject to the focal contract's transfer and margin requirements.
- **Representative equation:** `$pi_S = sum_i (w-c)D_i I_i;  pi_i = (p_i-w)D_i$ (Section 3, benchmark Model W, printed p. 4840 / PDF p. 5)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect channel equilibrium under wholesale, margin, and margin-plus-low-price contracts
- **Solution:** A guaranteed-margin contract can be anticompetitive when retailer competition is intense: it induces the supplier to use exclusive distribution, raises the retail price, and removes consumer access through the rival. With weak competition and a uniform wholesale price, the same contract retains both outlets, lowers prices relative to the wholesale benchmark, and increases market coverage. Allowing differentiated wholesale prices makes the anticompetitive price effect arise more broadly. Adding a supplier-funded low-price guarantee preserves both outlets but produces the highest equilibrium retail prices across the compared regimes, so outlet access alone is not a sufficient antitrust screen.
- **Evidence:** Demand is derived from a representative consumer's utility over differentiated retailer offerings.; The supplier decides whether to serve both retailers or partner exclusively with one and chooses wholesale price.; The dominant retailer can precommit to a guaranteed per-unit margin and, in the ML regime, a lowest-price obligation backed by supplier payments.; The paper compares equilibrium access, wholesale and retail prices, profits, and consumer outcomes across W, M, and ML.
- **Caveat:** The model has one supplier, two retailers, a dominant retailer able to move first, linear demand derived from a representative consumer, and stylized enforceable margin and low-price terms. It abstracts from upstream competition, retailer entry, direct channels, dynamic contracting, heterogeneous consumers beyond the demand system, and many legal and implementation details of real contracts.

### The Interplay Between Product Variety and Customer Retention: Theory and Evidence

Ulrich Kaiser; Reinhold Kesler; Markus Reisinger (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.00985](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00985). First published online: 2025-09-23.

- **Question:** Should a digital-product firm retain customers more aggressively or broaden its catalog, and how do market value and consumer heterogeneity change the equilibrium mix?
- **Players:** M competing multiproduct firms; retained and switching consumers assigned initially to firm customer bases
- **Timing:** Firms simultaneously choose product variety m_i, customer-retention investment r_i, and price p_i. Retained consumers buy from their incumbent firm, while nonretained consumers compare the products offered by all firms. Sales, revenue, and variety and retention costs are then realized.
- **Actions:** choose the number or mass of products; choose customer-retention investment; choose a common product price; buy from the incumbent or select among all available products
- **Information:** Market size, taste heterogeneity, cost functions, and competitors' feasible choices are common knowledge.; Firms act simultaneously and do not observe rivals' contemporaneous variety, retention, or price choices.; Each firm begins with an equally sized customer base in the baseline.; Consumer matching probabilities depend on all firms' product masses and prices.
- **Objective:** Each firm maximizes revenue from retained customers plus its share of switching-customer revenue, net of product-variety and retention costs.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi_i(m,r,p)=r_i p_i/M + [sum_j(1-r_j)/M] [p_i m_i(v-p_i)^(1/beta) / sum_j m_j(v-p_j)^(1/beta)] - f(m_i)-c(r_i)$ (Section 3, printed p. 4940 / PDF p. 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Interior Nash equilibrium in variety, retention, and price
- **Solution:** Product variety and customer retention are substitutes: stronger retention lowers a firm's incentive to expand its product line, and broader variety lowers the marginal value of retention. Equilibrium variety is inverted-U-shaped in market value because a larger market initially raises demand for breadth but eventually strengthens price and retention incentives; greater consumer heterogeneity raises variety. The Steam OLS and instrumental-variable specifications provide suggestive, nonstructural support for the predicted negative variety-retention relationship and the main market-value and heterogeneity patterns.
- **Evidence:** Firms simultaneously choose a continuous mass of products, a retention rate, and a common price.; Retained consumers buy from their incumbent firm, whereas nonretained consumers choose among all products according to matching probabilities.; The model predicts that variety and retention are strategic substitutes within a firm and links equilibrium variety to market value and taste heterogeneity.; The empirical analysis uses a large Steam title snapshot and instruments price and retention proxies with exchange-rate movements and SteamWorks diffusion.
- **Caveat:** The theoretical baseline assumes equal customer bases, a continuous product mass, a common price within firm, simultaneous choices, and restrictive curvature conditions. The empirical application is largely cross-sectional and vulnerable to remaining endogeneity, measurement, Steam survivorship and platform-selection concerns despite instruments and robustness checks; update frequency is an imperfect retention proxy.

### Two-Sided Benefits of Price Transparency in Smallholder Supply Chains

Yuan Shi; Joann F. de Zegher; Irene Y. Lo (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.01617](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01617). First published online: 2025-09-29.

- **Question:** How much rival-price information should a platform reveal to farmers if it needs to improve farmer welfare without driving procurement buyers away?
- **Players:** high-demand procurement buyer; low-demand procurement buyer; continuum of informed or uninformed smallholder sellers
- **Timing:** In each period buyers observe their realized procurement targets and simultaneously post per-unit prices. A fraction lambda of sellers observes both prices and chooses the utility-maximizing buyer after transport cost; remaining sellers observe only their loyal buyer's price. Supply shocks then realize, buyers purchase the resulting quantities, deliver them downstream, and incur shortage or surplus penalties. In the collusion extension this stage interaction repeats with discount factor delta.
- **Actions:** post a procurement price; compare both prices or follow a loyal relationship depending on information; choose which buyer receives the seller's output; cooperate on a joint price profile or deviate in the repeated-game extension
- **Information:** Each buyer observes its realized high or low contractual demand before pricing; in the baseline the two targets are opposite and sum to two.; The transparency parameter lambda is the fraction of sellers who observe both buyer prices and distances.; Uninformed sellers see only one price and remain with their loyal buyer.; Supply shocks are not observed at the time prices are set.; Market primitives and the distribution of demand and supply states are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** Each buyer chooses its procurement price to maximize expected single-period revenue net of purchase cost and expected underage or overage loss, taking the rival price and transparency regime as given.
- **Representative equation:** `$p_i^BR(p_j,lambda) in argmax_{p_i>=p_bar} pi_i(p_i,p_j,lambda), where pi_i=y(p_i,p_j,lambda)(1-p_i)-gamma E[(s_i+epsilon)^-]-h E[(s_i+epsilon)^+].$ (Equations (2)-(3), best-response problem, and equilibrium statement, printed p. 5217 / PDF p. 7, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Unique pure-strategy Bayes-Nash procurement-price equilibrium; subgame-perfect collusive equilibrium in the repeated extension
- **Solution:** Once transparency passes the competitive threshold, average procurement prices rise. Demand asymmetry creates price dispersion, and after both buyers price above the reservation price, further transparency weakly narrows that dispersion. With sufficiently asymmetric buyer demand, high overage cost, and low random supply variation, price differences direct supply toward the buyer that needs it most and reduce mismatch losses. Under the paper's sufficient conditions a nonempty interval of transparency benefits sellers and both buyers, but full transparency may go too far from buyers' perspective. Cooperative pricing can preserve two-sided gains when repeated-game incentives support it, and transparency-dependent uncertainty can strengthen or weaken the result.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 defines two buyers at opposite ends of a Hotelling line, a continuum of smallholder sellers, transparency lambda, asymmetric procurement targets, and stochastic supply with underage and overage penalties.; At the pricing stage each buyer chooses a best response to the competitor's price. Theorem 1 establishes, under its transport-cost threshold, a unique pure-strategy Bayes-Nash equilibrium for every positive transparency level.; Theorem 1 shows that above the competitive threshold average price rises with transparency. Proposition 1 shows that once both prices exceed the reservation price, further transparency weakly narrows price dispersion; demand asymmetry keeps the high-demand buyer's price above the low-demand buyer's.; Propositions 2-3 identify demand signaling: more transparency reduces expected mismatch loss, but the gain becomes harder to achieve as random supply uncertainty rises.; Theorem 2 gives sufficient conditions for an interval of transparency levels to be strongly Pareto improving for sellers and both buyers; Proposition 4 characterizes the bounds and comparative statics of that interval, which need not include full transparency.; Theorem 3 embeds cooperative prices in a repeated game and characterizes when a collusive outcome is sustainable. Later results allow transparency-dependent and supply-dependent uncertainty and buyers that reject excess supply.; Section 7 calibrates t from PemPem supply-elasticity estimates, back-engineers Delta from observed price dispersion, and fits sigma to bootstrapped transaction-level supply; h and gamma cannot be estimated and are set by assumption for the recommendations.
- **Caveat:** The baseline has two spatially differentiated buyers, a continuum of sellers with a common reservation price, opposite demand states, balanced expected supply and demand, additive symmetric uncertainty, myopic single-period pricing, acceptance of all supply, and no price discrimination. Equilibrium uniqueness needs a differentiation threshold, and the sufficient conditions for two-sided welfare gains are not universal. The collusion and uncertainty extensions depend on additional reduced-form assumptions. PemPem recommendations use reduced-form estimates for t, Delta, and sigma, whereas h and gamma are not identified from the platform data and are set by assumption.

### Dynamic Portfolio Selection Under Quantile Maximization

Xue Dong He; Zhaoli Jiang; Steven Kou (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.03182](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03182). First published online: 2025-10-21.

- **Question:** What dynamically credible portfolio policy follows when an investor judges terminal wealth by a quantile rather than expected utility, and can that equilibrium explain how risky-asset shares vary with household wealth?
- **Players:** the investor's current self at each time t; the same investor's future selves who control later portfolio actions
- **Timing:** Trading occurs continuously over [0,T]. At time t and a reachable wealth state, the current self can replace the candidate portfolio for an infinitesimal interval [t,t+epsilon), but cannot commit future selves. From t+epsilon onward, future selves use the candidate Markov strategy. The current self evaluates the alpha-quantile of terminal wealth and chooses whether to deviate.
- **Actions:** each time-t self chooses dollar investments in m risky assets for the current interval; future selves follow the candidate Markov strategy; the investor selects an endogenous portfolio-insurance floor among multiple median equilibria
- **Information:** Each self observes current wealth and the filtration generated by asset prices.; Drift, volatility, the risk-free rate, portfolio constraints, and the candidate future strategy are common knowledge across selves.; The equilibrium test is applied at wealth states reachable from the initial condition under the candidate strategy.; Terminal wealth remains stochastic because risky prices follow Brownian dynamics.
- **Objective:** Each time-t self maximizes the conditional alpha-quantile of terminal wealth; an intrapersonal equilibrium makes the gain from any feasible infinitesimal current deviation nonpositive when future selves follow the candidate strategy.
- **Representative equation:** `$G^p(t,x,alpha)=sup{y: F^p(t,x,y)<=alpha}; equilibrium p_hat satisfies G^{p_hat_{t,epsilon,pi}}(t,x,alpha)-G^{p_hat}(t,x,alpha)<=0 for every feasible pi and sufficiently small epsilon$ (Section 3, Equations (10)-(13) and Definition 1, printed p. 5812 / PDF p. 7, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Continuous-time intrapersonal equilibrium under quantile maximization
- **Solution:** Quantile choice has a sharp equilibrium implication. For alpha<1/2, every affine equilibrium leads to zero risky investment; for alpha>1/2, no affine intrapersonal equilibrium exists because the current self wants unbounded risk; and for alpha=1/2, every equilibrium is a constant-proportion portfolio-insurance strategy p_hat(t,x)=v*(x-xi) with an endogenous floor xi<x0. Calibrated variation in xi explains the newly documented 'portfolio share smile': risky shares first fall and then rise with household log net worth.
- **Evidence:** At every instant, the current self chooses risky investment for a short interval while correctly anticipating that future selves will revert to the proposed strategy.; Definition 1 requires no feasible infinitesimal deviation to raise the current self's conditional terminal-wealth quantile at any reachable state.; Within time-varying affine strategies, Theorem 1 gives portfolio-insurance equilibria only for the median, zero risky investment below the median, and nonexistence above the median.; The median equilibrium has an endogenously chosen wealth floor and coincides with a constant-proportion portfolio-insurance form.; Calibrating heterogeneous equilibrium floors to SCF data reproduces a U-shaped relation between risky portfolio share and log net worth.
- **Caveat:** The complete theorem is limited to time-varying affine strategies; nonaffine equilibria are not characterized. Asset returns follow a diffusion with deterministic coefficients, the constraint set is linear, and the equilibrium notion permits deviations only at reachable states for an infinitesimal interval. The wealth-floor heterogeneity is calibrated rather than structurally estimated from household preferences, and the cross-sectional portfolio-share explanation remains a model-consistent interpretation despite panel and education robustness checks.

### Incentivizing Resource Pooling

Chen Chen; Yilun Chen; Pengyu Qian (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.03550](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03550). First published online: 2025-11-10.

- **Question:** Can a simple token rule make anonymous self-interested computing servers share idle capacity as efficiently as a fully informed central dispatcher?
- **Players:** N strategic servers, each operating a private M/M/1 queue
- **Timing:** Jobs and service-capacity units arrive independently to every server in continuous time. At any time, a server may spend tokens to request help for one or more queued jobs and move them irrevocably to the shared pool. On a capacity arrival, it may serve a local job, offer help to the pool, or idle; offering help earns a token with probability φ. The process repeats indefinitely and each server minimizes long-run average cost.
- **Actions:** request help for one or more queued jobs subject to the token balance; retain jobs in the local queue; serve a local job; offer a capacity unit to the shared pool; idle and waste a capacity unit
- **Information:** A server privately observes its own queue length, tokens, arrivals, and interaction history.; Other servers' states and actions and the shared-pool queue length are hidden.; A server need not know the exact number of servers, only that the market is large.; Arrival/service rates, cost parameters, token protocol, and token-earning probability are common knowledge.; FMFE assumes a stationary history-independent distribution for the shared pool.
- **Objective:** Each server chooses a dynamic requesting and capacity-allocation strategy to minimize expected long-run average holding and processing costs.
- **Representative equation:** `$limsup_{t→∞} (1/t)V_i(t), where V_i(t) ≜ E[Σ_{j≤N_i^λ(t)} w_ij + c(L_i(t)+T_i(t))]$ (Section 2, server objective, p. 5 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Fluid mean-field equilibrium with asymptotically near-optimal best responses
- **Solution:** For small shared-pool delay, best responses are queue-threshold policies: servers serve local jobs whenever present and help only when empty, while their help-request threshold depends on φ. As N grows, any cooperative FMFE has O(1/N) shared-pool delay. The congestion-minimizing choice is φ=λ; then every incoming job is requested, every idle capacity unit is offered, and the decentralized system exactly matches centralized complete pooling in dynamics and performance. FMFE play is asymptotically a near-optimal best response in the original capped-token game. Adjusted φ also implements the first best when helping has an extra processing cost, and the mechanism remains nearly optimal with heterogeneous servers.
- **Evidence:** Each server receives independent job and capacity-unit Poisson processes and privately observes its own queue and token balance.; A server earns a token probabilistically by offering help and spends one token to move a job into a hidden shared pool.; The FMFE combines a stationary mean-field approximation with a fluid token-balance relaxation, yielding a queue-length threshold strategy.; Theorems 5.1-5.2 optimize the token earning probability and show that setting it equal to arrival rate implements complete resource pooling in large systems.
- **Caveat:** The exact PBE is not solved; FMFE uses stationary mean-field beliefs and a fluid relaxation and admits a no-cooperation equilibrium in addition to cooperative equilibria. Exact first-best implementation is an asymptotic large-market result. The baseline assumes homogeneous M/M/1 servers, pair-independent processing cost, a hidden FCFS pool, and an artificial token cap; the authors flag joint job-server heterogeneity and perishable tokens as future work.

### The Production and Consumption of Social Media

Apostolos Filippas; John J. Horton; Elliot Lipnowski; Prasanna Parasurama (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.00060](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00060). First published online: 2025-11-10.

- **Question:** Why do ordinary social-media users produce content and follow one another reciprocally, and how can platforms encourage engagement without destroying the audience value that sustains production?
- **Players:** a continuum of heterogeneous social-media users choosing unilateral and reciprocal following links
- **Timing:** Users choose bilateral attention-bartering relationships while anticipating optimal unilateral following. Conditional on the reciprocal network, each user unilaterally follows other users whose content yields positive consumption value. A new reciprocal relationship requires the prospective partner's consent, whereas either user may sever an existing reciprocal relationship unilaterally.
- **Actions:** follow another user unilaterally for consumption value; propose or consent to a reciprocal attention-bartering link; sever an existing reciprocal link
- **Information:** User types and type-contingent consumption values are publicly observable in the model.; Users know the current follower counts that determine marginal attention benefits.; A user anticipates unilateral-following best responses when evaluating a bilateral link.; Whether another user is willing to form a new reciprocal link is constrained by that partner's marginal payoff.; The empirical ability proxy is residualized list membership, not a directly observed primitive.
- **Objective:** A user chooses organic and reciprocal links to maximize consumption utility net of reciprocal-link monitoring cost plus a concave benefit from the attention supplied by followers.
- **Representative equation:** `$V(theta|f1,f2) = E_hat_theta[f2(theta,hat_theta)(u(theta,hat_theta)-c(theta)) + (1-f2(theta,hat_theta))f1(theta,hat_theta)u(theta,hat_theta)] + b(theta)A(m(theta|f1,f2))$ (Section 3.1, Notation 1, printed p. 6373 (PDF p. 6), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Pairwise-stability-like equilibrium in unilateral and reciprocal following networks
- **Solution:** Equilibrium attention bartering does not crowd out organic follows and raises users' utility; under the paper's follower-based interpretation, it can induce additional content production. The vertical model has an essentially unique network of stars, ability-ranked reciprocal clubs, and possibly lurkers; followers and follower-to-followee ratios rise with ability, while followees peak and then fall. #EconTwitter patterns and user surveys broadly match these predictions, and reciprocal following is a strong predictor of link formation.
- **Evidence:** Theorem 1 gives necessary and sufficient equilibrium conditions for unilateral following and reciprocal attention bartering.; Proposition 2 derives an essentially unique vertical-model network with stars, isolated attention-bartering clubs, and possibly lurkers.; Proposition 3 predicts increasing follower counts, a followee dip at high ability, and reciprocal relationships concentrated among intermediate-ability users.; A sample of 55,966 active #EconTwitter users displays the predicted follower, followee, ratio, and assortative-matching patterns.; Surveys of 496 Twitter and 505 Instagram users and a link-prediction exercise provide direct and behavioral evidence of reciprocal attention exchange.
- **Caveat:** The model is static, treats the platform as passive, and abstracts from content-production choices, interpreting a user as producing if and only if that user has followers. It uses public types and additively separable link payoffs and omits entry, exit, dynamic reciprocity, preferential attachment, and richer substitution across followed users. The empirical exercise is observational and qualitative rather than structural; reciprocal links and ability are inferred from network snapshots and proxies, so omitted variables and organic two-way following cannot be eliminated completely.

### Behavioral Simulation of Blockchain-Enabled Market for Supplier Capacity Trading Among Retailers

Kai Wendt; Volodymyr Babich; Daniel Hellwig; Arnd Huchzermeier (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.03771](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03771). First published online: 2025-11-17.

- **Question:** Can blockchain-based trading of supplier-capacity claims improve decentralized inventory allocation, and how do strategic human retailers actually order and trade when the market is thin?
- **Players:** N self-interested retailers with heterogeneous private retail prices and independent random demand
- **Timing:** At the start of a period, retailer i observes private retail price p_i and orders Q_i capacity tokens at wholesale price w. Demand D_i then realizes privately. In market treatments, retailers submit up to five blind buy and sell limit orders; the batch auction clears once at a common price m and assigns A_i. Retailers then use Q_i+A_i tokens to serve demand and receive profit; periods repeat without carryover.
- **Actions:** choose the initial token order Q_i; submit buy limit orders; submit sell limit orders; select limit prices and quantities
- **Information:** A retailer privately observes its own retail price before ordering and its own demand before trading.; Retailers do not observe rivals' prices, demands, initial orders, or order book.; The wholesale price, demand and price distributions, auction rules, and historical outcomes are known.; Trades are anonymous and the clearing mechanism is deterministic conditional on all submitted orders.; From one retailer's viewpoint, its allocation and the clearing price are random because rivals' policies are unobserved.
- **Objective:** Retailer i selects its first-stage order and contingent second-stage trading policy to maximize expected operating profit net of supplier purchases and batch-market trades.
- **Representative equation:** `$-wQ_i + E_{D_i}{E_{A_i,m}^{U_i}[-mA_i + p_i min(D_i,Q_i+A_i)]}$ (Section 3.2, Equation (2), p. 7 (PDF p. 7))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect Bayesian solution concept for the two-stage ordering and trading game; full equilibrium not computed
- **Solution:** Markets reduce leftover inventory and shortages and raise average retailer and total supply-chain profits. However, clearing prices anchor strongly to wholesale prices and fail to signal net demand in large markets. Clustering reveals spot buyers, spot sellers, and coopetitors; the coopetitive strategy performs best because it balances demand and market risk. Markets pull average orders toward mean demand but increase order dispersion, creating a bullwhip effect. Supplier revenue rises with high wholesale prices but falls with low wholesale prices.
- **Evidence:** Each retailer first orders supplier-capacity tokens using only its private retail price and later submits vectors of buy and sell orders after observing its own demand.; A deterministic blind batch-clearing rule converts all retailers' orders into one market price and individual net allocations.; The authors specify SPBE but explicitly state that computing the full equilibrium is challenging; predictions instead use reward-function structure and behaviorally reasonable strategies.; The experiment crosses two wholesale prices with no, three-retailer, and all-retailer markets and measures allocation, prices, ordering strategies, and profits.
- **Caveat:** The paper does not solve the stated SPBE; its predictions rely on reasonable trading strategies and the experiment documents boundedly rational behavior. Demand is known before trading, retailers do not compete downstream, the supplier and wholesale price are passive, products are fully substitutable as tokens, and the student sample uses only two wholesale prices. The authors explicitly leave full equilibrium with behavioral heterogeneity and strategic supplier intervention to future work.

### Whence LASSO? A Rational Interpretation

Wen Chen; Bo Hu; Liyan Yang (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.06127](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06127). First published online: 2025-11-17.

- **Question:** Can LASSO be rationalized as an equilibrium decision rule for strategic traders, and when does its competition-mitigation benefit exceed the bias it introduces?
- **Players:** N identical large traders using historical prices; unmodeled informed and noise order flow represented in the price process
- **Timing:** In round 1, traders submit orders before observing informative price history. The first price incorporates informed and noise order flow. In round 2, traders observe the first price or order flow and choose new orders, internalizing price impact and rival strategies. The asset then liquidates.
- **Actions:** each trader chooses a first-round order; after observing price history, each trader chooses a state-contingent second-round order; each trader robustly evaluates strategies over an ambiguity set
- **Information:** All modeled traders observe the same public price history.; They know pricing and informed-flow coefficients but are ambiguous about the scale of the Laplace asset-value distribution.; Each large trader accounts for its own effect on total order flow and price.; Noise and informed exogenous order flows are unobserved before trading.
- **Objective:** Each trader chooses first- and second-round order strategies to maximize worst-case expected trading profit over all asset-value scale parameters in the ambiguity set.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{Z_{1,n}\in S_1,Z_{2,n}(y_1)\in S_2}\;\min_{\xi\in[\underline\xi,\infty]}\mathbb E^{\xi}[(\tilde v-\tilde p_1)Z_{1,n}+(\tilde v-\tilde p_2)Z_{2,n}(y_1)]$ (Equation (11), printed p. 5 (PDF p. 5), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric Bayesian Nash equilibrium with max-min robust preferences
- **Solution:** Without ambiguity, symmetric equilibrium orders are proportional to an MSE forecast. Ambiguity creates conservative, LASSO-like trading with an inaction region, and the paper's linear strategy constraints yield an exact LASSO rule; related constraints rationalize elastic net. Shrinkage can raise aggregate trader profit by softening strategic competition, but estimation bias can offset that benefit, so LASSO is not uniformly more profitable.
- **Evidence:** Equation (11) defines each trader's max-min expected-profit problem over an ambiguity set for the asset-value distribution.; Proposition 1 gives the benchmark symmetric equilibrium based on the MSE estimate.; Proposition 2 shows that ambiguity creates an inaction region and an approximate LASSO strategy without trading constraints.; Proposition 3 shows that linear strategy constraints produce the exact LASSO form.; The profit analysis separates reduced competition from forecast bias, and extensions cover elastic net and alternative fat-tailed distributions.
- **Caveat:** The baseline takes linear price impact and informed-flow coefficients as given, models identical large traders and a stylized two-round market, and uses a Laplace scale ambiguity set. The exact LASSO result depends on specific linear strategy constraints, and equilibrium existence statements rely on sufficient parameter conditions rather than a universal market microstructure.

### Quality-Variety Tradeoffs in Recommendation Systems on Content Platforms

Tianxin Zou; Yue Wu; Miklos Sarvary (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2025.00300](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00300). First published online: 2025-11-19.

- **Question:** How does a recommendation system's emphasis on quality versus preference match change creators' strategic entry, content quality, platform value, and consumption variety?
- **Players:** N potential content creators strategically deciding entry and quality
- **Timing:** The platform's recommendation accuracies are fixed and publicly known. All creators simultaneously decide whether to produce and, conditional on entry, choose content quality. The recommender then allocates consumer impressions probabilistically, consumers consume the recommended content, and creators receive viewership net of production cost.
- **Actions:** each potential creator enters or stays out; each entering creator chooses content quality simultaneously with rivals
- **Information:** Creators know the recommendation rule, production-cost function, and other common primitives.; In the base model content types and realized qualities are observed by the reduced-form recommender.; Creators choose simultaneously and do not observe rivals' entry or quality choices beforehand.; The trendiness extension adds random postproduction quality shocks to a subset of creators.
- **Objective:** An entering creator chooses quality to maximize recommendation-driven viewership relative to rivals minus convex production cost.
- **Representative equation:** `$π_j(q_j) = 1/n + b_q(q_j - q̄_{-j}) - C(q_j)$ (Section 4, Equation (4), paper p. 7 (PDF p. 7))
- **Equilibrium:** Pure-strategy creator-entry and quality perfect Bayesian equilibrium
- **Solution:** Equilibrium quality is q*=C'^{-1}(b_q), whereas the equilibrium creator count is n*=1/C(q*). Thus increasing quality-based accuracy raises quality but lowers variety. Match-based accuracy always helps the platform in the base model, while greater quality emphasis can reduce platform value when the lost probability of offering consumers their preferred content outweighs quality gains. Random hit potential, endogenous platform demand, creator type flexibility, and multi-item consumption preserve the central possibility that excessive quality emphasis harms the platform; the paper also derives a U-shaped response of consumption variety.
- **Evidence:** A creator's viewership rises with its quality relative to other entrants, so quality choices are strategically interdependent.; Equations (4)-(6) derive equilibrium creator payoff, quality, and the zero-profit number of entrants.; Proposition 1 proves stronger quality emphasis raises equilibrium quality but reduces the number of creators.; Later propositions show when lower variety dominates quality gains for platform value and how random trendy content and endogenous demand modify the tradeoff.
- **Caveat:** The base model is a one-shot symmetric game with one content item per creator, one recommendation per consumer, fixed platform demand and content types, and a reduced-form linear recommender. Quality and match accuracies are treated as fixed when creators act. Extensions relax several assumptions, but the model still abstracts from repeated creator learning, exploration by the recommender, moderation, filter bubbles, strategic users, and direct empirical identification.

### Political Polarization and Nonmarket Strategy over the Policy Life Cycle

Thomas P. Lyon; John W. Maxwell (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2025.00819](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00819). First published online: 2025-11-27.

- **Question:** How should a firm coordinate resistance to activist pressure and lobbying over a policy life cycle whose public opinion is slowed by political polarization?
- **Players:** activist choosing campaign intensity; firm choosing whether to concede, how much harm to resist, and whether to lobby
- **Timing:** In every period the activist chooses effort before campaign harm is realized. After observing harm, the firm concedes or resists. Once majority beliefs cross the legislative threshold, a resisting firm can also lobby to block a bill; if lobbying fails and a bill arrives, adoption is mandated. Otherwise the game proceeds with updated public beliefs.
- **Actions:** activist chooses campaign effort e_t; firm selects a resistance threshold h_t^R and concedes or resists after observing harm; firm chooses lobbying expenditure L_t when legislation is viable; the legislature may introduce and pass a mandate if not blocked
- **Information:** The belief paths of majority and minority groups and the policy threshold are common knowledge.; Campaign harm is stochastic conditional on activist effort and is observed before the firm's resistance decision.; The firm's lobbying cost and its spillover from campaign harm are known.; Firm and activist strategies can depend on the full history of actions and public beliefs.
- **Objective:** A strategy profile is subgame perfect when each player's continuation strategy maximizes discounted payoff after every possible history of strategic choices and public beliefs.
- **Representative equation:** `$u^i(s^{*i},s^{*-i} | H_{t-1},b_t) ≥ u^i(ŝ^i,s^{*-i} | H_{t-1},b_t) for every player i and alternative strategy ŝ^i$ (Section 2.4, pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium condition, paper p. 6 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium of the infinite-horizon activist-firm game
- **Solution:** As Phase II approaches, the firm's resistance declines and activist effort also declines when effort and toughness are complements or campaign cost is sufficiently low. Once lobbying is feasible, low harm supports resistance plus lobbying, moderate harm can support resistance without lobbying when spillovers are large, and high harm induces concession. The prospect of future lobbying raises firm value and makes resistance tougher in both phases. Greater ideological or affective polarization delays viable legislation, intensifies early activism and resistance, lowers lobbying cost, prolongs lobbying, and can generate permanent legislative gridlock.
- **Evidence:** Each period the activist selects costly effort, stochastic harm is realized, and the firm concedes or resists and may lobby.; Public-belief convergence determines the endogenous date at which legislation becomes feasible.; Proposition 2 characterizes declining campaign effort and resistance during Phase I under its stated conditions.; Propositions 3-8 characterize resistance-lobbying repertoires, strategic complementarity, lobbying cessation, and the effects of both forms of polarization.
- **Caveat:** The baseline has one representative firm and one activist, exogenous public-belief diffusion, a binary full-adoption decision, and no formal welfare analysis. Self-regulation and strategic manipulation of public beliefs are discussed but not incorporated into the solved game. The pure-strategy results depend on maintained distributional and curvature conditions for campaign harm and lobbying cost.

### Board Fiduciary Duty, Communication, and Compensation

Lin Qiu (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.08559](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08559). First published online: 2025-12-03.

- **Question:** Can tighter board fiduciary-duty rules unintentionally reduce information gathering, equity value or welfare when the board and a biased CEO communicate strategically?
- **Players:** shareholders; a self-interested board of directors; a privately informed empire-building CEO
- **Timing:** Shareholders first choose the board's linear compensation. The board then chooses costly information-gathering effort and the CEO's compensation, and the CEO chooses effort. If board information fails, the CEO sends a cheap-talk report about the state; the board then chooses the investment level and payoffs are realized.
- **Actions:** shareholders choose the board equity share and fixed pay; the board chooses information effort, CEO compensation and the investment decision; the CEO chooses effort and, when asked, a state report
- **Information:** The CEO privately observes a noisy signal about the binary investment state.; The board independently discovers the state with a probability determined by costly effort.; Compensation contracts and model primitives are common knowledge.; When board information acquisition fails, the board updates beliefs from the CEO's cheap-talk message.
- **Objective:** Shareholders choose board compensation to maximize their expected utility subject to board participation and to the board optimally choosing CEO compensation and information effort.
- **Representative equation:** `$P_SH*: max_{alpha_B in [0,1], F_B>=0} EU_SH(alpha,F,b), subject to EU_B(alpha,F,b)>=0 and (alpha_C,F_C) in argmax EU_B(alpha,F,b)$ (Section 3, shareholder compensation program, printed p. 7 / PDF p. 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Perfect Bayesian equilibrium of the CEO-board cheap-talk subgame embedded in optimal hierarchical contracts
- **Solution:** The board may grant the CEO more equity than shareholders would choose because doing so improves communication and saves board information effort. Rational shareholders partially offset this incentive through the board's own equity stake. Relative to board discretion, a binding fiduciary-duty regime weakly raises shareholder payoff, but that gain is nonmonotone and can diminish as CEO bias grows; with severe agency conflict, the binding regime can weaken board effort and reduce total equity value and welfare.
- **Evidence:** The board may learn the investment state through costly effort or from a biased CEO's report.; The board chooses CEO equity to trade off effort and credible communication, while shareholders anticipate the board's private incentives.; The model compares shareholder value, total equity value and welfare under changes in the board's fiduciary constraint.
- **Caveat:** The model uses a binary state, linear compensation, binary CEO effort and a stylized dilution/quiet-life structure. Its formal governance comparison has two regimes rather than a continuously adjustable rule-intensity parameter. It abstracts from board turnover, repeated board-CEO relationships, heterogeneous directors and empirical identification, so its regulatory implications are comparative-static mechanisms rather than direct policy estimates.

### Deep Reinforcement Learning for Equilibrium Computation in Multistage Auctions and Contests

Fabian R. Pieroth; Nils Kohring; Martin Bichler (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.06771](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06771). First published online: 2025-12-05.

- **Question:** How can analysts compute and verify equilibrium strategy functions in multistage auctions, contests and pricing games whose continuous state and action spaces defeat standard analytic methods?
- **Players:** N strategic agents in a finite multistage game; nature, which generates chance moves but is not a strategic player; application-specific agents such as bidders, contestants, or pricing firms
- **Timing:** Within the underlying game, nature and the strategic agents move over finitely many stages; signals are generated from prior actions, each agent's behavioral strategy maps its current signal to an action distribution, and bounded utility evaluates the complete rollout. Outside the game, the analyst trains a candidate profile by self-play and then applies a separate unilateral-deviation verifier.
- **Actions:** each strategic agent chooses a signal-contingent, potentially continuous action at every stage where it moves; nature draws its prescribed chance actions from the history-dependent transition law
- **Information:** Signals can be private and continuous, with distributions specified by the multistage game.; Agents have perfect recall of their own actions and received information.; The game structure and priors are known to the computational analyst.; A strategy may condition on the full information history available to that player.
- **Objective:** A candidate profile is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium when no player can improve ex ante utility by more than epsilon through any unilateral strategy deviation.
- **Representative equation:** `$u_tilde_i(beta_i,beta^*_{-i}) <= u_tilde_i(beta^*) + epsilon for every player i and deviation beta_i$ (Section 3, Definition 2 and Equation (1), printed p. 6 / PDF p. 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Numerically learned and independently verified epsilon-Nash equilibrium
- **Solution:** The method recovers analytically known equilibria in benchmark games, learns approximate equilibria in previously intractable environments, and identifies new asymmetric bidding patterns in sequential second-price auctions. The verifier supplies a numerical exploitability bound whose approximation error vanishes with finer discretization and more samples under the stated regularity conditions.
- **Evidence:** Strategies map continuous signal histories to continuous actions at multiple stages.; The learning procedure trains neural policies against opponents generated by self-play.; A separate verifier estimates profitable deviations and has an error bound under Lipschitz continuity, discretization and sampling.; Applications recover known equilibria and produce new numerical equilibrium candidates where analytic solutions are unavailable.
- **Caveat:** The output is an approximate ex ante Nash profile, not a proof of subgame-perfect, sequential, or perfect Bayesian equilibrium. The verifier's upper-bound result is asymptotic and restricted to pure Lipschitz-continuous deviations under compactness, continuity, signaling, and transition assumptions; it does not prove that policy-gradient self-play converges. Multiple asymmetric equilibria and initialization can affect equilibrium selection.

### Public Signals, Default Risk, and Voluntary Disclosure

Davide Cianciaruso; Dor Lee-Lo; Sri S. Sridhar (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.01332](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.01332). First published online: 2025-12-10.

- **Question:** How should managers of levered firms adjust voluntary disclosure after earnings news or analyst reports when extreme surprises change investors' beliefs about both expected cash flow and default risk?
- **Players:** manager of a levered firm, possibly privately informed about terminal cash flow; risk-neutral competitive investors setting the equity price
- **Timing:** A public signal s is realized. With exogenous probability q, the manager privately learns the terminal cash flow x. If informed, the manager chooses truthful disclosure of x or nondisclosure; an uninformed manager cannot certify being uninformed. Competitive investors update from the public signal and the disclosure decision and price equity at conditional expected residual value. Terminal cash flow is then realized.
- **Actions:** informed manager truthfully discloses private cash-flow information or withholds it; investors update beliefs after disclosure or nondisclosure; competitive investors set the stock price equal to expected equity value
- **Information:** The public signal is observed by the manager and investors before disclosure.; The manager privately observes terminal cash flow with probability q.; Disclosed private information is verifiable and must be truthful.; Investors cannot distinguish an uninformed manager from an informed manager who withholds.; Investors update both the mean and variance of cash flows from public signals and observed silence.
- **Objective:** The manager chooses disclosure to maximize the market price of equity, which competitive investors set equal to expected residual cash-flow value conditional on the public signal and the manager's disclosure or silence.
- **Representative equation:** `$P(I) = E[max{x-delta,0} | I], where I = {s,d}$ (Section 2, stock-price definition, printed p. 5 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Unique Bayesian cutoff equilibrium in voluntary disclosure
- **Solution:** Higher interim default risk always lowers disclosure probability. With variance uncertainty, low-prior-risk firms have a hump-shaped disclosure response to the public signal, whereas high-prior-risk firms have a U-shaped response. Public-signal quality, analyst consensus, and dispersion affect disclosure through their combined mean-variance effect; when ex ante cash-flow uncertainty is sufficiently high, greater analyst precision or coverage raises disclosure under low interim default risk and lowers it under high interim default risk. Under unlimited liability or known variance, these nonmonotonicities disappear or collapse to simpler benchmarks.
- **Evidence:** Lemma 1 establishes that, under limited liability, disclosure probability and default probability move in opposite directions after public news.; Proposition 1 shows hump-shaped disclosure in the public signal when prior default risk is low and U-shaped disclosure when prior default risk is high.; Proposition 2 shows that higher public-signal quality amplifies favorable and unfavorable news in different regions.; Proposition 3 separates the effects of analyst consensus and dispersion on disclosure; conditional on sufficiently high ex ante cash-flow uncertainty, Proposition 4 shows how analyst precision and coverage affect disclosure depending on interim default risk.; Appendices verify the cutoff result and examine endogenous financing, unlimited liability, and prefinancing disclosure.
- **Caveat:** The main model is static and postfinancing, treats debt face value and the manager's information-arrival probability as exogenous, assumes a perfectly informative private signal when information arrives, and imposes a specific t-distribution structure linking signal surprises to cash-flow variance. Investors are risk neutral and competitive, and strategic behavior among analysts is abstracted away. Appendices relax some liability and financing assumptions but not all of these restrictions.

### A Theory of Front-Line Management

Daniel Bird; Alexander Frug (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.08424](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08424). First published online: 2025-12-18.

- **Question:** How can front-line managers use small, nonwage, perishable perks to motivate extra effort, and when do their information and relative impatience generate conditional rewards or informal seniority systems?
- **Players:** front-line manager who benefits from worker effort and controls perishable compensation; worker who chooses effort and bears its cost; organization as an extension-level designer that evaluates payoff streams and chooses the manager's effective discount rate
- **Timing:** At the start, the manager commits to a history-dependent work schedule and compensation policy. Over an infinite continuous-time horizon, opportunities arrive according to a Poisson process. If an opportunity arrives, the worker chooses effort; at every instant, the manager's committed policy specifies a bounded flow compensation. Under observable opportunities, the manager observes arrival and effort; under concealable opportunities, only effort is public and the worker can hide an opportunity by exerting zero effort.
- **Actions:** manager commits to a history-dependent required-effort schedule; manager commits to a flow-compensation policy bounded between zero and one; worker exerts zero, partial, or full effort when an opportunity arrives; worker may conceal a privately observed opportunity by choosing zero effort; organization chooses the manager's effective discount rate in the organizational-design extension
- **Information:** Worker effort is perfectly observed under both information structures.; Opportunity arrivals are either publicly observed by the manager or privately observed and concealable by the worker.; Histories of observed arrivals and effort determine continuation promises and policies.; The Poisson process makes past private opportunity information payoff irrelevant once histories advance.; Model primitives and discount rates are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** The manager chooses an incentive-compatible dynamic contract to maximize the expected discounted benefit from effort at opportunity times net of the discounted flow cost of compensation.
- **Representative equation:** `$V_M = E[sum_k exp(-r_m T_k) B alpha(h_Tk) - integral_0^infinity exp(-r_m t) phi(h_t) dt]$ (Section 2 payoff primitives and contract definition, printed pp. 4-5 (PDF pp. 4-5), with the discounted-payoff representation made explicit in Appendix A)
- **Equilibrium:** Manager-optimal incentive-compatible dynamic contract
- **Solution:** With observable opportunities, a patient manager uses finite conditional promises that reset after new effort, whereas an impatient manager creates a tenure-based seniority path. With concealable opportunities, a patient manager accumulates promises and cycles between full and reduced effort; an impatient manager creates performance-based seniority, with two or three tiers depending on relative impatience. Lumpier opportunities lower managerial value, information frictions can benefit an organization with different intertemporal preferences, and the organization may optimally shift the manager's effective discount rate toward the worker's.
- **Evidence:** Proposition 1 shows that a patient manager facing observable opportunities uses resettable conditional promises and a constant effort requirement.; Proposition 2 shows that an impatient manager facing observable opportunities uses a tenure-based system that progresses from work without perks to perks with work and finally perks without work.; For concealable opportunities, Lemma 1 reduces the optimal contract to effort and compensation thresholds in the worker's continuation utility.; Propositions 3-5 show accumulating promises and nonmonotonic effort for a patient manager and performance-based seniority for an impatient one.; Proposition 6 shows that lumpier opportunities reduce the manager's value except under observable opportunities with equal discount rates; Proposition 7 characterizes the organization's preferred manager discount rate in the organizational-design extension.
- **Caveat:** The model has one manager and one worker, linear effort and perk payoffs, exogenous Poisson opportunities, perfectly observed effort, stationary exponential discounting, and a manager with full commitment to a highly stylized bounded flow perk. Teams, endogenous opportunities, hidden effort, type uncertainty, promotions, and most intertemporal consequences of perks are omitted. The paper argues that relational contracts and costly storage preserve the qualitative mechanisms, but the exact contracts change.

### Platform Expansion Through Asset Provision: Ownership, Commitment, and Flexibility

Heikki Peura; S. Alex Yang (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.00170](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00170). First published online: 2025-12-24.

- **Question:** When should a service platform expand capacity by financing provider-owned assets, employing providers with platform-owned assets, or renting assets to independent providers?
- **Players:** a service platform; a continuum of prospective new service providers; a competitive bank
- **Timing:** In the investment stage, the platform selects an asset-provision mechanism, expansion quantity and long-term terms; prospective providers choose the platform program or bank financing, and the competitive bank decides whether to lend at a break-even rate. In the operating stage, the platform first sets customer price and provider wage. Each new provider's outside option is revealed only after the wage is set; providers then choose platform work or the outside option, productivity is realized, and any loan repayment or default occurs.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses mechanism, investment quantity, contract terms, service price and provider compensation; prospective providers choose a platform program, bank financing when available, and platform versus outside work; the bank supplies a loan only when expected repayment breaks even
- **Information:** The mechanism, contract terms and demand primitives are common knowledge.; A provider's outside option is unknown when the platform sets the wage and is revealed before the provider's operating participation decision.; Asset productivity is uncertain when investment and financing decisions are made.; Providers are symmetric ex ante, and the platform anticipates their aggregate supply response.
- **Objective:** Given available incumbent and newly induced capacity, the platform chooses its operating wage and customer price to maximize service margin times demand while satisfying the supply requirement.
- **Representative equation:** `$Pi_B(w,p)=D(p)(p-w)=(alpha-p)(p-w), subject to D(p)<=S_0+S(w)$ (Section 3, Equation (5), printed p. 5 / PDF p. 5)
- **Equilibrium:** Pareto-selected symmetric pure-strategy equilibrium solved by backward induction
- **Solution:** Simple interest-only platform financing often fails because providers can free ride, whereas tying repayment discounts to on-platform activity can restore value. Employment is preferred when demand is high and investment cost is low; financing or rental becomes more attractive as demand weakens or investment becomes costly. Under Proposition 11's conditions, a moderate minimum wage can expand feasible investment and can raise platform profit under platform financing or rental, even while benefiting providers. Employment gains ground when providers' outside opportunities depend less on access to the asset.
- **Evidence:** The platform chooses capacity expansion and contract terms before setting its operating price and wage.; Potential providers compare platform participation with heterogeneous outside options, and the bank lends only under its break-even condition.; Closed-form equilibrium comparisons identify when employment, financing or rental is preferred and how minimum wages alter commitment.
- **Caveat:** The baseline studies one platform under Assumptions 1-2, with deterministic linear demand, a uniform outside-option distribution, binary asset productivity, zero resale value, and an asset-dependent outside option. It abstracts from platform competition and provider price discretion, and the paper identifies empirical validation as future work; the mechanism rankings are therefore structural predictions rather than direct estimates.

### Spatial Information Sharing on On-Demand Service Platforms

Swanand Kulkarni; Basak Kalkanci (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2021.03426](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.03426). First published online: 2026-01-14.

- **Question:** How much spatial demand-supply information should an on-demand platform reveal so that drivers relocate without abandoning locally valuable demand?
- **Players:** an on-demand service platform precommitted to an information-sharing mechanism; drivers initially located in two nonsurge zones
- **Timing:** The platform is precommitted to truthful surge, full, or local disclosure. At the start of Stage 1, demand in all zones is realized and the selected policy releases its signal. Drivers simultaneously stay or relocate to Zone 3. Stayers can serve a Stage-1 request in their origin; movers incur their origin-specific cost and spend Stage 1 relocating, so they cannot serve then. In Stage 2, the same realized zone demands are matched against the updated driver pools, including arrivals in Zone 3.
- **Actions:** commit to surge, full, or local information sharing; stay in the initial zone; relocate to the surge zone
- **Information:** Initial driver supplies, relocation-cost parameters, and the demand distribution are common knowledge.; Surge sharing reveals the excess-demand zone to all drivers, full sharing reveals mismatch in all zones, and local sharing reveals the surge only to sufficiently nearby drivers.; Drivers observe the policy-released signal but not peers' contemporaneous relocation choices.; The platform truthfully reports the mismatch information specified by its mechanism.
- **Objective:** Each driver chooses stay or move to maximize expected net earnings, accounting for congestion from all drivers' relocation choices and subtracting the relevant relocation cost.
- **Representative equation:** `$choose move iff E[earnings in Zone 3 | signal, others' moves] - r_i >= E[earnings from staying in Zone i | signal, others' moves]$ (Section 3, driver decision problem, printed p. 6 / PDF p. 6; equilibrium indifference conditions (3)-(4), printed p. 7 / PDF p. 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Pure-strategy driver-relocation equilibrium under each information-sharing mechanism
- **Solution:** In the rational benchmark, full information has lower expected matching efficiency than surge disclosure when relocation costs are low, because surge already attracts enough drivers and revealed favorable origin demand can keep some drivers away from Zone 3; as costs rise, full information can outperform surge. Local disclosure never strictly dominates the public mechanisms in that benchmark: it is strictly dominated by full or surge when nearby supply is limited and otherwise is weakly dominated by, or ties, surge. In the laboratory, drivers overrelocate relative to theory under surge and local disclosure. Overall efficiency is marginally below theory under surge, marginally above under full, and significantly above under local; full performs marginally better than surge and local is statistically comparable to surge. A fitted behavioral equilibrium with loss aversion through mental accounting and decision errors describes these deviations better than the rational model.
- **Evidence:** Drivers start in two nonsurge zones and choose whether to relocate to a third zone with excess demand.; Earnings from staying or moving depend on local demand, driver supply, and how many peers relocate.; The platform commits to truthful surge, full, or distance-targeted local information.; Laboratory choices are compared with rational equilibria and a behavioral specification featuring loss aversion, mental accounting, and decision errors.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses three stylized zones, homogeneous driver cohorts within origins, independent uniform demand held fixed across two stages, fixed surge-payment rules, truthful platform messages, a stay-versus-one-destination action, and no endogenous information-policy choice, commission, learning, or repeated relocation. Laboratory behavior may not transport directly to professional drivers or real spatial networks, and the behavioral specification is one of several possible explanations for overrelocation.

### Optimal Contests with Negative Prizes: Theory and Experiment

Lingbo Huang; Jingjing Zhang; Jun Zhang (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2023.03580](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03580). First published online: 2026-02-04.

- **Question:** Can a contest designer use entry fees and negative prizes to maximize both the winner's effort and total participation effort?
- **Players:** a contest designer; N privately informed contestants
- **Timing:** The designer commits to an entry fee, effort reserve, and shared prize. Contestants privately observe ability and simultaneously choose whether to enter and, if entering, how much effort to exert. Prizes depend on whether the highest effort meets the reserve.
- **Actions:** the designer chooses entry fee, reserve effort, and below-reserve shared prize; contestants choose entry; entrants choose effort
- **Information:** Contestant ability is private and i.i.d.; The ability distribution, prize budget, cost technology, and liability bound are common knowledge.; The baseline designer knows the common liability level.
- **Objective:** The designer chooses a modified all-pay contest to maximize either expected total effort or expected winner effort.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{(E,\widehat e,S)}\ \mathbb E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N} e_i\right]\quad\text{or}\quad\max_{(E,\widehat e,S)}\ \mathbb E\left[\max_i e_i\right]$ (Section 2 and Proposition 1, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 4), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric Bayesian all-pay contest equilibrium with endogenous entry
- **Solution:** The optimal entry fee always equals liability, and the reserve is weakly higher than without negative prizes. If liability exceeds the derived threshold, one contest maximizes both total and winner effort; below it, numerical differences across the two optimal designs remain under 8.4% in the reported simulations. In the lab, High_TW raises winner effort by 45.8% versus Zero_W and total effort by 48.5% versus Zero_T. Aggregate effort tracks theory, but low-ability entry is much lower than predicted; risk aversion, negative entry experience, and beliefs about competition explain much of the deviation.
- **Evidence:** Proposition 1 derives the optimal modified all-pay contest for total-effort and winner-effort objectives.; Proposition 2 gives full-participation equilibrium effort and monotonicity in liability.; Eighteen sessions with 432 subjects compare six treatments; an additional forced-entry treatment diagnoses behavioral deviations.
- **Caveat:** The baseline assumes risk neutrality, i.i.d. one-dimensional ability, symmetric mechanisms, a common publicly known liability, and small contests. The experiment uses undergraduate subjects and groups of three; low-type participation departs sharply from equilibrium. Heterogeneous private liabilities create a multidimensional mechanism-design problem left for future work.

### An Economic Analysis of Online Ad Fraud Deterrence

Min Chen; Subodha Kumar; Abhishek Ray (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2022.02201](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.02201). First published online: 2026-02-06.

- **Question:** How should an ad network coordinate publisher payments and fraud-detection strictness, and can removing malicious publishers backfire?
- **Players:** an ad network; malicious and nonmalicious publishers; advertisers
- **Timing:** The ad network first chooses publisher payments and detection sensitivities. Publishers then decide participation and, if malicious, fraud quantity. Valid and charged traffic are realized; advertisers update per-unit valuation from campaign performance, and payoffs follow.
- **Actions:** the ad network chooses payments by classified publisher type; the ad network chooses detection configurations; nonmalicious publishers choose participation; malicious publishers choose fraud traffic; advertisers update ad valuation
- **Information:** Publisher type is imperfectly classified.; Traffic-level fraud detection is imperfect and summarized by an ROC curve.; Advertisers observe charged traffic and assess valid traffic to update valuation.; Whitelisted nonmalicious publishers are known with certainty.
- **Objective:** The ad network chooses publisher payments and type-specific fraud-detection configurations to maximize ad revenue plus retained penalties minus the cost of mislabeling valid traffic.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p_W,\{p_j,s_j\}_{j\in\{M,N\}}}\ \pi=(\widetilde v-p_W)n_{gW}+\sum_j(\widetilde v-p_j)[n_{gj}(1-y_j)+n_{fj}(1-s_j)]+\theta w\sum_j p_j\left(s_jn_{fj}+y_j\sum_i n_{gij}\right)-k\sum_j y_jn_{gj}p_j$ (Equation (6), printed p. 10 (PDF p. 10), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium of the three-stage ad-network game
- **Solution:** Better detection always induces stricter configurations, but equilibrium publisher payments can rise or fall. More efficient fraud generation likewise calls for stricter detection and can optimally be paired with higher payments when detection quality is high. Although marginal returns to detection quality can diminish, better fraud-generation technology amplifies the value of continued detection investment. Removing malicious publishers can increase remaining publishers' fraud enough to raise total fraud and can reduce network profit under stated conditions.
- **Evidence:** Equations (1)-(6) specify publisher utilities, fraud technology, advertiser valuation updating, and the ad network's profit.; Lemma 1 characterizes interior and boundary equilibrium configurations.; Propositions 1-5 study technology quality, fraud-generation efficiency, investment returns, malicious-publisher exclusion, fraud volume, and network profit.
- **Caveat:** The main results use binary publisher types, a whitelist, uniform reservation utilities, quadratic fraud cost, a linear ROC approximation, interior participation/configuration conditions, and one coordinating network. Publisher competition, repeated enforcement, endogenous technology investment cost, advertiser strategic contracting, and empirical validation are left for future work.

### Multidimensional Signaling with Supplier Credit Guarantees

Huihui Liu; Haotian Song; Wenqiang Xiao (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.07052](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07052). First published online: 2026-02-06.

- **Question:** When should an informed supplier guarantee a capital-constrained buyer's bank loan, and how can the guarantee credibly signal buyer quality without distorting operations?
- **Players:** an informed upstream supplier; a capital-constrained downstream buyer; a competitive bank
- **Timing:** The supplier observes buyer type and offers wholesale price and guarantee. The bank observes the contract, updates beliefs, and quotes a break-even interest schedule. The buyer chooses order quantity and borrows; production then succeeds or fails, determining repayment and guarantee liability.
- **Actions:** the supplier chooses wholesale price and guarantee; the bank forms a belief and sets break-even interest; the buyer chooses order quantity and loan size
- **Information:** Buyer success type is known to the supplier but hidden from the bank.; The bank observes the contract and updates by Bayes' rule.; The buyer's type and contract are common knowledge between supplier and buyer.
- **Objective:** Given bank belief and the buyer's best-response order, the supplier chooses wholesale price and guarantee to maximize sales profit net of expected guarantee and financing costs.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{w,G}\ \Pi_{i\tau}(w,G)=(w-c)q^*_{i\tau}-(1-\beta_i)\left[\min\{wq^*_{i\tau},G\}+h\left(\min\{wq^*_{i\tau},G\}-(w-c)q^*_{i\tau}\right)^+\right]$ (Supplier profit displayed in Section 3, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 6), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Refined perfect Bayesian signaling equilibrium
- **Solution:** Under complete information, guarantees increase quantity holding price fixed, but the supplier responds with a higher wholesale price; a positive guarantee never strictly improves operational efficiency and is strictly worse when supplier financing cost is positive. Under asymmetry, wholesale price alone supports a refined pooling equilibrium, whereas adding guarantees yields a refined separating equilibrium with a partial or full guarantee. The high type can keep wholesale price at its full-information optimum and distort only the guarantee. Guarantee adoption is not uniformly win-win: supplier and buyer gains depend on financing cost, prior belief, and product profitability.
- **Evidence:** Section 4 solves the complete-information partial- and full-guarantee benchmark.; Propositions 2-3 characterize the refined pooling equilibrium with wholesale price alone and separating equilibrium with a guarantee.; Propositions 4-9 compare supplier and buyer welfare, portfolio choices, differentiated demand, and trade credit.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses exogenous default risk independent of order quantity, two buyer types, linear demand with zero revenue in failure, a competitive risk-neutral bank, and wholesale-price/guarantee contracts. Endogenous default, revenue sharing, sales rebates, richer contracts, and continuous multidimensional private information are left for future work.

### A Note on “Corporate Provision of Public Goods”

Thomas Eichner; Mark Schopf (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2025.03558](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03558). First published online: 2026-02-11.

- **Question:** Does delegating shareholders' public-good contributions through a company necessarily make citizens willing to fund the venture in refined equilibrium?
- **Players:** N citizens choosing venture shares or bonds; a manager acting for n shareholders; N-n bondholders contributing individually to the public good
- **Timing:** At Stage 1, each citizen invests one dollar either in the venture or in a bond. The company is founded if at least n citizens invest; if more than n do so, n investors are randomly selected as shareholders and all others are bondholders. At Stage 2, the manager chooses the firm's public-good contribution on the n shareholders' behalf while the N-n bondholders simultaneously choose individual contributions. The game is solved backward, and the funding subgame is refined by trembling-hand perfection.
- **Actions:** fund the venture and become a shareholder; purchase bonds and remain a bondholder; choose the manager's corporate public-good contribution; choose an individual bondholder contribution
- **Information:** Citizens are identical and utility and budget primitives are common knowledge.; The number of shareholders n and the continuation-game consequences of funding are anticipated at Stage 1.; Manager and bondholders observe the established ownership structure before contributing simultaneously.; There is no private information in the baseline.
- **Objective:** In the continuation game, the manager chooses the corporate contribution to maximize aggregate shareholder utility, while each bondholder chooses an individual contribution to maximize own utility subject to the relevant budget.
- **Representative equation:** `$max_alpha sum_{j in N\B} u(c_j, alpha+sum_{i in B} beta_i) s.t. sum_{j in N\B} c_j+alpha=n*pi; each i in B maximizes u(c_i,alpha+sum beta_j) s.t. c_i+beta_i=pi$ (Section 2.1, printed p. 2 / PDF p. 2)
- **Equilibrium:** Trembling-hand perfect funding equilibrium followed by a Nash public-good equilibrium
- **Solution:** With positive bondholder contributions, corporate delegation makes the shareholders' per-capita contribution exceed both the funded-equilibrium and business-as-usual bondholder contributions, but remaining bondholders free ride because contributions are strategic substitutes.
