- **Actions:** seller selects the price increment and runs the descending procedure; agents report demanded or strictly preferred objects; the mechanism lowers personalized prices; the mechanism reallocates objects along improvement cycles
- **Information:** Each agent privately knows a classical utility function over objects and discrete payments.; The price grid and auction rules are common knowledge.; The mechanism elicits partial demand information rather than full utility functions.; The seller need not assume quasilinear utility but uses a domain-wide wealth-effect bound for incentive guarantees.
- **Objective:** At a discrete price vector, an agent demands any object that beats nonparticipation and remains optimal even when every alternative object is made one price increment more expensive.
- **Representative equation:** `$D_i^epsilon(p) = {ell in L: u_i(ell,p_ell) >= u_i(0,0) and u_i(ell,p_ell) >= u_i(ell',p_ell' + epsilon) for every ell' in M}$ (Section 2.2, discrete demand set, PDF p. 6, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Tight equilibrium implemented by a sequential descending-price auction
- **Solution:** The sequential descending auction reaches a tight equilibrium in finitely many steps. Tight-equilibrium allocations are efficient, prices remain within explicit geometric-in-d bounds of the continuous minimum-price benchmark, and any tight-equilibrium mechanism is bounded compensating strategy-proof; in the quasilinear case the manipulation bound becomes 2m epsilon.
- **Evidence:** Definition 7 refines discrete equilibrium by local connectedness and the absence of improvement cycles.; Theorem 1 proves that the sequential descending auction terminates finitely at a tight equilibrium.; Theorem 2 establishes efficiency of every tight-equilibrium allocation under the maintained assumptions.; Theorems 3 and 4 bound deviations from minimum equilibrium prices and establish bounded compensating strategy-proofness.
- **Caveat:** Efficiency and incentive guarantees rely on strict preferences, objects being strictly good, unit demand, and a fixed announced price increment. Variable increments and broader preference domains require modified analysis.

### Left-Digit Bias, Quality Choice, and Channel Coordination

Xuefeng Peng; Zemin (Zachary) Zhong (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2025.00771](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00771). First published online: 2026-07-17.

- **Question:** How should a manufacturer and retailer jointly adapt quality, wholesale price, and retail price when consumers underreact to right-hand price digits, and when does 99-ending rigidity worsen or alleviate double marginalization?
- **Players:** one upstream manufacturer; one downstream retailer; a unit mass of heterogeneous consumers whose purchase decisions generate demand
- **Timing:** The manufacturer first chooses product quality q and wholesale price w. Observing these choices, the retailer chooses the posted retail price p, represented by a left block n and right digits Delta. Consumers then decide whether to buy from their perceived price and quality. The manufacturer anticipates the retailer's best response, and the equilibrium is solved by backward induction.
- **Actions:** the manufacturer chooses product quality; the manufacturer chooses a linear wholesale price; the retailer chooses the left block and right digits of the retail price; consumers buy when perceived utility is nonnegative
- **Information:** The manufacturer and retailer know the demand, cost, and left-digit-bias parameters in the baseline.; Consumer willingness to pay theta is heterogeneous and uniformly distributed on [0,1], but the firms optimize against aggregate demand.; Consumers perceive the left block fully and discount the right digits according to lambda.; The manufacturer anticipates the retailer's retail-price best response.
- **Objective:** The retailer maximizes its downstream margin times demand over the retail price, while the manufacturer chooses quality and wholesale price to maximize its upstream margin times that same demand, anticipating the retailer's response.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{n\in\mathbb N^+,\,\Delta\in[0,1)}\pi_r^{DN}=(n+\Delta-w)\left(1-\frac{\widetilde p(n,\Delta,\lambda)}{q}\right);\qquad \max_{q,w}\pi_m^{DN}=(w-cq^2)\left(1-\frac{\widetilde p(n,\Delta,\lambda)}{q}\right)$ (Equations (4)-(5), printed p. 9 / PDF p. 9, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium of the manufacturer-retailer channel
- **Solution:** Left-digit bias raises optimal quality at interior prices but lowers it at 99-ending prices. Price rigidity at 99 endings makes cost shocks more likely to produce shrinkflation; in a decentralized channel, the manufacturer lowers quality and raises the wholesale price while the retail price stays fixed. At interior prices the bias can intensify double marginalization through a markup prisoner's dilemma, whereas a binding 99-ending retailer response can force a lower wholesale price and improve coordination. When lambda exceeds a threshold bounded above by 0.088, the full endogenous-quality model has only 99-ending pricing and both channel members outperform the rational benchmark. A consumer 'triple win' is possible only for a downward move to a lower 99-ending price under sufficiently mild bias; stronger bias induces larger quality cuts and lowers consumer surplus.
- **Evidence:** Equation (1) makes perceived price equal to the fully attended left block plus only a fraction of the right digits, creating a discrete demand change at integer thresholds.; Equations (4)-(5), printed p. 9 / PDF p. 9, give the retailer's retail-price objective and the manufacturer's quality-and-wholesale-price objective; the paper explicitly solves the decentralized channel by backward induction.; Lemma 3 characterizes the retailer-price equilibrium conditional on exogenous quality, including interior and 99-ending regimes and the manufacturer's wholesale-price response.; Lemma 4 and Proposition 3 endogenize manufacturer quality; above a bias threshold whose upper bound is 0.088, only a 99-ending equilibrium arises and both channel members earn more than in the rational benchmark.; Proposition 1 and Corollary 8 show that 99-ending price rigidity redirects cost-shock adjustment toward quality; in the decentralized channel, the manufacturer lowers quality and raises the wholesale price while the retail price remains fixed.
- **Caveat:** The exact regime boundaries rely on a stylized uniform-WTP demand system, a single manufacturer and retailer, a linear wholesale contract, and a particular baseline perceived-price function. Many threshold derivations are placed in the online appendix rather than the downloaded main article. The main paper reports robustness to a generalized perception function and discusses menu costs, but no new empirical test establishes that left-digit bias is the principal cause of observed shrinkflation.

### Credit Ratings and Investments

Anna Bayona; Oana Peia; Razvan Vlahu (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.06886](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06886). First published online: 2026-07-28.

- **Question:** Do potentially inflated credit ratings improve or distort capital allocation when bond investors must coordinate, and through which beliefs do ratings affect investment?
- **Players:** credit rating agency observing firm fundamentals; firm issuing bonds and choosing low-risk, high-risk, or default; continuum of privately informed investors in theory and groups of five in the experiment
- **Timing:** At t=0 the CRA observes fundamentals theta and, when present, assigns a rating. Investors observe independent noisy private signals and the public rating, then simultaneously buy or decline the bond. At t=1 the firm uses internal and external funds to choose the low-risk project, high-risk project, or default. At t=2 project cash flow and bond repayment are realized.
- **Actions:** CRA chooses rating 0, q, or p; investors choose whether to buy the bond; firm chooses low-risk project, high-risk project, or default; experimental investors state beliefs about fundamentals and peers' investment
- **Information:** The CRA perfectly observes fundamentals and anticipates the firm's strategy.; Each investor sees x_j=theta+epsilon_j but not theta.; The rating, if provided, is a public signal observed by all investors.; Investor actions are strategic complements because financing changes the firm's feasible project.; The firm observes total available financing before choosing its project.
- **Objective:** Given external financing generated by investor coordination, the firm chooses the low-risk project, high-risk project, or default to maximize expected payoff.
- **Representative equation:** `$u_F = p[V-I+K(theta)-W(theta)F] for LR; q[H+K(theta)-W(theta)F] for HR; 0 for default, where K(theta)=theta+W(theta)B$ (Section 2.1.2, Equations (2)-(3), PDF p. 4, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Unique monotone perfect Bayesian threshold equilibrium
- **Solution:** Potentially inflated ratings increase investor coordination and external funding. Good ratings induce both more efficient low-risk projects and some inefficient high-risk gambling by weak firms, whereas bad ratings coordinate noninvestment and curtail risky financing. In the experiment the overall real effect is positive, driven primarily by beliefs about peers' behavior rather than beliefs about fundamentals.
- **Evidence:** Without a CRA, Theoretical Prediction 1 gives a unique investor-signal and firm-fundamental cutoff equilibrium.; With a CRA, Theoretical Prediction 2 adds an equilibrium p-or-zero rating rule and new investor and firm thresholds.; The five-player experiment runs 15 independent random-matching rounds in baseline and CRA treatments.; Ratings mainly move investment through beliefs about other investors, producing both beneficial low-risk investment and harmful gambling-for-resurrection effects, with positive effects dominant overall.
- **Caveat:** Laboratory behavior is not quantitatively extrapolated to real bond markets; the elicited beliefs were not incentivized, the simplified theory does not reproduce every focal effect of bad ratings, and the study does not compare potentially inflated ratings with a fully accurate rating regime.

### Information Asymmetry at Debt Rollover and Startup Loans

Chong Huang; Fei Li; Haibo Xu (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mnsc.2024.07999](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07999). First published online: 2026-07-30.

- **Question:** How much project-quality information should be disclosed when a startup rolls over debt so that it can raise the most initial funding without sacrificing more social welfare than necessary?
- **Players:** entrepreneur seeking a startup loan and later choosing effort; initial winning creditor that becomes a privately informed insider; continuum of outside creditors competing to refinance
- **Timing:** Before financing, a regulator or third-party intermediary commits to a monotone public signal structure. At day 0, the entrepreneur needs B and creditors simultaneously offer startup loans; the lowest requested day-1 repayment wins and that creditor becomes the insider. At day 1, project quality p and independent creditor liquidity shocks are realized; the entrepreneur and insider observe p, whereas outsiders observe only signal s. Outsiders simultaneously make refinancing offers, and an unshocked insider then matches the lowest outside offer or exits, or sets its own offer when no outsider participates. If refinancing succeeds, the day-1 loan is repaid and production continues. At day 2, the entrepreneur works or shirks; cash flow and limited-liability repayments are realized.
- **Actions:** the signal designer selects a monotone disclosure rule; creditors choose whether and on what repayment terms to offer the startup loan; outside creditors choose refinancing offers after observing the public signal; the unshocked insider matches, exits, or sets a monopoly refinancing offer; the entrepreneur chooses whether to incur the effort cost
- **Information:** Project quality p is drawn from a continuous distribution G on [0,1] and is realized at day 1.; The entrepreneur and the insider observe p perfectly; outsiders observe only the public signal sigma(p).; The insider observes the lowest outside refinancing offer before responding, while outsiders do not observe whether the insider received a liquidity shock.; Outsiders update beliefs about p by Bayes' rule from the common signal structure.; Loan terms, the prior, effort technology, and liquidity-shock probability are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** Choose the pass-or-fail quality threshold, together with the supporting short-term loan contract, to maximize cash-flow pledgeability and therefore the entrepreneur's borrowing capacity.
- **Representative equation:** `$p_T^* in arg max_{p_T in [c/v,1]} V(p_T), where V(p_T) = integral_{p_T}^1 p(v-c/p_T)dG(p) + (1-lambda) integral_{c/v}^{p_T} (pv-c)dG(p)$ (Proposition 3, Equation (2), printed p. 8 / PDF p. 8, visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Perfect Bayesian equilibrium of the startup-loan and debt-rollover game
- **Solution:** Among all monotone disclosures, a minimally informative pass-or-fail signal maximizes borrowing capacity. A pass pools p at or above p_T, attracts outside refinancing, and induces effort at exactly the same threshold; a fail deters outsiders and leaves refinancing to an unshocked insider. The optimal p_T^* balances the rent-preserving benefit of a stricter pass against the extra liquidation risk. It falls when liquidity shocks become more likely, rises with effort cost, and borrowing capacity falls with both parameters. In the no-moral-hazard and no-liquidation-risk polar cases, nonrevealing disclosure is optimal, although it induces opposite outsider participation. For any B no greater than maximum capacity, the smallest p_T(B) satisfying B = V(p_T) also maximizes welfare; this threshold rises with B, lambda, and c, while welfare falls.
- **Evidence:** Section 2 defines creditor and entrepreneur behavior strategies, Bayesian updating by outsiders, and perfect Bayesian equilibrium E(B; sigma).; Proposition 3 proves that, among monotone signal structures, a binary pass-or-fail signal with an optimally chosen quality threshold maximizes borrowing capacity.; Lemmas 1-2 decompose the informed creditor's equilibrium return with and without outsider participation and support the pooling argument behind the optimal binary signal.; Proposition 5 shows that for every feasible borrowing need, a borrowing-dependent pass-or-fail threshold also maximizes the entrepreneur's ex ante payoff and social welfare.; Corollaries 1-2 trace how liquidity-shock risk, effort cost, and borrowing need change the optimal threshold, borrowing capacity, and welfare.
- **Caveat:** The main result is proved within weakly increasing, right-continuous signal structures and treats the regulator or intermediary's disclosure rule as committed and exogenous to the game players. The baseline assumes short-term debt, zero liquidation value, risk neutrality, no discounting, homogeneous competitive creditors, independent liquidity shocks, and an insider second-mover and tie-breaking advantage. The downloaded main article describes but does not contain the online-appendix proofs and extensions to long-term loans, renegotiation, public shocks, and nonmonotone signals. The numerical figure is illustrative rather than empirical validation.

## Marketing Science

### The Role of Messenger in Advertising Content: Bayesian Persuasion Perspective

Jiwoong Shin; Chi-Ying Wang (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0405](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0405). First published online: 2024-01-16.

- **Question:** How should a firm jointly choose an advertising messenger and product price when messenger type changes the product-match signal structure and consumers must pay a deliberation cost to process the ad?
- **Players:** a monopolistic firm; a unit mass of consumers with latent product-match values; Nature, which draws match values and private ad signals
- **Timing:** Stage 0: Nature draws each consumer's match value. Stage 1: the firm chooses a high- or low-type messenger and a price. Stage 2: after observing messenger and price, each consumer decides whether to incur the deliberation cost and attend to the ad; an attentive consumer receives a private good or bad match signal. Stage 3: the consumer updates beliefs and decides whether to buy. The firm anticipates these downstream responses.
- **Actions:** the firm chooses messenger type m_j in {m_L,m_H}; the firm chooses product price p; consumers choose whether to pay attention to the ad; consumers choose whether to purchase after any Bayesian updating
- **Information:** The match-value distribution F and production cost k are common knowledge, but neither the firm nor consumers initially know an individual's realized match value.; Messenger type and price are observed costlessly before the attention decision.; An attentive consumer privately observes a binary product-match signal and updates by Bayes' rule.; The firm knows each messenger's signal technology but observes neither consumer attention nor realized private signals.
- **Objective:** The firm chooses price and messenger to maximize expected unit margin times the demand induced by consumers' attention and purchase rules.
- **Representative equation:** `$\mathbb{E}\Pi=D(p,m_j)\cdot(p-k)$ (Equation (10), printed p. 851 (PDF p. 12))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the sequential messenger-price, attention, and purchase game
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 links relative signal elasticity to posterior informativeness. Lemmas 1-3 derive attention and price thresholds. Propositions 2 and 3 show which messenger commands the larger price premium with and without attention. Proposition 4 gives the main profit-maximizing coverage and messenger regions: high production cost favors attention and a higher price, while higher deliberation cost makes full coverage more attractive; a low-type messenger can be optimal when a high type's generally positive signals obscure match information.
- **Evidence:** Closed-form Bayesian updating, attention thresholds, price thresholds, and profit comparisons; Section 4 uses two binary-signal examples to illustrate when high- or low-type messengers dominate
- **Caveat:** The focal model is a monopoly, single-product setting with two exogenously available messenger signal technologies, no initial private product information, homogeneous deliberation cost, and rational Bayesian consumers. The paper explicitly leaves brand positioning and target-audience fit outside the model, and notes that its clean rankings rely on particular global relationships between the two signal-elasticity functions.

### Peer-to-Peer Markets with Bilateral Ratings

T. Tony Ke; Monic Sun; Baojun Jiang (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0158](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0158). First published online: 2024-03-01.

- **Question:** How do bilateral ratings that reveal provider quality and customer service cost reshape application sorting, provider pricing, platform commission revenue, and competition relative to unilateral provider ratings?
- **Players:** high- and low-quality service providers; customers heterogeneous in cost to serve
- **Timing:** First, all providers simultaneously post publicly observed prices. Second, all customers simultaneously submit at most one application, using mixed application strategies when indifferent. Third, each capacity-one provider receiving applications accepts the lowest-cost applicant. Service is delivered and the provider pays commission delta to the platform. The game is solved backward in symmetric large-market equilibrium.
- **Actions:** providers choose posted prices; customers choose whether and to which provider type to apply; providers select the lowest-cost applicant when oversubscribed
- **Information:** Under bilateral ratings, provider quality q and each customer's service-cost type theta are publicly revealed.; All posted prices are observed before customers apply.; Agents know the population distributions, quality shares, customer-provider ratio, and commission rate.; Under the unilateral-rating benchmark, provider quality remains observable but customer service cost is not, forcing random applicant selection.
- **Objective:** A provider of type j chooses its posted price to maximize expected transaction margin, integrating over the density of the lowest-cost applicant it ultimately accepts.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_j^0(p_j^0;p_H,p_L)=\int_{\theta^0}^{\bar{\theta}}\left[(1-\delta)p_j^0-\theta g(q_j)\right]\left(-\frac{db_j^0(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)d\theta$ (Equation (4), printed p. 1085 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric pure-strategy Nash pricing equilibrium with directed-search application and acceptance subgames
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 characterizes cost-based application segmentation. Propositions 2 and 3 establish multiple bilateral-rating price equilibria and the associated queues, acceptance rates, and customer utility. Proposition 4 shows the pricing game is supermodular: prices rise with market tightness n, fall with the high-quality share gamma, and for sufficiently large n fall with maximum service cost and commission. Proposition 5 gives a unique unilateral-rating equilibrium; numerical comparisons show bilateral ratings can segment customers, soften provider competition, and raise prices.
- **Evidence:** Large-market directed-search model with analytical customer application and provider pricing conditions; Numerical equilibrium comparisons for comparative statics and bilateral versus unilateral ratings
- **Caveat:** The main analysis is a one-shot, large-market approximation with capacity one, fully revealing and truthful bilateral ratings, complete market coverage, and exogenous platform commission. Several closed-form results require uniform service costs and sufficiently many customers. Provider and customer entry, optimal commission with endogenous entry, and a formal repeated matching game are outside the focal model.

### Media Formats of Advertising

Song Lin (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0356](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0356). First published online: 2024-03-07.

- **Question:** How should a medium allocate advertising and content over time when media technology constrains its control, consumers choose where to direct attention, and the medium cannot perfectly observe ad processing?
- **Players:** a medium that allocates advertising and media content; a consumer who allocates attention; an advertiser whose match value is monetized by the medium but who has no focal strategic action; Nature, which governs signal arrival, match realization, and random termination
- **Timing:** At each continuous time t, the medium chooses an allocation d(t) allowed by its format: simultaneous ad and content under static, either ad or content under sequential, or all three choices under interactive advertising. The consumer observes d(t) and chooses whether to attend to the ad, consume content, or take an outside option. A product-match signal may arrive while the ad is processed, after which attention and medium policy continue. The equilibrium solves the medium's allocation and the consumer's attention policy together.
- **Actions:** the medium chooses ad A, content M, or the option set {A,M}, subject to the format's feasible set; the consumer chooses attention to A, M, or outside option B when available; under interactive advertising the medium chooses a minimum forced-ad duration and when to introduce skip control
- **Information:** The consumer observes the medium's current allocation before choosing attention.; Static and sequential media do not observe the consumer's attention action; an interactive medium partially observes it after presenting a choice.; The medium never directly observes whether the product-match signal has arrived.; Signal arrival is stochastic with common-knowledge exponential rate lambda, and all players share discount or termination rate r.
- **Objective:** The medium extracts consumer and advertiser surplus and chooses an allocation policy to maximize discounted total value. Under static advertising and the attention condition lambda v_c>m, its advertising payoff has the following closed form; otherwise the ad-free payoff is m/r.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_{Static}^{*}=\int_0^{\infty}\left(v_c+v_a+\frac{m}{r}\right)e^{-rt}dF(t)=\frac{\lambda[r(v_c+v_a)+m]}{r(\lambda+r)}$ (Equation (4), printed p. 1037 (PDF p. 7))
- **Equilibrium:** Continuous-time media-policy and consumer-attention equilibrium
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 says a static medium offers content with the ad exactly when lambda v_c>m and otherwise turns advertising off. Proposition 2 says a sequential medium runs no ad when lambda v_c<=b; otherwise it runs the ad first for S^*=max{lambda^{-1} ln[lambda(v_c+v_a)/m],0} and then supplies content. Lemma 4 and Proposition 4 show that an interactive medium imposes a positive minimum ad duration only when lambda v_c<m<lambda(v_c+v_a), then grants skip control; the forced duration is zero for highly informative ads. Proposition 5 ranks format profits: interactive equals static for highly informative ads, equals sequential for moderately informative ads, and all three coincide when advertising is too weak to use.
- **Evidence:** Continuous-time control and stopping analysis for static, sequential, and interactive advertising formats; Analytical format-profitability and consumer-externality comparisons
- **Caveat:** The paper explicitly describes the model as preliminary: it has one representative consumer, one advertiser and one medium, no consumer heterogeneity or product pricing, an exponential single-signal information process, and fully rational forward-looking attention. Competition among media, imperfect targeting, richer signal processes, fatigue, and interaction between ads and content remain outside the focal model.

### Self-Preferencing in E-Commerce Marketplaces: The Role of Sponsored Advertising and Private Labels

Fei Long; Wilfred Amaldoss (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0262](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0262). First published online: 2024-03-29.

- **Question:** When should an e-commerce marketplace place its private label in the sponsored top slot rather than auction that slot to third-party sellers, and how does this choice affect prices, platform revenue, sellers, and consumers?
- **Players:** an e-commerce platform that may sell a private label; two strategic third-party sellers; consumers with horizontally differentiated product preferences
- **Timing:** At T=0 the platform sets commission, decides whether to introduce a private label and sponsored slot, and if both exist whether to concede the slot or contest it for the private label. At T=1 each third-party seller chooses participation relative to its outside option. At T=2 participating sellers and the private label simultaneously set prices, and sellers submit ad-auction bids. At T=3 the second-price auction outcome is realized. At T=4 consumers observe listings and buy or exit. The platform anticipates all later subgames.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses commission, private-label entry, sponsored-slot availability, and whether to concede or contest the slot; third-party sellers choose whether to participate; the platform/private label and third-party sellers choose product prices; third-party sellers choose ad-auction bids; consumers choose among products in their consideration sets or the outside option
- **Information:** The platform publicly commits to marketplace configuration before seller participation and pricing.; Prices and the realized product ranking are observed before consumers purchase.; The distribution of consumer locations and consideration sets is common knowledge, while each consumer knows her own tastes and distances.; Each seller has an exogenous outside-option profit pi_0 and anticipates equilibrium demand, prices, and bids.
- **Objective:** In the contest subcase, the platform's total revenue is private-label sales revenue plus commission on the two third-party products; the private-label price is chosen anticipating the third-party sellers' simultaneous equilibrium prices.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_P^{Contest}=p_l^{Contest}D_l+2\phi p_i^{Contest}D_i$ (Section 4.4.2.2, printed p. 937 (PDF p. 13))
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction platform-configuration equilibrium with simultaneous pricing and locally envy-free auction bidding
- **Solution:** Lemmas 2-5 characterize equilibrium price rankings across advertising, private-label, concede, and contest subgames. Proposition 1 shows the platform concedes the slot when ad effectiveness alpha exceeds a threshold and self-preferences when alpha is lower, because ad and commission revenue can outweigh private-label margin. Proposition 2 shows self-preferencing lowers consumer surplus and has asymmetric effects on third-party sellers. Proposition 3 identifies when sponsored advertising and the private label are complements rather than substitutes for platform profit; later propositions show robustness to endogenous commission and model extensions.
- **Evidence:** Backward-induction analysis of platform design, seller participation, pricing, bidding, and consumer choice; Pure-strategy price equilibria paired with locally envy-free second-price auction bids
- **Caveat:** The focal model assumes a monopoly platform, two symmetric third-party sellers, one equally positioned private label, zero marginal costs, horizontal rather than vertical differentiation, a single prominent slot, and moderate product valuation. The authors explicitly leave platform competition, endogenous entry and product-line length, organic-ranking manipulation, richer private-label quality differences, and empirical testing for future work.

### Don’t Hurry, Be Happy! The Bright Side of Late Product Release

Mushegh Harutyunyan; Chakravarthi Narasimhan (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0393](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0393). First published online: 2024-04-30.

- **Question:** Can a firm profitably delay a ready product solely to soften later price competition, and how do consumer waiting, market growth, horizontal differentiation, and quality differences determine equilibrium release timing?
- **Players:** two competing durable-goods firms; first-period and second-period cohorts of forward-looking consumers
- **Timing:** The two firms first choose release periods R_i in {1,2} simultaneously. At the beginning of each period, all firms whose products have been released simultaneously choose current prices. Consumers entering that period observe current prices and buy, wait when feasible, or take the outside option. First-period consumers form expectations of second-period prices, and equilibrium requires those expectations to equal the subsequent price equilibrium.
- **Actions:** each firm chooses an early or late product-release period; released firms choose prices in each period; first-period consumers choose whether to buy now or wait; consumers choose which differentiated product to buy or whether to exit
- **Information:** Firms and consumers know the market primitives, release choices, current prices, and horizontal differentiation level.; Each consumer knows her own location and hence relative product fit.; First-period consumers do not observe future prices but form rational expectations that must equal equilibrium second-period prices.; The main model assumes firms correctly assess differentiation and consumers know their product preferences.
- **Objective:** In the asymmetric-release subgame, the early firm chooses its period-1 price to maximize profit over both periods, taking the consumer waiting cutoff and second-period equilibrium profits into account.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p_{11}\ge 0}\;\pi_1^{(1,2)}=\pi_{11}^{(1,2)}+\pi_{12}^{(1,2)},\qquad \pi_{11}^{(1,2)}=\alpha\hat d\,p_{11}$ (Section 4.2, printed p. 1195 (PDF p. 8))
- **Equilibrium:** Rational-expectations equilibrium of the release-timing and dynamic pricing game
- **Solution:** Lemmas 1-3 solve prices and profits for same-period and staggered release subgames. Proposition 1 shows late release occurs when the early-consumer share is not too high and horizontal differentiation is sufficiently strong but below the full-coverage bound; waiting then softens second-period price competition. Proposition 2 shows the late firm's profit can rise with the early-consumer share even as its sales fall, and Proposition 3 shows a larger early cohort can expand the late-entry region. Proposition 4 adds vertical differentiation: very large quality gaps induce both firms to enter early, whereas a moderate quality advantage can make the high-quality firm the late entrant.
- **Evidence:** Two-period Hotelling duopoly solved by backward induction with rational consumer expectations; Figures illustrate equilibrium price and profit regions for stated parameter values
- **Caveat:** The focal result requires a two-period durable-goods market with strategic consumer waiting, nonextreme horizontal differentiation, unit demand, and no resale. The paper states that the mechanism need not apply to very highly differentiated local monopolies or repeat-purchase categories. Used-goods markets, boundedly rational expectations, and price preannouncement are discussed as open extensions rather than solved in the main model.

### Designing Loot Boxes: Implications for Profits and Welfare

Jin Miao; Sanjay Jain (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0007](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0007). First published online: 2024-05-07.

- **Question:** How should a seller choose loot-box price and product-allocation probabilities, when will consumers repeatedly purchase, and when can probabilistic selling outperform deterministic pricing in profit and welfare?
- **Players:** a monopolist selling two symmetric products; loyal consumers in segments A and B; switcher consumers in segment M
- **Timing:** The firm first commits to a single loot-box price p and announced probability phi of product 1 (and 1-phi of product 2). Consumers observe the mechanism and decide whether to buy. After each purchase the product outcome is revealed; loyal consumers dynamically decide whether to stop or buy again, taking future repurchases into account, while switchers buy at most once in the focal profitable regime. The firm chooses p and phi anticipating these self-selection and continuation decisions.
- **Actions:** the firm chooses loot-box price p; the firm chooses allocation probability phi for product 1; consumers choose whether to make an initial purchase; loyal consumers choose after each realized outcome whether to repurchase or exit
- **Information:** The firm publicly preannounces truthful allocation probabilities, which consumers observe before purchase.; A consumer learns the exact product only after purchasing the loot box.; Consumers know their own segment and valuations and are rational and forward-looking in the main model.; The firm knows segment sizes and valuation parameters but cannot directly price discriminate by segment or condition price on purchase history.
- **Objective:** The firm maximizes expected revenue from repeated purchases by the two loyal segments and one purchase by switchers, subject to incentive constraints that make each loyal segment repurchase and switchers willing to buy.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{\phi,p}\;\pi(\phi,p)=\frac{\alpha p}{\phi}+\frac{\alpha p}{1-\phi}+(1-2\alpha)p\quad\text{s.t. }p\le\phi(v-w),\;p\le(1-\phi)(v-w),\;p\le\beta$ (Equations (13)-(16), printed p. 1247 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Incentive-compatible loot-box mechanism with optimal sequential consumer repurchase
- **Solution:** Lemma 1 solves the deterministic-pricing benchmark. Proposition 1 shows the optimal loot box uses equal probabilities when switcher value is high but can deliberately use asymmetric probabilities when switcher value is low. Proposition 2 identifies low less-preferred-product value and intermediate loyal-segment sizes and switcher values as conditions under which loot boxes earn more through time-based price discrimination and market expansion. Proposition 3 shows the base loot-box policy weakly raises social welfare and can raise consumer welfare. Extensions show addiction raises profit, positive production cost narrows the profitable region, longer product lines change optimal probability polarization, and a finite winning guarantee can raise profit while lowering consumer welfare.
- **Evidence:** Dynamic consumer value functions and incentive constraints for repeated loot-box purchase; Closed-form constrained optimization of price and allocation probability with welfare comparisons
- **Caveat:** The base model is a monopoly with two symmetric virtual products, zero marginal cost, three homogeneous segments, rational consumers, unlimited repeat-purchase budgets, truthful fixed odds, no resale, and no purchase-history pricing. The paper studies many robustness extensions, but competing loot-box sellers, multiple simultaneous loot-box designs, and empirical validation are explicitly left for future research.

### Dual Role and Product Featuring Strategy of Digital Platform

Ruitong Wang; Ye Qiu (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0338](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0338). First published online: 2024-05-17.

- **Question:** When a marketplace also sells its own product, how does that dual role alter which products it features, seller price competition, self-preferencing, and consumer welfare?
- **Players:** the monopoly digital platform, acting as marketplace operator and possibly private-label seller; third-party merchants with heterogeneous product fit probabilities; a representative consumer
- **Timing:** First, given the private-label fit, commission rate, and upper bound on merchant fit, the platform decides whether to feature its private label and selects featured third-party products. Second, featured sellers simultaneously choose prices. Third, the consumer costlessly learns the fit and price of featured products and chooses whether and from whom to buy. The authors solve the game by backward induction.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses its featuring set and whether to self-preference its private label; featured third-party merchants and the platform's private label choose prices, generally using mixed strategies; the consumer chooses a fitting product or exits
- **Information:** The platform and each merchant know merchant fit probabilities, but the consumer does not know fit before inspecting featured products.; The consumer observes realized fit and prices of featured products at the purchase stage.; The commission rate, fit ceiling, product valuation, and private-label fit are common model primitives.; The platform anticipates equilibrium seller pricing when it chooses the featuring set.
- **Objective:** Under sole-marketplace operation, the platform chooses the fit levels of two featured merchants to maximize expected commission revenue after accounting for their equilibrium mixed pricing.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{q_1,q_2}\; E\pi_l=\beta(1-q_2)(q_1+q_2)\quad\text{s.t. }0\le q_2\le q_1\le \bar q$ (Platform featuring problem immediately before Proposition 1, printed p. 1172 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect equilibrium with mixed-strategy seller pricing
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 shows that a marketplace-only platform may deliberately feature an inferior second merchant to soften price competition, creating intermediary bias. Proposition 2 characterizes when a dual-role platform features its private label and how the commission rate changes the rival it features. Proposition 3 shows dual role can either amplify or mitigate intermediary bias; Proposition 4 likewise finds that dual role can intensify rather than always soften price competition. Proposition 5 identifies regions in which dual role raises consumer welfare, so banning platform participation is not uniformly welfare improving.
- **Evidence:** Closed-form mixed-strategy pricing and featuring characterizations in the main model; Numerical region comparisons for prices and consumer welfare where closed-form signs are unavailable
- **Caveat:** The main model uses one representative consumer, zero production cost, an exogenous commission, a continuum of products summarized by exogenous fit probabilities, and prohibitive search cost outside the featured set. The sharp dual-role benchmark assumes perfect imitation by the private label. Extensions relax search and imitation assumptions, but the analysis remains a stylized one-category monopoly-platform model without empirical estimation; it does not endogenize merchant product innovation, the commission rate, or competition among platforms, which the authors identify as limitations.

### Agency Market Power and Information Disclosure in Online Advertising

W. Jason Choi; Amin Sayedi (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0039](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0039). First published online: 2024-06-03.

- **Question:** When should an online publisher disclose targeting information to an advertising agency, given that better information improves allocation but also lets the agency coordinate client bids more effectively and extract a larger share of auction surplus?
- **Players:** an online publisher that owns one advertising slot; an advertising agency representing delegated advertisers; three competing advertisers
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the publisher chooses reserve price R and information policy I. Stage 2: the agency sets fee F. Stage 3A: advertisers choose direct bidding, agency delegation, or nonparticipation. Stage 3B: the impression arrives and click-through rates are realized; they are privately known by the publisher under withholding and common knowledge under disclosure. Stage 4: the agency chooses which delegated bids to submit. Stage 5: the auction is run and payoffs are realized.
- **Actions:** the publisher chooses a reserve price and whether to disclose click-through-rate information; the agency sets an upfront delegation fee; each advertiser chooses whether to bid directly, delegate to the agency, or abstain; the agency chooses the subset of delegated advertiser bids submitted to the auction; participating advertisers bid in the publisher's auction
- **Information:** The publisher's reserve-price rule and disclosure policy are observed before the agency and advertisers act.; Advertiser click-through rates are binary random variables; under withholding they are privately observed by the publisher, whereas under disclosure they are common knowledge and usable for targeting.; Advertisers choose their bidding channels before the impression-specific click-through rates are realized.; The agency observes its clients and, when information is disclosed, can select the client with the highest realized click-through rate.
- **Objective:** When information is withheld and the agency submits one randomly selected client, its commission-relevant expected payoff is the expected auction surplus of that submitted advertiser; this payoff comparison drives random bid rotation.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_{ag}^{(1)}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\sigma-R\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\sigma-R\right)\mathbb{I}_{\{R\leq 1/2-\sigma\}}$ (Displayed agency payoff in Section 3.2.1, immediately before Proposition 1, printed p. 1286 (PDF p. 8); the paper suppresses the infinitesimal commission alpha in this expression.)
- **Equilibrium:** Pure-strategy subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium
- **Solution:** Without an agency, the publisher is indifferent between disclosure and withholding (Lemma 1). With an agency, withholding induces random bid rotation and an equilibrium with two delegating advertisers and one direct bidder (Lemma 2 and Proposition 1), whereas disclosure induces selective rotation and all three advertisers delegate, leaving auction density one (Lemma 3 and Proposition 2). Withholding is inefficient and its loss rises with sigma (Proposition 3). The publisher nevertheless withholds when sigma <= 1/22 to curb agency market power, and discloses otherwise when the efficiency gain dominates (Proposition 4). The analytical extensions preserve the central efficiency-versus-surplus-extraction tradeoff while changing threshold regions.
- **Evidence:** Pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibria are derived by backward induction for the no-agency benchmark and the agency game.; Analytical extensions cover campaign-management costs, first-price auctions, N advertisers, and heterogeneous per-click values correlated with click-through rates.
- **Caveat:** The main model is a stylized single-slot environment with one publisher, one agency, three symmetric advertisers, binary independent click-through rates, homogeneous per-click value, a second-price auction, an infinitesimal agency commission, and pure strategies. The paper analytically relaxes the auction format, number of advertisers, campaign-management costs, and the relationship between valuations and click-through rates, but it does not empirically estimate the magnitude of the predicted disclosure effects.

### On the Profitability of Loyalty

Ying Lei; Ji Shen; Ei Yang; Xin Zhai (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0109](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0109). First published online: 2024-06-11.

- **Question:** When does observed repeat-purchase loyalty increase firm profits, and how do switching costs, the strength of brand preferences, and the persistence of those preferences change equilibrium prices, switching, loyalty duration, and profit?
- **Players:** firm A selling one horizontally differentiated brand; firm B selling one horizontally differentiated brand; a unit mass of long-lived, forward-looking consumers
- **Timing:** The game repeats over an infinite horizon. In each period, consumer preferences either persist or change according to the specified stochastic process; the two firms simultaneously choose prices using open-loop strategies; each consumer observes current prices and chooses one brand, paying switching cost s if changing from the previously purchased brand. Purchases determine the next period's old- and new-buyer customer bases. The analysis focuses on a stationary symmetric steady state.
- **Actions:** each firm chooses its period price; each consumer chooses whether to remain with the previously purchased brand or switch to the rival brand; consumers condition purchase choices on current preference, prices, switching cost, and discounted continuation values
- **Information:** Current prices, switching cost, discount parameters, and the preference-transition process are common knowledge.; Consumers know their current preference type and previously purchased brand when choosing between firms.; Under global preference change, a fraction kappa redraws preference independently from the symmetric distribution F; under local change, future preference depends on current type through a Markov process.; Open-loop firm strategies depend on time rather than on a complete history of realized market states.
- **Objective:** Firm A chooses its entire open-loop price sequence to maximize its normalized infinite-horizon discounted revenue, with the customer base in each future period determined by equilibrium switching flows.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{\{p_A^{t+s}\}_{s=0}^{\infty}} \; \delta\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}(1-\delta)^s p_A^{t+s}N_A^{t+s}$ (Equation (7), printed p. 311 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric steady-state open-loop equilibrium
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 gives a unique symmetric price equilibrium and switching cutoff. Equation (17) turns equilibrium switching into average repeat-purchase duration. Proposition 2 shows that higher switching costs lengthen repeat purchases but lower equilibrium price and profit, so switching-cost-driven behavioral loyalty is unprofitable. Under global preference change, a more concentrated preference distribution raises loyalty but lowers profits (Proposition 3), while preference instability lowers price and has a U-shaped effect on loyalty (Proposition 4). The local-change analyses preserve the negative switching-cost result (Proposition 5) and show that strong, stable preferences can raise both loyalty and profits, whereas the loyalty effect of dispersion depends on the preference-transition regime (Proposition 6).
- **Evidence:** The continuous-type global-preference model yields analytical switching cutoffs, a unique symmetric price equilibrium, repeat-purchase duration, and comparative statics.; A three-type local-preference model provides further analytical comparisons, and a generalized continuous-type local model is examined numerically for finer comparative statics.
- **Caveat:** The focal results use a symmetric, fully covered duopoly with zero marginal cost, no price discrimination, long-lived consumers, and a stationary open-loop equilibrium. The conclusion notes that non-steady-state settings such as entry deterrence and asymmetric customer bases remain outside the analysis. Endnote 14 further cautions that open-loop equilibria are not necessarily subgame perfect; the paper can verify subgame perfection only under stated conditions in the tractable three-type extension.

### Overdiagnosis and Undertesting for Infectious Diseases

Tinglong Dai; Shubhranshu Singh (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0038](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0038). First published online: 2024-06-13.

- **Question:** Should a policymaker require a testing laboratory to report fine-grained viral-load information, and how do the laboratory's diagnostic cutoff and future capacity respond when positive diagnoses create contact-tracing demand but quarantining reduces organic infection-driven demand?
- **Players:** a policymaker choosing whether CT-value disclosure is mandatory; a commercial laboratory choosing disclosure, diagnostic cutoff, and future testing capacity; a physician who diagnoses in the patient's interest when the CT value is disclosed
- **Timing:** In period 1, the policymaker first chooses whether CT-value reporting is mandatory. The laboratory then chooses whether to disclose voluntarily, sets its diagnostic cutoff kappa_l when retaining the diagnosis right, and chooses period-2 capacity C_2. Patients are tested; if CT is disclosed, the physician applies cutoff kappa_p, otherwise the physician follows the laboratory's binary diagnosis; positive patients are quarantined. At the start of period 2, symptom and contact-tracing demand realizes. The laboratory again chooses disclosure and cutoff, testing and diagnosis occur, positive patients are quarantined, and payoffs are realized. The paper solves this sequential-move game by backward induction.
- **Actions:** the policymaker mandates or does not mandate CT-value reporting; the laboratory discloses the CT value or reports only a binary diagnosis; the laboratory chooses a CT cutoff when it retains diagnostic authority; the laboratory invests in period-2 testing capacity; the physician chooses a patient-welfare-maximizing CT cutoff when fine-grained information is available
- **Information:** The realized CT value x is private information of the laboratory unless it is disclosed on the test result.; The conditional CT distributions, disease and symptom parameters, payoff parameters, and policy are common knowledge.; The physician observes a disclosed CT value but otherwise observes only the laboratory's binary diagnosis and can decide whether following it minimizes expected diagnostic error cost.; The basic reproduction number R_0 and hence period-2 testing demand are uncertain when the laboratory chooses capacity.
- **Objective:** In period 1 the laboratory jointly chooses its diagnostic cutoff and future capacity to maximize expected net testing revenue less capacity-expansion cost and the expected patient costs of false-positive and false-negative diagnoses.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi(\kappa_l,C_2)=r\,\mathbb{E}\min\{C_2,z_1(\kappa_l)+z_2(\kappa_l)R_0\}-\gamma(C_2^2-C_1^2)-C_1\{c_{FP}H(\kappa_l)+c_{FN}[1-G(\kappa_l)]\}$ (Equation (15), printed p. 361 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium of the two-period sequential-move game
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 gives optimal capacity for an exogenous cutoff, and Proposition 2 jointly characterizes the laboratory's cutoff and capacity when it retains diagnosis rights. Under the sufficient contact-tracing condition, the laboratory chooses a cutoff above the patient-optimal cutoff, builds more capacity, and withholds CT information (Proposition 3). This overdiagnosis reduces tested-patient welfare (Proposition 4) and generates demand that even the higher capacity cannot fully absorb. Mandatory CT reporting raises tested-patient utility and service level but increases subsequent infection and lowers capacity (Proposition 5), explaining why a policymaker may initially decline to mandate disclosure. The prevalence-dependent and nonprofit extensions preserve the core overdiagnosis mechanism under their stated conditions.
- **Evidence:** A two-period sequential model is solved by backward induction to characterize diagnostic cutoff, disclosure, capacity, service level, and patient-welfare outcomes.; Real-world COVID-19 parameter estimates are used only to discuss plausibility of a sufficient condition; the paper does not estimate or calibrate the model.; Analytical extensions study a prevalence-dependent cutoff and a nonprofit unconstrained laboratory.
- **Caveat:** The model is a stylized two-period, single-laboratory setting with exogenous test price, no competition among laboratories, specific triangular CT distributions, random rationing under shortages, and an exogenous contact-tracing-demand intensity. The conclusion explicitly notes that the model does not separate organizational incentives from individual morality, does not model interactions between organic and induced testing demand, and leaves endogenous test pricing, laboratory heterogeneity, and empirical validation for future work.

### Competitive Model Selection in Algorithmic Targeting

Ganesh Iyer; T. Tony Ke (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0175](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0175). First published online: 2024-06-25.

- **Question:** How does market competition alter a firm's optimal choice between a flexible but high-variance targeting algorithm and a simpler, more biased but more predictable model?
- **Players:** two competing firms that choose algorithm designs and consumer targets
- **Timing:** The two firms first simultaneously choose private nonnegative Lasso tuning parameters. Each then receives an independent private data set, and its analyst computes penalized profitability estimates. Using those estimates and beliefs about the rival, the firms simultaneously choose which consumers to target; overlapping targets split their business between the firms.
- **Actions:** each firm selects a Lasso regularization parameter that determines model complexity and bias; each firm allocates a fixed targeting capacity across the two consumer segments
- **Information:** Each firm's tuning parameter and realized data set remain private throughout the game.; The private data sets are independent across firms, so a firm uses the prior rather than updating about its rival from its own realization.; Firms observe each consumer's binary characteristic before targeting and know the common distributions of segment profitability and estimation noise.; A firm anticipates the distribution of its rival's targeting action but not the rival's realized estimate.
- **Objective:** At the model-selection stage, each firm chooses its regularization parameter to maximize expected profit, taking the rival's equilibrium design and induced targeting distribution as given.
- **Representative equation:** `$\lambda_j^*=\arg\max_{\lambda_j}\Pi_j(\lambda_j),\qquad j=1,2.$ (Equation (13), p. 1234 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Bayesian Nash equilibrium in algorithm selection and targeting
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 establishes that a monopolist chooses λ=0, favoring an unbiased, flexible estimator despite greater variance. Proposition 2 shows that if a pure-strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium exists, the segment shares and targeting capacity are not knife-edge symmetric, and estimation noise is sufficiently high, at least one competing firm chooses λ>0. Corollary 1 implies positive regularization in a symmetric pure-strategy equilibrium. The mechanism is competition softening: regularization spreads targeting more evenly, reducing expected overlap. Numerical examples show regularization generally rises with data noise and is strongest where uniform targeting produces the largest overlap reduction.
- **Evidence:** Proposition 1 proves that a monopoly firm chooses zero regularization and therefore the most flexible, least biased model.; Equations (11) and (13) jointly determine targeting probabilities and regularization choices in Bayesian Nash equilibrium.; Proposition 2 proves that, under the stated asymmetry and noise conditions, at least one competing firm chooses positive regularization in every pure-strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium.; Corollary 1 applies the result to a symmetric pure-strategy equilibrium, and Figure 3 supplies numerical comparative statics for market reach, segment sizes, and data noise.; Discussion sections examine additional predictors, overparameterized models, other competitive actions, and data generated endogenously by an earlier targeting round.
- **Caveat:** The baseline intentionally uses one binary predictor, two training observations, independent private data, a fixed targeting capacity, and no endogenous price decision. The main positive-regularization proposition is conditional on pure-strategy equilibrium existence and sufficiently large noise, although a mixed equilibrium preserves the qualitative conclusion. The authors note that the result need not extend to the overparameterized double-descent region and leave a general oligopoly model with richer algorithms and strategic variables for future work.

### Influencers: The Power of Comments

Cristina Nistor; Matthew Selove (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0186](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0186). First published online: 2024-06-25.

- **Question:** Why are microinfluencers often more selective than celebrities, and how do the informativeness of follower comments and the cost of reading them affect an influencer's endorsement policy, a seller's prices, consumer learning, and joint endorsement profit?
- **Players:** an influencer choosing which product qualities to endorse; a monopolist seller choosing prices and sharing endorsement profit with the influencer; first-period followers who purchase and leave comments; second-period followers who can read comments before purchasing
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the influencer publicly chooses a binding policy to endorse all products or only high-quality products. Stage 2: Nature draws quality, observed by the seller and influencer; if the draw is excluded by the policy, the game ends, otherwise a fixed payment proportionally splits expected endorsement profit. Stage 3: the seller sets first-period price P_1. Stage 4: early followers read the post, choose whether to buy, observe their own fit after purchase, and leave comments. Stage 5: the seller sets second-period price P_2. Stage 6: later followers read the post and price, may sequentially read comments, and choose whether to buy.
- **Actions:** the influencer chooses an all-products or high-quality-only endorsement policy; the seller and influencer agree to a fixed transfer that proportionally splits expected endorsement profit; the seller sets first- and second-period prices; first-period followers purchase or abstain and leave informative or uninformative comments; second-period followers choose whether to buy immediately, read comments until learning fit, or abstain
- **Information:** The endorsement policy is publicly observed and binding in the main model.; Product quality is observed by the seller and influencer but not directly by followers.; Followers observe prices and infer expected product quality from the public endorsement policy and equilibrium or off-path pricing beliefs.; An informative comment privately reveals whether the product is a good fit for the follower reading it; an uninformative comment conveys no fit information.; Perfect Bayesian equilibrium requires correct on-path beliefs and sequentially rational actions after every history.
- **Objective:** Because the transfer makes the seller and influencer share expected profit proportionally, the influencer chooses the policy that maximizes joint expected profit. Equation (6) is the incremental expected profit from endorsing all products rather than only high-quality products for a microinfluencer.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Delta\mathbb{E}[\pi]=(1-\alpha)\left[\underline{q}-\beta C-(1-\beta)\underline{q}C-\frac{R(1-\beta)}{\bar{\lambda}}\right]M_V$ (Equation (6), printed p. 1161 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Perfect Bayesian equilibrium
- **Solution:** Lemma 1 gives the late follower's choice among immediate purchase, comment reading, and nonpurchase. With few informative comments, celebrity posts support pooling prices and no comment reading (Lemma 2); a celebrity endorses all products exactly when low-quality expected fit exceeds marginal cost (Proposition 1). With sufficiently inexpensive access to informative comments, late followers of a microinfluencer read until learning fit and equilibrium prices compensate their expected reading cost (Lemma 3). A microinfluencer therefore endorses only high-quality products when the follower reading-cost burden of low-quality endorsements exceeds their incremental surplus (Proposition 2). The commenting-utility and specialization extensions preserve the celebrity-microinfluencer contrast under stated conditions (Propositions 3 and 4), and Online Appendix extensions show how reputation can sustain selectivity and why comment-deletion incentives differ by influencer type.
- **Evidence:** A two-cohort incomplete-information model is solved for perfect Bayesian equilibrium under celebrity and microinfluencer comment compositions.; Section 4.4 uses a numerical example and comparative-static figures to illustrate equilibrium endorsement policies, prices, and profits.; Analytical extensions endogenize commenting incentives and influencer specialization; the Online Appendix also treats repeated-game reputation and deletion of uninformative comments.
- **Caveat:** The main model assumes a monopolist seller, two product-quality levels, a continuum of followers, exogenous early and late cohorts, a binding endorsement policy, and that every early follower comments. Its clean celebrity and microinfluencer results focus on low and high informative-comment shares; the paper notes that intermediate shares can support other equilibria, including price signaling. Extensions relax commenting incentives, policy commitment, expertise, and comment deletion, but the paper leaves empirical testing and richer dynamic reputation as future research.

### Endogenous Inequality in Decentralized Two-Sided Markets

Dmitri Kuksov (2024). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0236](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0236). First published online: 2024-07-02.

- **Question:** Can a fully decentralized two-sided search market generate persistent inequality between ex ante identical groups, and do cheaper search or side payments reliably reduce that inequality?
- **Players:** an infinite population I of agents searching for partners in population J; an ex ante identical infinite population J searching for partners in population I
- **Timing:** An unmatched agent pays a per-meeting search cost to meet a random member of the other population. At the meeting, each participant privately observes the payoff that the match would give that participant and simultaneously accepts or rejects. A match forms only if both accept; otherwise both remain unmatched and may pay to search again. Stationary reservation thresholds are mutually consistent in Bayesian Nash equilibrium.
- **Actions:** agents decide whether to continue searching and pay for another meeting; each agent adopts a population-level reservation threshold; meeting partners simultaneously accept or reject after observing their own match payoff; in an extension, agents may offer a monetary transfer conditional on acceptance
- **Information:** At a meeting, each agent privately observes only the payoff that the proposed match would yield to that agent.; Match payoffs are independently and identically distributed across directions and pairs in the symmetric benchmark.; Agents know the payoff distribution, search cost, and the other population's stationary acceptance rule.; An agent does not observe the counterpart's match payoff before the simultaneous acceptance decision.
- **Objective:** Population I's equilibrium reservation threshold equates the current meeting cost to the probability that a J-agent accepts times the expected surplus from draws above I's threshold; population J satisfies the mirror condition.
- **Representative equation:** `$s=(1-F(R_J))\int_{x>R_I}(x-R_I)\,dF(x).$ (Equation (3), p. 1303 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Asymptotically stable Bayesian Nash equilibrium in reservation acceptance rules
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 shows that the stable Pareto equilibrium is unique up to relabeling, asymmetric when s<1/(α-1), and symmetric otherwise. Propositions 2 and 3 show that reducing search cost can trigger inequality and, once the asymmetric regime applies, make the disadvantaged side worse off as inequality grows. Propositions 4 and 5 show that the asymmetric outcome and cheaper search may raise or lower welfare depending on the Pareto shape parameter. Proposition 6 ties symmetric stability to a decreasing mean-excess function: thin-tailed normal, logit, and uniform examples preserve symmetry, whereas sufficiently heavy-tailed cases can break it. Proposition 7 shows by construction that monetary offers can further disadvantage the low-payoff side.
- **Evidence:** Proposition 1 characterizes the unique stable equilibrium up to renaming the two populations and shows it is asymmetric below the Pareto search-cost threshold.; Propositions 2 and 3 show that lowering search costs can create and magnify inequality, helping one population while hurting the other.; Propositions 4 and 5 characterize when the stable asymmetric outcome has higher or lower welfare and when cheaper search reduces total welfare.; Proposition 6 generalizes the stability criterion to the shape of the match-payoff distribution through its mean-excess function.; Proposition 7 constructs a discrete-payoff example in which allowing monetary acceptance offers increases inequality and lowers the disadvantaged side's payoff.
- **Caveat:** The benchmark assumes infinite stationary populations, iid directed match payoffs, random meetings, and no transfers, and it selects locally stable equilibria through a best-response dynamic rather than modeling a finite learning process. Under symmetric primitives the model predicts inequality but cannot predict which labeled population becomes advantaged. The sharp closed forms rely on Pareto payoffs; distributional robustness is conditional on the mean-excess shape, and the monetary-transfer extension is established by an example rather than a general closed-form solution.

### Asymmetric Impact of Matching Technology on Influencer Marketing: Implications for Platform Revenue

Jessie Liu; Yi Liu (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0211](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0211). First published online: 2024-07-17.

- **Question:** Does a more accurate influencer-marketer recommendation technology always increase platform revenue, and how should a platform adjust its commission when improved matching intensifies competition among influencers?
- **Players:** a continuum of heterogeneous niche-to-general influencers that set endorsement prices; a continuum of marketers with heterogeneous campaign costs that choose an influencer or do not participate; in Section 4.2's endogenous-commission extension, the platform that chooses its commission rate
- **Timing:** Given a public matching-accuracy level, the platform's AI recommends influencers to each marketer. Influencers simultaneously post take-it-or-leave-it endorsement prices. Marketers then choose whether to participate and, if so, buy at most one endorsement. Matched influencers produce sponsored content, converted revenue is realized, and the platform retains its commission share. Extensions let the platform choose the commission rate.
- **Actions:** each influencer posts an endorsement price and participates if the resulting payoff exceeds the outside option; each marketer chooses whether to launch a campaign and which recommended influencer to hire; in the endogenous-commission extension, the platform chooses its commission rate
- **Information:** Matching accuracy and the commission rate are public model primitives.; Influencers differ in content broadness and implied follower reach; marketers differ in campaign fixed cost.; Each marketer knows its campaign cost and evaluates the converted revenue generated by each recommended influencer.; Equilibrium prices and participation thresholds are mutually anticipated, and nonparticipants receive stated outside options.
- **Objective:** The platform's expected revenue is the commission share of every participating influencer's equilibrium campaign price, integrated over the active influencer set.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi=\int_{n\in\mathcal{N}}\delta p(n)\,dn.$ (Equation (7), p. 71 (PDF p. 7))
- **Equilibrium:** Competitive pricing and market-clearing participation equilibrium
- **Solution:** Lemma 2 establishes a unique cutoff equilibrium for active marketers and influencers. Proposition 1 shows that matching accuracy can reduce platform revenue at intermediate follower density because niche entry intensifies competition enough to outweigh matching and market-expansion gains. Proposition 3 shows that when opportunity cost is constant, an optimally adjusted commission makes revenue nondecreasing in accuracy, but Proposition 4 shows this remedy can fail when outside options rise with follower count. Proposition 5 confirms nonmonotonicity even when influencers have equal follower counts; when only follower density varies and content broadness is fixed, improved matching instead always raises revenue.
- **Evidence:** Lemma 2 characterizes a unique pair of influencer and marketer participation thresholds, equilibrium prices, and a market-clearing condition.; Proposition 1 proves that platform revenue can fall as matching accuracy improves when follower density is intermediate.; Propositions 2–4 study positive and size-dependent influencer opportunity costs and show when endogenous commission adjustment can or cannot remove the negative revenue effect.; Proposition 5 and alternative heterogeneity models show that the nonmonotonicity depends on heterogeneity in content broadness rather than follower-size heterogeneity alone.; Numerical figures decompose matching-enhancement, competition, and market-expansion effects and illustrate the nonlinear platform-revenue response.
- **Caveat:** The baseline is static, places marketers' target consumers at a common location, gives each influencer and marketer at most one campaign partner, uses posted flat fees rather than bargaining, and treats matching accuracy, influencer positioning, and the commission as exogenous. The paper endogenizes the commission and handles some other departures in extensions but leaves dynamic repositioning, celebrity bargaining power, richer competition among brands with different target segments, and endogenous restrictions on recommended influencer sets for future research.

### Product Safety and Liability with Deceptive Advertising and Moral Hazard

Xu Guan; Huan Cao; Krista J. Li; Yucheng Ding (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0173](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0173). First published online: 2024-07-25.

- **Question:** Should product failures be governed by strict liability or comparative negligence when firms privately know quality, can advertise deceptively, and consumers choose how carefully to use the product?
- **Players:** a monopolist firm whose product can be high or low quality and that chooses an advertising message and price; a unit mass of consumers that update quality beliefs, buy, and choose precaution effort
- **Timing:** Nature first draws binary product quality, observed only by the firm. The firm sends a public high- or low-quality advertising message. Consumers update their belief; the firm then sets price and consumers decide whether to buy. Buyers choose precaution effort based on the posterior. Product failure may occur, after which the firm compensates consumers according to the preannounced liability rule.
- **Actions:** the informed firm reports a high- or low-quality advertising message and sets price; consumers update beliefs, choose whether to purchase, and select precaution effort
- **Information:** The firm privately observes the binary product quality before advertising.; Consumers observe the public message and price, know the prior probability of low quality, and update beliefs rationally.; The firm's mixed advertising probability is not directly observed, but consumers' equilibrium conjecture must be correct.; The liability regime is known ex ante; comparative negligence assumes the court can verify quality and consumer effort after a failure.
- **Objective:** When a low-quality firm advertises high quality under strict liability, profit equals the price that extracts perceived consumer surplus minus the expected compensation paid at the actual low-quality failure rate.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_L^S(\lambda,m_H)=v-G(\lambda,m_H)(l-s)-c(e^S)-F_L(e^S)s.$ (Equation (11), p. 295 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Perfect Bayesian pooling, hybrid, or separating advertising equilibrium
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 shows that comparative negligence always produces pooling, whereas strict liability moves from pooling to a unique hybrid equilibrium and then separation as compensation rises. Proposition 2 shows that compensation does not affect comparative-negligence profit but can raise, lower, or nonmonotonically change strict-liability profit in the hybrid region, depending on the quality gap. Propositions 3 and 4 identify conditions under which strict liability raises firm profit and lowers the expected failure rate relative to comparative negligence. Proposition 6 shows that strict liability can also produce higher consumer surplus with heterogeneous willingness to pay. Proposition 7 cautions that if quality and precaution are complements rather than substitutes, pooling returns under both rules and comparative negligence dominates in firm profit.
- **Evidence:** Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 isolate the roles of private quality information and endogenous precaution by studying transparent-quality and fixed-effort benchmarks.; Proposition 1 characterizes pooling under comparative negligence and pooling, unique hybrid, or separating equilibria under strict liability as the compensation level changes.; Propositions 2 and 3 characterize nonmonotone effects of liability on firm profit and conditions under which strict liability outperforms comparative negligence.; Proposition 4 compares expected failure rates and shows when a higher strict-liability payment improves safety by inducing more truthful advertising.; Extensions study price signaling, a separate deceptive-advertising fine, heterogeneous willingness to pay, and complementarity rather than substitutability between quality and precaution.
- **Caveat:** The main model reduces safety quality to two types, assumes the high-quality firm reports high quality, gives homogeneous consumers full market participation, treats the quality message as cheap talk, and suppresses price signaling. It also assumes quality and precaution are substitutes and that comparative-negligence courts can verify quality and effort after failure. Extensions show robustness to several departures, but the complements case reverses core liability comparisons.

### Endogenous Costs, Market Competition, and Disclosure

Xi Li (2025). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2022.0346](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.0346). First published online: 2024-07-29.

- **Question:** When should competing manufacturers reveal sourcing information that changes suppliers' wholesale-price decisions, and how do supplier structure and the form of market competition alter the answer?
- **Players:** two competing downstream manufacturers; two independent upstream suppliers or one common supplier
- **Timing:** In stage 1, manufacturers simultaneously choose whether to disclose their sourcing information. In stage 2, suppliers observe the disclosures available to them and set input prices. In stage 3, manufacturers compete simultaneously in quantities or prices. Payoffs are then realized.
- **Actions:** each manufacturer chooses disclosure or nondisclosure; each independent supplier, or the common supplier, sets input prices; manufacturers choose Cournot quantities or Bertrand prices
- **Information:** Disclosure is truthful, credible, costless, and chosen before suppliers price inputs.; A disclosure reveals the focal manufacturer's sourcing information to the rival manufacturer and relevant supplier.; Nondisclosure leaves the corresponding cost information unavailable; passive off-path beliefs support the equilibrium analysis.; Demand and the game's structural parameters are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** Under disclosure and quantity competition, manufacturer i chooses output to maximize downstream margin given its own input cost and the rival's quantity; the supplier then sets the input price anticipating this response.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{q_i^D}\;\pi_i^D=(1-q_i^D-\theta q_j^D-c_i^D)q_i^D.$ (Manufacturer profit-maximization expression immediately before Equation (1), printed p. 380 (PDF p. 7))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect disclosure, supplier-pricing, and downstream-competition equilibrium
- **Solution:** With independent suppliers, both manufacturers disclose in the unique quantity-competition equilibrium (Proposition 1), whereas neither discloses under price competition (Proposition 3). With a common supplier, neither discloses under either quantity competition (Proposition 5) or price competition (Proposition 7). Propositions 2, 4, 6, and 8 show that manufacturers' equilibrium choices need not always maximize total channel profit. Proposition 9 finds that consumer-surplus and social-welfare rankings align with manufacturers' equilibrium disclosure behavior in the focal cases, and Proposition 10 characterizes supplier-initiated disclosure.
