- **Timing:** Given an exogenous common commission rate r, the content developer first chooses quality q. Platforms a and b then simultaneously choose device prices p_A and p_B. A unit mass of consumers distributed on a Hotelling line chooses device A or B. The game is solved by backward induction from consumer device demand to platform prices and then developer quality.
- **Actions:** the developer invests in content quality; the two platforms simultaneously set device prices; consumers choose between the two hardware ecosystems; a regulator or platform changes the common commission rate in comparative statics
- **Information:** Quality and device prices are observed before consumers choose.; Consumer Hotelling locations are privately realized and uniformly distributed.; Revenue asymmetry, commission, cost parameters, and demand primitives are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** The developer chooses common quality to maximize its retained content revenue across both platform installed bases less quadratic quality-investment cost.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_D=(1-r)q(m_A+\alpha m_B)-kq^2$ (Section 2.2, printed p. 251 (PDF p. 3))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the developer-platform pricing game
- **Solution:** Higher content quality makes both platforms cut device prices, especially platform b, and this strategic response is stronger at higher commission rates. When commission is below a threshold, cutting it reduces equilibrium quality because platforms respond with higher device prices and shrink the installed base that is most valuable to the developer. At still lower rates the developer's own profit can also fall; at intermediate rates profit rises even while quality falls. Conversely, for a range above the quality threshold, a commission cut raises quality yet lowers consumer surplus because higher device prices dominate the quality benefit. These mechanisms survive several extensions, although full market coverage is important for the intensive-margin channel.
- **Evidence:** A sequential developer-platform-consumer game is solved by backward induction.; Closed-form comparative statics characterize content quality, developer profit, device prices, market shares, and consumer surplus as the commission changes.; Extensions examine platform vertical differentiation, platform-specific qualities, content utility, asymmetric commissions, and an open platform.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses two hardware-gated platforms, one developer, a common exogenous commission, full Hotelling market coverage, alpha>1, symmetric device values, one common quality, and consumer device utility independent of quality. Interior restrictions are required. Extensions relax several assumptions, but developer competition, entry, endogenous commission-setting, partial coverage, and richer content demand are not jointly modeled.

### Data and Algorithms: Strategic Disclosure of Competitiveness on Platforms Through Marketplace Analytics

Yi Liu; Fei Long (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2024.0960](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2024.0960). First published online: 2025-12-09.

- **Question:** Why might an e-commerce platform permit third-party marketplace analytics despite having better data and its own analytics product, and how should it design its algorithm and API access?
- **Players:** an e-commerce platform choosing data access and designing platform analytics; two symmetric sellers choosing analytics adoption and product prices
- **Timing:** The platform chooses a restrictive or open data-access policy and designs its platform algorithm's true-positive and true-negative rates. Sellers simultaneously choose whether to adopt the available analytics service before observing the platform's chosen algorithm, while rationally anticipating it. Market competitiveness theta realizes and analytics signals arrive. Sellers update beliefs and simultaneously set prices without observing the rival's adoption choice. Consumers purchase according to the differentiated-demand system, and the platform earns commissions.
- **Actions:** the platform opens or restricts third-party data access; the platform chooses the accuracy structure of its own algorithm; sellers adopt platform analytics, third-party analytics, or no analytics; sellers update beliefs after analytics signals; sellers simultaneously set prices; the platform designs third-party API data accuracy in an extension
- **Information:** Market competitiveness theta is binary and initially unknown to all players.; Platform analytics can have asymmetric true-positive and true-negative rates chosen strategically.; The platform's algorithm is unobservable to sellers before adoption but can be learned through use; sellers form rational expectations at adoption.; Third-party analytics is honest because it serves sellers individually, but its accuracy is capped by data access.; Sellers do not observe one another's adoption decisions when setting prices.
- **Objective:** Given posterior probability eta that competition is intense, seller i chooses its price to maximize expected profit across bad and good market states.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_i(p_1,p_2;\eta)=\eta\pi_{iB}+(1-\eta)\pi_{iG}=((1-\delta)p_i-m)[1-(1+\eta\theta_B)p_i+\eta\theta_Bp_j]$ (Equation (8), printed p. 660 (PDF p. 8))
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric perfect Bayesian adoption-pricing equilibrium with platform persuasion
- **Solution:** The platform truthfully reports a good market (alpha_G*=1) but underreports a bad, highly competitive market; its optimal bad-state accuracy is below the sellers' preferred level and may be zero when the bad-market prior is small. Sellers adopt platform analytics only when its adoption value VOP covers cost, and VOP is inverted-U shaped in the prior; third-party adoption follows the analogous VOT condition. Open access strictly benefits the platform exactly when third-party analytics is adopted, platform analytics would be rejected, and third-party information beats no analytics, which occurs in moderately low or moderately high competition-prior regions. Better third-party technology or lower adoption cost can move open access from irrelevant to beneficial and then detrimental. If the platform controls API accuracy, the adoption constraint can make optimal data accuracy rise with seller marginal cost. More accurate third-party analytics lowers consumer surplus, yet restricting the platform's API can still hurt consumers by forcing the platform to tolerate even more accurate scraping. Coexistence, multiple-tool adoption, and analytics pricing preserve the core open-access mechanism.
- **Evidence:** A binary-state Bayesian-persuasion problem is embedded in sellers' simultaneous analytics-adoption and pricing decisions.; The platform compares equilibrium revenue under restrictive access, platform analytics, open access, third-party analytics, and no adoption.; Extensions endogenize API accuracy, derive consumer surplus, allow coexistence and multiple analytics adoption, and price analytics services.
- **Caveat:** The baseline has a monopolistic platform, two symmetric sellers, binary competition states, reduced-form linear demand, symmetric adoption, at most one analytics tool, an honest representative third party, and an algorithm that sellers learn after adoption. A conservative selection rule is imposed, and the learning mechanism is not modeled as a full repeated game. The paper leaves competing platforms, richer analytics tasks, dynamic trust, privacy, seller heterogeneity, and consumer-level demand for future research.

### Strategic Capacity Commitment: A Channel Competition Perspective

Shuguang Zhang; Wei Shi Lim; Lucy Gongtao Chen (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0139](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0139). First published online: 2026-01-12.

- **Question:** When does committing to a sales capacity create strategic value for a manufacturer, and how does that value depend on whether the rival channel is centralized or decentralized?
- **Players:** a centralized manufacturer cm selling directly to consumers; a decentralized manufacturer dm selling through a retailer; the retailer r setting the decentralized channel's retail price; a unit mass of Hotelling consumers choosing between the two channels
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the centralized and decentralized manufacturers simultaneously choose capacity commitment C or flexibility F. Stage 2: any manufacturer choosing C sets its capacity after observing the rival's commitment strategy. Stage 3: the decentralized manufacturer sets an observable wholesale price w. Stage 4: the centralized manufacturer and retailer simultaneously set retail prices. Consumers choose, efficient rationing applies if capacity binds, and the four strategy subgames are solved by backward induction.
- **Actions:** each manufacturer chooses commitment or flexibility; a committing manufacturer selects capacity; the decentralized manufacturer sets wholesale price; the centralized manufacturer and retailer simultaneously set retail prices; consumers choose a channel; capacity-constrained demand is efficiently rationed
- **Information:** Commitment strategies and capacities are observable in the baseline before wholesale and retail pricing.; The wholesale price is observed by the rival centralized channel.; Each consumer privately knows a Hotelling location representing relative product preference.; Channel structure, differentiation, costs, and demand are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** When it commits, the centralized manufacturer chooses capacity to maximize retail revenue, subject to sales not exceeding committed capacity.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{k_{cm}}\;q_{cm}p_{cm}\quad\text{s.t. }q_{cm}\le k_{cm}$ (Equation (6), printed p. 619 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the four-stage capacity-channel game
- **Solution:** In the asymmetric-channel equilibrium, the centralized manufacturer commits to a limiting capacity, while the decentralized manufacturer is indifferent between flexibility and a nonbinding high capacity. The commitment credibly weakens the centralized manufacturer's competitiveness, induces a higher wholesale price, softens retail competition, and raises both manufacturers' profits; the retailer benefits only when differentiation is low, and consumer surplus falls. With two centralized channels, both commit when differentiation is low, but only one commits when differentiation is high. With two decentralized channels, commitment is dominant for both because each downstream retailer absorbs the rival commitment's price effect. Quantity competition, retailer commitment, asymmetric selling costs, and unobservable commitment preserve the base equilibrium. Costly capacity with a long lead time can make the decentralized manufacturer strictly prefer commitment because the commitment converts a future marginal capacity cost into a sunk cost.
- **Evidence:** A four-stage asymmetric-channel game is solved by backward induction across FF, CF, FC, and CC capacity-strategy subgames.; Alternative models characterize symmetric centralized and symmetric decentralized channel competition.; Extensions analyze quantity competition, retailer commitment, asymmetric selling costs, unobservable commitment, and costly capacity with short or long lead times.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses two substitutable products, Hotelling demand with full coverage, one centralized and one decentralized channel, zero production and selling costs, costless observable commitment, an observable wholesale price, no outside wholesale market, and efficient rationing. The paper varies many of these assumptions in extensions, but complementary products, multiple firms per channel, uncertain demand, and empirically estimated commitment costs remain outside the model.

### Bargaining and Network Effects in Two-Sided Platforms: Evidence from Online Healthcare

Xu Zhang; Junhong Chu; Puneet Manchanda (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2024.0922](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2024.0922). First published online: 2026-02-23.

- **Question:** How do participant-specific network effects alter negotiated commission rates and the growth-profitability trade-off for a platform that bargains individually with strategic sellers?
- **Players:** an online healthcare platform bargaining over commission rates and allocating sales effort; individual hospitals and clinics deciding whether to join and bargaining over commission; consumers deciding whether to adopt the platform
- **Timing:** The platform's sales team sequentially approaches hospitals. A hospital first decides whether to join under free registration and often a zero initial commission. As the platform brings consumers to the hospital, the platform and hospital bargain and periodically renegotiate the commission rate. Consumer and hospital adoption in each city depends on lagged same-side and cross-side installed bases. The estimated network effects enter the platform's bargaining payoff as the hospital's contribution to future growth and monetization.
- **Actions:** consumers join or do not join the platform; approached hospitals join or reject the platform; the platform and each hospital bargain over the commission rate; the platform chooses which hospital types and cities to target in policy simulations; the platform and hospitals accept agreement or retain their outside options
- **Information:** The platform and hospital bargain using observed sales, hospital attributes, installed bases, market share, and outside-option proxies.; Consumer and hospital adoption include private Type-I extreme-value utility shocks.; Lagged city-level consumer and hospital bases are observed state variables generating direct and cross-network effects.; Hospital network effects are heterogeneous functions of size, public ownership, and online rating.; Unobserved endogeneity in installed bases is addressed with instruments and control functions rather than treated as complete information.
- **Objective:** The negotiated commission maximizes the generalized Nash product of the hospital's and platform's gains from agreement over disagreement, weighted by their relative bargaining powers.
- **Representative equation:** `$(\Pi_{jt}^{H}-\Pi_{jt}^{H,0})^{\delta_{jt}}(\Pi_{jt}^{F}-\Pi_{jt}^{F,0})^{1-\delta_{jt}}$ (Equation (10), printed p. 368 (PDF p. 10))
- **Equilibrium:** Generalized Nash bargaining solution embedded in structural two-sided adoption
- **Solution:** Consumer-side direct and hospital-to-consumer cross-network effects are positive: a 1% larger consumer base raises next-month new-consumer share about 0.58%, and a 1% larger hospital base raises it about 0.19% on average. Hospital-to-consumer effects are larger for bigger hospitals and average 0.71 for public versus 0.24 for private hospitals. Consumer-to-hospital cross-network effects are positive; the average hospital-side direct effect is insignificant but masks strong heterogeneity, with private hospitals averaging 0.36 and public hospitals -0.11. In bargaining, a one-unit cross-network effect is valued like 6.1% more commission revenue and a one-unit direct effect like 3.3% more, so high-network-effect hospitals receive lower commissions. Estimated hospital bargaining power declines from public A to public B/C, private, and clinic types, and a 10% increase in platform consumer share lowers hospital bargaining power about 1.5%. Simulations show public-hospital seeding maximizes growth but is costly, clinic seeding favors short-run liquidity, public-first targeting raises consumers while private-first targeting raises hospital count, and small-city emphasis can greatly accelerate consumer growth.
- **Evidence:** The data cover August 2015-December 2019, approximately three million registered consumers, 1,154 joining hospitals, 202 cities, and 11,433 sales-team visits to 2,484 hospitals.; Consumer and hospital adoption are estimated with utility-based models, IV/control-function corrections, rich fixed effects, and robustness checks.; Generalized Nash bargaining parameters are estimated from 5,838 original and renegotiated contracts using network effects generated by the adoption models and two-stage bootstrap inference.; Counterfactuals compare hospital seeding, approach sequences, and large- versus small-city entry strategies.
- **Caveat:** The data come from one Chinese online health-checkup platform during its early growth stage. The model omits long-run hospital competition, hospital exit, strategic interaction across hospitals, detailed actions of competing platforms, exclusive contracting, and consumer choice among health-checkup packages. Network contributions to future platform value are reduced form, offline checkup data are unavailable, and the no-cannibalization and near-zero variable-cost assumptions rely partly on interviews and institutional context.

### The Design of Centralized Matching Systems on Two-Sided Platforms: Evidence from the Ride-Hailing Market

Xueli Zhang, Wei Miao, Junhong Chu, and Ivan Png (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0561](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0561). First published online: 2026-03-03.

- **Question:** Does removing drivers' right to reject e-hail requests improve matching efficiency, earnings, and rider welfare enough to compensate for the loss of agent autonomy?
- **Players:** strategic taxi drivers choosing acceptance and relocation; riders choosing e-hail, street-hail, or an outside option
- **Timing:** At each five-minute period, riders choose a transport mode; the platform broadcasts e-hail requests; drivers decide whether to enter each e-hail matching pool; unmatched drivers search for street-hail riders; matched drivers travel and unmatched drivers choose where to relocate. This repeats over a finite day shift, and beliefs, wait times, demand, and spatial supply must be mutually consistent.
- **Actions:** riders choose e-hail, street-hail, or the outside option; drivers accept or ignore an e-hail request under driver-accept dispatch; unmatched drivers choose a neighboring location or stay put; the counterfactual dispatcher automatically assigns requests to nearby drivers
- **Information:** Drivers observe their own location and request destination and form beliefs about aggregate spatial industry states rather than tracking every rival.; Riders know fares and form rational expectations about wait times generated by equilibrium driver supply.; The driver-accept model includes idiosyncratic acceptance and relocation shocks.; The auto-accept counterfactual removes the individual screening decision and its attention cost.
- **Objective:** A vacant driver values street-hail search as the expected payoff and continuation value when matched plus the best relocation continuation value when unmatched; this Bellman expression is the core dynamic objective behind acceptance and relocation decisions.
- **Representative equation:** `$V_{o,h}^{t}(\widetilde S)=\frac{m_{o,h}^{t}}{v_{o,h}^{t}}\sum_d M_{od,h}^{t}(\pi_{od,h}^{t}+V_d^{t+\tau_{od}}(\widetilde S)) + \left(1-\frac{m_{o,h}^{t}}{v_{o,h}^{t}}\right)\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_k}\left[\max_{k\in A(o)}\{V_k^{t+\tau_{ok}}(\widetilde S)-c_{ok}+\varepsilon_k\}\right].$ (Equation (4), driver value function, printed p. 826 (PDF p. 11))
- **Equilibrium:** Finite-horizon mean-field competitive two-sided-market equilibrium
- **Solution:** With rider demand held fixed, auto-accept cuts average e-hail wait time from 3.97 to 3.44 minutes, raises consumer surplus by 0.11%, and raises average shift earnings by 16.61%, mainly through lower pickup and vacant time. With demand adjusting, e-hail wait time is 3.45 minutes, hourly e-hail demand rises 5.30%, consumer surplus rises 0.18%, and shift earnings rise 18.33%. Gains are uneven: the reallocation toward e-hail raises street-hail wait time by 1.20% and lowers hourly street-hail demand by 0.23% in the long-run equilibrium.
- **Evidence:** The demand side is a random-coefficient discrete-choice model estimated from Singapore taxi trips and GPS traces.; The supply side is a finite-horizon dynamic driver game solved with backward induction and forward updating inside a mean-field fixed point.; Counterfactuals compare driver-accept and nearest-driver auto-accept dispatch with fixed demand and with endogenous rider demand.
- **Caveat:** The setting is one Singapore taxi operator in 2016-2017 with regulated fares, fixed driver participation, a finite day shift, discretized space and time, and an oblivious or mean-field information approximation. The auto-accept policy is simulated as nearest-driver assignment; long-run entry, multihoming, endogenous platform pricing, driver dissatisfaction, and broader labor-market responses are outside the model.

### Consumer-Driven Class Pricing

Zuhui Xiao (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0133](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0133). First published online: 2026-03-12.

- **Question:** Why might a firm deliberately assign the same price to products with different costs even when fine-grained pricing is technologically feasible?
- **Players:** a multiproduct monopolist choosing prices; loss-averse consumers forming credible plans and choosing products
- **Timing:** The firm commits to prices for N products. Consumers then form state-contingent consumption plans that generate reference distributions. Each consumer privately observes the realized ideal taste and finally chooses a product; a credible plan is a personal equilibrium when the realized choice is optimal and consistent with the plan in every state.
- **Actions:** the firm chooses one price for each product, subject to weakly increasing prices in costs; each consumer forms a state-contingent planned product choice; after taste realization, each consumer chooses the utility-maximizing product; not buying serves as the participation benchmark
- **Information:** The firm knows the distribution of stochastic tastes but not individual realizations.; Consumers know prices and their prior taste interval when forming plans, then privately learn realized tastes.; Reference points are endogenous distributions generated by credible expectations rather than fixed external benchmarks.; The monopolist anticipates the demand induced by personal-equilibrium constraints.
- **Objective:** The monopolist chooses the vector of product prices to maximize expected margins over demand generated by credible consumer plans, subject to ordered prices and personal-equilibrium constraints.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p_1,\ldots,p_N}\;\Pi(p_1,\ldots,p_N)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}(p_i-c_i)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\int_{a_j}^{a_{j+1}}\mathbf 1\{M_j(x)=i\}\,\frac{dx}{m},\quad \text{s.t. }p_1\le\cdots\le p_N\text{ and PE constraints}.$ (Section 3.3, firm's optimization problem, printed p. 778 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Price-commitment subgame with consumer personal equilibria
- **Solution:** Loss aversion makes a price difference reduce willingness to pay for the cheaper product more strongly than it raises willingness to pay for the expensive product. When this demand-side asymmetry is sufficiently strong relative to the cost difference, the monopolist optimally sets equal class prices despite heterogeneous costs (Proposition 3). Under class pricing, stronger loss aversion can raise optimal profit while reducing consumer surplus (Proposition 4). In the N-product extension, products are partitioned into consecutive pricing classes whose sizes depend on loss aversion and cost differences.
- **Evidence:** Proposition 1 characterizes the two-product personal equilibrium and its demand cutoff.; Propositions 2 and 3 connect loss aversion to cross-price responsiveness and establish when equal class prices are optimal.; Proposition 4 studies profit and consumer surplus, and the N-product section characterizes equilibrium class structure and size.
- **Caveat:** The mechanism relies on expectations-based reference dependence, a specific additive gain-loss formulation in price and taste dimensions, uniform ex ante taste intervals, complete market coverage, firm commitment, and ordered exogenous product locations and costs. The model is monopolistic and analytical: it excludes seller competition, impulse purchases, long purchase journeys with dynamically updated plans, endogenous locations, and empirical estimation of loss aversion or observed class-pricing choices.

### Algorithmic Targeting and the Precision-Recall Tradeoff

Ganesh Iyer, Yunfei (Jesse) Yao, and Zemin (Zachary) Zhong (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2024.0930](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2024.0930). First published online: 2026-03-23.

- **Question:** How does competition change the precision-recall balance of targeting algorithms, especially when rival firms' consumer-level predictions are correlated?
- **Players:** two competing firms choosing consumer-level targeting policies
- **Timing:** For each consumer, firms receive possibly correlated predicted conversion probabilities from their algorithms and simultaneously choose whether to target, possibly mixing as a function of the prediction. Payoffs depend on true interest, targeting cost, and whether one or both firms target the consumer. Extensions let firms first invest in lowering correlation and jointly choose prices and targeting.
- **Actions:** each firm chooses a targeting probability q_i(p) for consumers assigned prediction p; in the data extension, each firm invests in private information to reduce prediction correlation; in the pricing extension, each firm chooses a price and a targeting policy
- **Information:** Each firm's prediction p is a calibrated probability that the consumer is interested.; The unconditional prediction distribution is identical across firms, but predictions coincide with probability rho and otherwise draw from type-consistent conditional distributions.; Firms know model primitives and the joint prediction structure but do not observe true consumer interest when targeting.; Targeting makes an interested consumer aware of the product; untargeted consumers do not purchase in the base model.
- **Objective:** For a consumer with predicted interest probability p, a firm's expected net payoff from targeting equals the expected joint-target payoff plus the sole-target payoff minus the targeting cost; mixing requires this payoff to equal zero.
- **Representative equation:** `$[\rho q(p)+(1-\rho)R]pw+[1-\rho q(p)-(1-\rho)R]pv-c=0.$ (Section 3.2, mixed-strategy indifference condition, printed p. 848 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Unique symmetric mixed-strategy targeting equilibrium
- **Solution:** Competition produces higher precision and lower recall than monopoly (Proposition 1): overlap lowers targeting returns, so firms concentrate on consumers predicted to be more likely to convert. Greater prediction correlation reduces recall and, once correlation is sufficiently high, also reduces precision because equilibrium targeting probabilities flatten. Firms may invest in private information to lower correlation when the initial correlation is already low enough to support positive operating profit (Proposition 2). The precision-over-recall result survives endogenous pricing and asymmetric equilibria.
- **Evidence:** Lemma 2 establishes the unique symmetric mixed-strategy equilibrium.; Proposition 1 compares duopoly precision and recall with monopoly.; Proposition 2 studies investment that reduces prediction correlation, and Proposition 3 establishes an asymmetric targeting equilibrium.
- **Caveat:** The base model assumes binary interest, calibrated continuous predictions with identical marginal distributions, a stylized one-parameter correlation structure, awareness only through targeting, fixed targeting payoffs, and symmetric firms. The paper does not estimate an algorithm or test the welfare predictions empirically, and consumer welfare from targeting information is discussed rather than fully solved in the base model.

### Optimizing Reserve Prices in Display Advertising Auctions

Hana Choi and Carl F. Mela (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2023.0002](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0002). First published online: 2026-05-06.

- **Question:** How should a publisher set reserve prices in real-time display auctions when advertisers strategically adjust bids to satisfy campaign-level reach constraints?
- **Players:** a publisher choosing reserve prices; many advertisers bidding for impressions over campaign horizons
- **Timing:** The publisher moves first and chooses a reserve price. For repeated impression arrivals, advertisers observe their private values, the reserve, and a stationary distribution of the maximum competing bid and choose bids subject to minimum-impression and participation constraints. The induced bid distribution must be consistent with advertisers' conjectures, and the publisher anticipates that equilibrium response.
- **Actions:** the publisher selects a reserve price; each advertiser selects a valuation-contingent bid function; advertisers participate across repeated second-price auctions during their campaigns
- **Information:** The publisher knows the distribution of advertiser valuations but not each realized private value.; An advertiser observes its own valuation and can infer the reserve price from repeated auction experience.; Advertisers know the stationary distribution of the maximum competing bid rather than rivals' individual states.; Advertiser conjectures about the competing-bid distribution are correct in fluid mean-field equilibrium.
- **Objective:** The publisher chooses the reserve price to maximize the long-run expected revenue rate from advertiser payments plus the outside value of unsold impressions, subject to advertisers' equilibrium complementarity conditions for impression constraints.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_r\;\eta\sum_{\theta}\lambda p_{\theta}s_{\theta}G_{\theta}(\boldsymbol\mu,r)+\eta cI(\boldsymbol\mu,r),\quad \text{s.t. }\mu_{\theta}\ge0\;\perp\; y_{\theta}\le\eta s_{\theta}\mathbb E_{V,D}[\mathbf 1\{V+\mu_{\theta}\ge D\}],\;\forall\theta\in\Theta.$ (Equation (3), publisher reserve-price problem, printed p. 9 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Fluid mean-field equilibrium of repeated display-ad auctions
- **Solution:** The first experiment shows that positive reserve prices raise publisher revenue by about 35% relative to zero reserves. Bid responses are consistent with minimum-impression rather than budget constraints: when reach becomes binding, advertisers add a constant premium above value. Accounting for that behavior in reserve optimization raises the estimated gain to 44%, nine percentage points above a model that ignores campaign constraints. The validation experiment finds revenues generally highest near the model-recommended reserve levels.
- **Evidence:** An initial reserve-price experiment identifies advertiser bid responses and a 35% revenue lift over zero reserve prices.; The structural model infers advertiser valuations and binding minimum-impression constraints from auction outcomes.; A model-guided counterfactual adds nine percentage points of revenue gain, and a later field experiment validates that revenues peak near the recommended reserves.
- **Caveat:** The fluid mean-field equilibrium uses large-market, stationary-bid-distribution, and ex ante stochastic-fluid approximations and may not suit small or short-lived auction markets. The analysis is partial equilibrium, so advertisers' budgets, targeting, and channel allocation do not adapt in the long run. It studies second-price auctions and does not jointly model budget and minimum-impression constraints or direct sales; reserve prices are inferred rather than announced, and the empirical setting is one publisher and ad exchange from an earlier programmatic-advertising period.

### Consumer Impatience, Technological Innovation, and Market Structure

Chaewon Seol, Federico Rossi, Sara Valentini, and Elisa Montaguti (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2024.0885](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2024.0885). First published online: 2026-06-04.

- **Question:** How does consumers' dislike of waiting shape local price competition and survival, and how would much faster delivery change market concentration and platform profits?
- **Players:** competing pizzerias simultaneously setting weekly prices
- **Timing:** In each weekly market, differentiated pizzerias simultaneously set prices given marginal costs and the estimated consumer choice system. Consumers then choose a pizzeria or the outside option based on quality, price, and expected delivery time. Counterfactuals change delivery times or service menus and resolve the Bertrand-Nash pricing equilibrium.
- **Actions:** each pizzeria chooses its price; in counterfactuals, an exogenous technology changes delivery times and per-order costs before pizzerias reoptimize prices; the platform offers a faster premium-delivery option and fee
- **Information:** Pizzerias are modeled as knowing the demand system and competitors' available products when setting prices.; Consumers observe platform listings and use distance and experience to form expected delivery times.; Researchers observe orders, prices, store and consumer locations, and actual delivery times but recover unobserved quality and marginal costs structurally.; Demand includes consumer-level heterogeneity and type-I extreme-value choice shocks.
- **Objective:** Pizzeria j chooses its weekly price to maximize its margin times market size and its demand share under differentiated Bertrand competition.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_{jt}=(p_{jt}-mc_{jt})M_t s(p_{jt}).$ (Equation (4), supply-side profit, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 8))
- **Equilibrium:** Static differentiated Bertrand-Nash price equilibrium
- **Solution:** The median consumer values a 50% delivery-time reduction at more than 20% of the order price, and cross-price substitution falls sharply with distance. Faster delivery therefore has a nonmonotone effect on structure: moderate reductions erode downtown proximity advantages and reduce concentration, but reductions beyond roughly 75% increasingly concentrate demand among high-quality pizzerias and push many low- and midquality firms toward exit. With a fixed platform cost of EUR0.80 per premium order, a premium option that is 10% faster for a fee equal to 10% of the order price raises simulated platform profit by 18.7% while also increasing consumer welfare.
- **Evidence:** The data contain 97,552 orders by 6,851 consumers across 51 pizzerias, including consumer and store locations.; Demand uses random coefficients for quality, price, and delivery time; cost shifters instrument for endogenous prices.; Counterfactuals recompute equilibrium prices and demand after delivery-time reductions and evaluate a paid faster-delivery option.
- **Caveat:** The evidence comes from one northern Italian city's pizza-delivery platform in 2010-2011 and omits phone and in-person orders. The model treats weekly prices as a static single-product Bertrand game, approximates expected delivery time from distance, holds basket choice and product quality fixed, and imposes broad technology adoption. Exit follows a heuristic 30% profit-loss threshold, while technology costs and premium-service design are simulated rather than observed responses to an actual delivery breakthrough.

### On the Value of Coalition Loyalty Programs

Yan Liu, Jingmai Wang, Yulan Wang, and Dan Zhang (2026). DOI: [10.1287/mksc.2024.1138](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2024.1138). First published online: 2026-06-17.

- **Question:** When should firms replace proprietary loyalty programs with a coalition, and how should the coalition set price, reward, and membership size to discriminate among customers?
- **Players:** a coalition program designer acting for participating firms; forward-looking heterogeneous customers choosing whether to purchase
- **Timing:** Given an exogenous exponential reward-expiration rate, the coalition chooses a constant price, reward, and number of participating firms. Over an infinite continuous-time horizon, customers arrive at coalition firms according to Poisson processes and choose whether to buy with or without a valid reward. Rewards are earned on purchase, may be redeemed at any member before expiration, and customers discount future surplus.
- **Actions:** the coalition chooses price and reward for a fixed membership size and then selects coalition size; each arriving customer chooses whether to purchase based on valuation, reward state, and continuation value; the analysis compares the optimized coalition outcome with proprietary and no-reward program benchmarks
- **Information:** The program designer knows the population shares of four valuation-shopping-intensity segments.; A customer knows her valuation, shopping intensity, current reward state, price, reward, expiration rate, and coalition size.; Customer arrivals and reward expiration are stochastic, but their rates are common knowledge.; The base coalition is symmetric and abstracts from direct competition among participating firms.
- **Objective:** For a fixed coalition size, the designer chooses price and reward to maximize long-run average profit per firm from frequent customers and high-valuation infrequent customers, accounting for their different discounted reward-redemption probabilities.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi^*(n)=\beta\lambda_F\left(v_L+\frac{n\lambda_F}{\delta+n\lambda_F+\mu}r^*-\frac{n\lambda_F}{n\lambda_F+\mu}r^*\right)+(\alpha-\gamma)\lambda_I\left(v_L+\frac{n\lambda_F}{\delta+n\lambda_F+\mu}r^*-\frac{n\lambda_I}{n\lambda_I+\mu}r^*\right).$ (Equation (4), optimal per-firm coalition profit, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Coalition-optimal design with dynamic customer best responses
- **Solution:** A profitable coalition targets all frequent customers plus high-valuation infrequent customers and discriminates by shopping intensity rather than directly by valuation. Relative to no reward program, a negative correlation between valuation and shopping intensity is necessary for coalition adoption (Proposition 1). In valuation-driven markets, per-firm profit rises with coalition size and a properly designed coalition beats a proprietary program. In intensity-driven markets, profit can be hump-shaped in membership, so an intermediate coalition or even a proprietary program can be best (Proposition 2). Without customer discounting, per-firm profit no longer falls with coalition size.
- **Evidence:** Lemma 1 characterizes the optimal price, reward, and per-firm profit for fixed coalition size.; Proposition 1 compares coalition programs with no reward program and identifies the role of valuation-shopping-intensity correlation.; Proposition 2 characterizes optimal coalition size and the comparison with proprietary programs; later sections relax discounting, symmetry, and reward-renewal assumptions.
- **Caveat:** The base model assumes symmetric coalition firms, no direct member competition, exogenous customer arrivals and valuations, zero marginal cost, a constant state-independent price, one nonaccumulating reward, exogenous exponential expiration, and a stylized four-segment market. Coalition formation, member bargaining, program-administrator incentives, and empirical validation are outside the model; its prescriptions isolate price discrimination rather than loyalty, search-cost, or cross-selling effects.

## Information Systems Research

### Blessing or Curse? Implications of Data Brokers for Publisher Competition

Xin Zhang; Wei Thoo Yue; Ran (Alan) Zhang; Yugang Yu (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2022.0227](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2022.0227). First published online: 2024-04-01.

- **Question:** When should a data broker sell collective insights exclusively or nonexclusively to competing publishers, and how do those choices affect publisher competition, advertiser surplus, and aggregate welfare?
- **Players:** monopoly data broker; large publisher (Publisher 1); small publisher (Publisher 2); a unit mass of heterogeneous advertisers
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the data broker sets the price w per analyzed data set. Stage 2: each publisher chooses individual insights O or collective insights B. Stage 3: the two publishers simultaneously set advertising prices p_i. Stage 4: advertisers choose the publisher that gives them the higher utility. The broker anticipates all downstream responses.
- **Actions:** the data broker chooses the insight price and thereby implements an OO, OB, BO, or BB selling regime; each publisher chooses individual or collective insights; each publisher chooses its advertising price; advertisers choose where to buy targeted advertising
- **Information:** The broker's analytics capability alpha, publisher data sizes, data externality gamma, and the pricing menu are common knowledge.; Publishers observe the broker's price before selecting insights and observe purchasing choices when competing in advertising prices.; Advertisers know publishers' insight-purchase decisions and prices. Each advertiser has a traffic valuation v drawn from the common-knowledge uniform distribution U[0,1]; the model does not require an advertiser's individual draw to be publicly observed.
- **Objective:** Publisher i maximizes advertising revenue net of its data-insight fee; anticipating publisher purchase and pricing responses, the data broker chooses w to maximize its fee revenue.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_i(s_i)=\begin{cases}p_iD_i-w,&s_i=O,\\ p_iD_i-2w,&s_i=B.\end{cases}$ (Section 3.2, p. 266 (PDF p. 6); the broker's corresponding revenues 2w, 3w, and 4w are stated in Section 3.1, p. 265 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the broker-led data-insight pricing game
- **Solution:** Lemma 2 shows that price thresholds generate nonexclusive BB, exclusive OB or BO, and individual-only OO purchase equilibria. Proposition 1 shows that the broker may profitably make collective insights exclusive to either the large or small publisher rather than sell them to both. Propositions 2-4 trace how analytics capability and data externality move the market across regimes and can create discontinuous changes in advertiser and publisher payoffs. Proposition 5 shows that data sharing always raises advertiser surplus relative to prohibited sharing, while aggregate welfare rises in BO and rises in OB or BB only when data externality is sufficiently strong.
- **Evidence:** Four-stage game with a monopoly data broker, two asymmetric publishers, and a unit mass of heterogeneous advertisers; Closed-form advertising-price equilibria and publisher data-purchase regions, followed by the broker's optimal pricing regime; Parameter-region and welfare figures illustrate the analytical regime changes; no structural estimation is performed
- **Caveat:** Section 6.3 identifies two principal limitations: the baseline has a monopoly data broker acting as leader, and the broker's analytics capability is exogenous. The baseline also imposes a flat-fee menu and full advertiser coverage; Section 5 relaxes independent pricing, market coverage, purchase participation, and advertiser multihoming, but the model should not be read as evidence for markets with competing brokers or endogenous analytics investment.

### Navigating Platform-Led Affiliate Marketing: Implications for Content Creation and Platform Profitability

Meilin Gu; Dengpan Liu; Subodha Kumar (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2022.0620](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2022.0620). First published online: 2024-07-05.

- **Question:** When should a UGC platform adopt affiliate marketing, how should it split commissions with creators, and how does the model affect content quality, consumer welfare, and affiliated and nonaffiliated creators?
- **Players:** UGC platform; m affiliated content creators; n-m nonaffiliated content creators; content consumers represented in aggregate
- **Timing:** With affiliate marketing, stage 0 has the platform announce commission-split rate alpha. In stage 1, affiliated and nonaffiliated creators simultaneously choose production efforts. In stage 2, consumers observe resulting content quality, allocate consumption time across creators, and may purchase through affiliate links. Without affiliate marketing, the platform has no stage-0 commission decision.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses the commission share retained from affiliate transactions; each creator chooses content-production effort; consumers choose time spent on each creator's content and make purchases during shoppable-content consumption
- **Information:** Creators observe the platform's commission share before choosing effort.; Consumers observe realized content quality before allocating attention.; The numbers of creators, affiliate eligibility, cost and demand parameters, and content substitutability are common knowledge in the baseline.
- **Objective:** The platform chooses its commission share to maximize traffic revenue plus affiliate commissions, net of the per-unit incentive paid to creators, while anticipating creator effort and consumer attention.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{\alpha}\;\pi=\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_i+\alpha(\omega+\lambda\eta)\sum_{i\in M}t_i-\xi\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_i$ (Equation (5), p. 810 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium of the platform-led affiliate-marketing game
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 shows that affiliate marketing raises content quality and consumer welfare only when base marginal commission revenue exceeds threshold omega_1. Proposition 2 shows that the platform adopts only above a second threshold omega_2 because commission revenue may fail to offset lost traffic. Proposition 3 finds affiliated creators are always better off, whereas nonaffiliates benefit only below omega_1. Proposition 4 shows that more intense creator competition calls for a lower platform commission share when shoppable-content nuisance is large, but a higher share when nuisance is small. Proposition 5 and its corollaries show that intensified competition need not make affiliated creators increase effort and that the response depends on whether competition rises through creator count or substitutability.
- **Evidence:** Three-stage platform-creator-consumer game comparing regimes with and without platform-led affiliate marketing; Closed-form creator effort, consumer attention, commission split, and stakeholder payoffs; Four extensions test creator heterogeneity and endogenous mechanisms; selected extensions use numerical analysis rather than field estimation
- **Caveat:** The main model uses one platform, aggregate consumers, symmetric creators, an exogenous number of affiliate participants, and an exogenous platform incentive. Section 7 relaxes creator cost symmetry, endogenizes incentives and participation, and varies the quality-commission link, but the results do not establish behavior under heterogeneous consumer tastes or direct competition among UGC platforms.

### Dynamics of Shared Security in the Cloud

Nan Clement; Daniel Arce (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2023.0256](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0256). First published online: 2024-07-29.

- **Question:** How do cloud providers' and users' joint security investments, cloud usage, provider competition, and switching costs shape the long-run paths of cloud security, vulnerability, lock-in, and user welfare?
- **Players:** Cloud Service Provider 1; Cloud Service Provider 2; n users initially subscribed to each provider
- **Timing:** In each period t, each CSP first chooses security investment s_csp,j,t. Given the provider's investment, its users choose their own security investments s_i,t. Users then choose cloud-service usage y_i,t under the resulting security umbrella; stay/switch choices must satisfy no-switching and participation constraints. Accumulated security S_j,t and vulnerability V_j,t become the next period's Markov states.
- **Actions:** each CSP chooses period security investment; each user chooses period security investment; each user chooses cloud-service usage; users may stay with or switch from the incumbent CSP subject to security-linked switching costs
- **Information:** At the beginning of period t, players observe the incumbent CSP's accumulated vulnerability and security states (V_j,t-1,S_j,t-1).; Strategies condition on the Markov states rather than the full history.; The numbers of users, state transition functions, cost and benefit functions, and security responsibilities are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** Each user maximizes the discounted stream of cloud-service benefits net of expected breach loss, security investment cost, and any security-linked switching cost.
- **Representative equation:** `$U_{i,j}=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\delta^t u_{i,t},\qquad u_{i,t}=[1-p(V_{j,t})c]b(y_{i,t})-ks_{i,t}-\lambda S_{j,t-1}$ (Equation (4), p. 924 (PDF p. 9), and the lifetime payoff definition, p. 926 (PDF p. 11))
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric stationary Markov-perfect equilibrium with CSP no-switching constraints
- **Solution:** Propositions 1-3 show that others' security can raise a user's current payoff, yet user-user and CSP-user security investments are strategic substitutes; greater CSP responsibility intensifies that substitution. Propositions 4-7 characterize the Euler path: security raises usage, and greater use by others raises a user's vulnerability, so accumulated vulnerability can either converge or increase depending on persistence and forward-looking incentives. Proposition 8 establishes that competing CSPs' minimum security levels are strategic complements. Proposition 9 shows sufficiently strong security-linked switching cost makes participation rather than switching the binding constraint, generating effective lock-in. The later CSP-profit results and robustness sections show competition can improve user welfare while security-based lock-in attenuates competitive pressure.
- **Evidence:** Infinite-horizon model with two CSPs, evenly divided identical users, accumulated security, and accumulated vulnerability; Euler-equation and value-function analysis of the equilibrium vulnerability and usage paths; Weakest-link security and quadratic security-cost variants test robustness; no field estimation is reported
- **Caveat:** Section 7.2 states that users are homogeneous despite provider-user asymmetry, so the model omits sorting by heterogeneous security preferences. It also leaves government/open-standard intervention, multihoming costs, interoperability, and alternative technology paths for future work. The baseline duopoly and additive security aggregation therefore should not be generalized directly to heterogeneous multi-cloud markets.

### Better Is Better? Signaling Paradoxes in Performance-Based Advertising

Ran Pan; Juan Feng (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2021.0419](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2021.0419). First published online: 2024-07-31.

- **Question:** How do product reputation and advertising reach affect the ability of performance-based advertising to signal quality, and which attribution/payment rules preserve credible signaling?
- **Players:** privately informed product-selling firm, whose type is high or low quality; heterogeneous consumers
- **Timing:** Nature determines quality q in {H,L}, observed by the firm but not consumers. The firm chooses whether to incur performance-based advertising expenditure as a quality signal; the analysis asks which per-unit fee a can sustain separation. In period 1, consumers observe whether the advertising signal is present, form quality perceptions, and decide whether to purchase. In period 2, loyal consumers repurchase and a quality-dependent share of other first-period buyers repurchases; the exogenous attribution rule determines which sales enter advertising expenditure.
- **Actions:** the informed firm chooses whether to use costly performance-based advertising as a quality signal; consumers update perceived quality after observing the signal and choose whether to purchase in period 1; eligible first-period buyers choose or realize repeat purchase in period 2; consumer purchases and repurchases generate the actions counted by the exogenous advertising-payment rule
- **Information:** The firm privately knows whether product quality is H or L.; Consumers have an equal prior over the two qualities and observe the advertising signal but not true quality before purchase.; Consumer willingness to pay is private and uniformly distributed; price P is exogenous and public.; Product-reputation factor beta and ad-signal reach eta determine which consumers are loyal or exposed to the signal.
- **Objective:** A separating equilibrium requires advertising to be profitable for the high-quality type after its performance fee but unprofitable as a mimicking strategy for the low-quality type.
- **Representative equation:** `$\exists a>0:\quad \ddot{\pi}(\beta,\eta;H)-A(a;H)>\dot{\pi}(\beta,\eta;H),\qquad \ddot{\pi}(\beta,\eta;L)-A(a;L)\le\dot{\pi}(\beta,\eta;L)$ (Equation (7), p. 1221 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Separating sequential equilibrium of the performance-based advertising signaling game
- **Solution:** Lemma 1 gives the baseline separating-equilibrium interval. Proposition 1 establishes the product-reputation paradox: except under a stated quality-demand condition, higher reputation makes separation harder because loyal sales inflate the high type's advertising bill. Proposition 2 establishes the reach paradox: broader signal reach can likewise make separation harder by increasing charged repeat purchases. Scheme I excludes loyal and repeat purchases; Proposition 3 shows it resolves the reputation paradox, but Proposition 4 shows the reach paradox remains. Scheme II charges only incremental first-period sales caused by advertising, and Proposition 5 gives a separating condition independent of beta and eta, eliminating both attribution distortions subject to the quality-cost condition.
- **Evidence:** Two-quality, two-period signaling model with reputation-affected, advertising-affected, and residual consumer segments; Incentive-compatibility inequalities characterize when a separating equilibrium exists; Two modified performance-payment schemes isolate which attributed sales generate the reputation and reach paradoxes
- **Caveat:** The conclusion states two limitations: the model abstracts from advertising-auction pricing and competition, and it treats product price as exogenous. It also uses binary quality, an equal prior, uniform willingness to pay, and stylized two-period attribution, so the separating conditions should not be carried directly to endogenous-price or multi-advertiser auction environments.

### How to Make My Bug Bounty Cost-Effective? A Game-Theoretical Model

Leting Zhang; Emre M. Demirezen; Subodha Kumar (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2021.0349](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2021.0349). First published online: 2024-09-03.

- **Question:** How should an organization set a bug bounty when researcher productivity, crowd size, security posture, patching complexity, postdiscovery leakage, and legal protection jointly affect vulnerability lifecycle costs?
- **Players:** organization running the bug-bounty program; n external security researchers with heterogeneous productivity
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the organization publicly commits to bounty b. Stage 2: after observing b, researchers simultaneously choose effort in a Bayesian winner-take-all tournament. The earliest valid report arrives at time I; the organization then patches for omega beta time, after which the modeled vulnerability no longer creates loss.
- **Actions:** the organization chooses the bounty amount; each researcher chooses search effort; the first successful researcher submits the valid vulnerability report; the organization undertakes remediation during the postdiscovery patching interval
- **Information:** The bounty and legal-protection level are public.; Each researcher's productivity a_i is privately known; the uniform productivity distribution and number of researchers are common knowledge.; The organization's security posture, damage, leakage, and patching parameters are common knowledge in the baseline.; Researchers form winning probabilities from the symmetric best-response performance function.
- **Objective:** The organization chooses bounty b to minimize the bounty itself plus expected damage before discovery, expected leakage during patching, and expected damage during the patching interval.
- **Representative equation:** `$\min_b\;\Pi=b+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_0^I c_a\beta\,dt+\int_I^{I+\omega\beta}c_p n g l\beta\,dt+\int_I^{I+\omega\beta}c_a\beta^2\,dt\right]$ (Equation (1), p. 1039 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect leader-follower outcome with a symmetric Bayesian tournament equilibrium among researchers
- **Solution:** Lemma 1 shows bounty and legal protection raise equilibrium search effort; Lemma 2 derives the optimal bounty. Proposition 1 finds greater patching complexity lowers the bounty, while weaker security posture can raise or lower it depending on patching complexity. Propositions 2-3 show productivity heterogeneity and researcher count have nonmonotone effects on the bounty. Proposition 4 shows improving novice productivity can increase total cost when postdiscovery leakage cost is high, whereas improving expert productivity always reduces total cost. Proposition 5 identifies conditions under which adding researchers raises rather than lowers total BBP cost. Proposition 6 shows stronger legal protection can raise or lower both the bounty and total cost because incentive, prediscovery, and leakage effects move in different directions.
- **Evidence:** Two-stage organization-researcher game with a winner-take-all tournament among n privately productive researchers; Expected cost integrates bounty, prediscovery damage, postdiscovery leakage, and patching-period damage; Closed-form equilibrium effort and bounty support comparative statics; figures illustrate thresholds without estimating the model
- **Caveat:** Section 5.3 calls for empirical measurement of BBP returns and costs, social-welfare analysis with users, multiple firms or bounty platforms, and a richer model of researchers choosing whether to report, exploit, or sell a discovered vulnerability. The baseline also focuses on one vulnerability, costless entry, uniform private productivity, and exogenous security posture, although online extensions relax several of these assumptions.

### Player-vs.-Player Game Design and Pricing: A Tournament Design Perspective

Haowen Deng; Yifan Dou; Zenan Wu; Cheng Zhang (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2023.0258](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0258). First published online: 2024-10-25.

- **Question:** How should a PvP game developer jointly design version quality, prices, and competitive balance to monetize paying players without driving away free or budget-constrained players?
- **Players:** monopolistic PvP game developer; a unit mass of potential players with heterogeneous quality valuation and game budget
- **Timing:** Stage 1: anticipating downstream demand, the developer chooses the number of versions K, qualities s_i, prices p_i, and antisymmetric competitive-balance matrix T. Stage 2: players form expectations about the installed-base composition, observe version attributes and pairwise advantages, and choose the affordable version giving highest net utility or remain out. Realized version shares must equal expected shares.
- **Actions:** the developer chooses the product line, intrinsic qualities, prices, and pairwise winning advantages; each player chooses one affordable game version or the outside option; players are randomly matched for one-on-one battles, generating version-specific network utility
- **Information:** The developer knows the distributions of player quality valuations and budgets but not individual types.; Each player knows the developer's full strategy profile, the competitive advantage of every version, and the player's own valuation and budget.; Players form beliefs about all other players' version choices; equilibrium requires expected and realized player composition to coincide.; When multiple stage-2 equilibria exist, the model selects the one most favorable to the developer.
- **Objective:** The developer jointly chooses the number and design of versions, their prices, and the tournament-balance matrix to maximize sales revenue under equilibrium version demand.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{\{K,\mathbf{s},\mathbf{p},\mathbf{T}\}}\;\Pi=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{K}}p_iQ_i$ (Developer's profit-maximization problem, p. 1465 (PDF p. 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Developer-optimal product and tournament design subject to a fulfilled-expectations player version-choice equilibrium
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 shows that without tournament design the developer offers two paid versions and excludes free-only players. Proposition 2 constructs an optimal four-version design with two free and two paid versions, using tilted win probabilities to segment both player groups; the resulting profit weakly exceeds the fair-game benchmark and strictly exceeds it when budget-constrained players exist. Propositions 3-4 show multiple optimal designs are possible but every optimum with tournament design uses freemium and multiple free versions. Propositions 5-6 show tournament design insulates installed base and profit from reluctance to pay and accommodates positive tight budgets. Proposition 7 establishes a Pareto improvement relative to fair play: developer profit rises and every player's surplus weakly rises.
- **Evidence:** Two-stage developer-player model with endogenous version-specific network effects generated by pairwise winning probabilities; Closed-form optimal versions, qualities, prices, balance matrices, and equilibrium market segments; A stylized two-group parameter example motivates the mechanism; no player-level estimation is reported
- **Caveat:** The conclusion identifies three extensions: competition among multiple developers, heterogeneous player skill with endogenous matchmaking, and bounded rationality. The baseline instead has one developer, random matching, fully rational players who accurately compare versions, and developer-favorable equilibrium selection when network effects create multiplicity.

### To Partner or Not to Partner? The Partnership Between Platforms and Data Brokers in Two-Sided Markets

Xin Zhang; Lihong Cheng; Yugang Yu; Yong Tan (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2022.0470](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2022.0470). First published online: 2024-11-04.

- **Question:** When should competing advertising platforms partner with a data broker, and how do targeting improvements, data fees, and privacy concerns affect platform profit, user welfare, and privacy protection?
- **Players:** two competing digital platforms A and B; a unit mass of single-homing consumers; single-homing and multihoming advertisers
- **Timing:** In stage 1, the two platforms simultaneously choose whether to partner with the data broker. In stage 2, they simultaneously set advertiser prices. In stage 3, consumers and advertisers choose platforms given partnership and price choices, with rational expectations about participation on the opposite side. The privacy-protection extension adds high-versus-low protection choices when both platforms partner.
- **Actions:** each platform chooses whether to partner with the data broker; each platform chooses its advertising price; consumers choose one platform; single-homing advertisers choose one platform and multihoming advertisers use both; platforms choose high or low privacy protection in the extension
- **Information:** Partnership decisions and advertising prices are observed before users choose platforms.; Consumers know whether a platform partners with the broker and anticipate the privacy cost associated with advertiser participation.; Consumers and advertisers form rational expectations about cross-side demand that are fulfilled in equilibrium.; Market primitives and the exogenous data price are common knowledge in the baseline.
- **Objective:** Given its partnership status, platform i earns advertising revenue and, if partnered, pays the broker per consumer record; in the pricing stage it chooses p_i to maximize this profit while anticipating both market sides.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p_i}\;\pi_i=p_i y_i-I_i\gamma x_i$ (Platform profit definitions in Section 3.1, p. 1442 (PDF p. 6), together with the stage-2 pricing problem in Section 4.1)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium with rational-expectations platform participation
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 moves the equilibrium from neither platform partnering, to asymmetric partnership, to both partnering as privacy concern or targeting improvement rises. Proposition 2 identifies a region in which bilateral partnership is a prisoner's dilemma. Proposition 3 shows that bilateral partnership lowers consumer surplus in the ad-sponsored baseline, raises advertiser surplus only when privacy concern is small, and raises social welfare exactly when targeting improvement exceeds the privacy increment. Proposition 4 finds high-high, asymmetric, and low-low privacy-protection equilibria as the privacy increment rises. The mixed subscription-advertising extension can reverse the consumer-surplus result because partnership intensifies consumer-price competition.
- **Evidence:** A three-stage game compares no, unilateral, and bilateral data-broker partnership configurations.; Closed-form advertising-price equilibria feed into discrete partnership choices and welfare comparisons.; A separate privacy-protection game permits symmetric high or low protection and asymmetric protection.; Extensions change the business model, advertiser homing, payment contract, targeting technology, and platform symmetry.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses symmetric Hotelling platforms, full market coverage, free consumer access, an exogenous multihoming share, exogenous per-record broker pricing, and additive targeting/privacy effects. Extensions relax many of these assumptions, but the study remains a stylized two-platform model rather than an empirical estimate of a particular broker market.

### Should Ad Exchanges Subsidize Advertisers to Acquire Targeting Data?

Wangsheng Zhu; Shaojie Tang; Vijay Mookerjee (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2023.0126](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0126). First published online: 2024-11-26.

- **Question:** When should an ad exchange subsidize advertisers' third-party targeting-data costs, how large should that subsidy be, and should eligibility depend on whether an informed advertiser wins or loses the auction?
- **Players:** one ad exchange that chooses a subsidy mechanism and subsidy amount; N ex ante symmetric advertisers that choose whether to acquire targeting data and submit bids
- **Timing:** The ad exchange first announces a subsidy amount under the selected all-subsidized, loser-subsidized, or winner-subsidized framework. Advertisers next decide whether to incur the targeting-data cost. After a user generates an impression, each advertiser selects an ad and submits a bid using the information available to it. The exchange allocates the impression through a second-price auction, collects the second-highest bid, and pays subsidies according to the announced framework.
- **Actions:** the ad exchange selects the subsidy framework and commits to a nonnegative subsidy; each advertiser chooses whether to acquire additional targeting data; each advertiser selects an ad and submits an impression-specific bid; the exchange allocates the impression, charges the auction payment, and pays eligible subsidies
- **Information:** The distribution of impression values and all model primitives are public knowledge.; Whether the current impression is high or low value for a particular advertiser is that advertiser's private information when it acquires the feature data.; An uninformed advertiser observes only the prior and bids the expected value of its best average ad.; Advertisers' targeting features and impression values are independent across advertisers in the main model.
- **Objective:** Under the all-subsidized framework, the platform chooses the subsidy to maximize the expected second-highest bid net of the subsidy paid to every advertiser that acquired data, conditional on the acquisition profile.
- **Representative equation:** `$\mathbb{E}\!\left[SH(b_1,\ldots,b_N)-s\sum_{i=1}^{N}d_i\mid d_1,\ldots,d_N\right].$ (Equation (5), p. 1510 (PDF p. 9))
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium of platform subsidy, advertiser data acquisition, and auction bidding
- **Solution:** Theorem 1 shows that all-subsidized support can raise platform net revenue only in intermediate data-cost regions; very low costs already induce acquisition, while sufficiently high costs make inducement unprofitable. Theorem 2 shows that subsidy-induced competition can lower naturally informed advertisers' payoffs while benefiting advertisers that remain uninformed. Proposition 2 and Theorem 3 show that loser subsidies soften bidding competition and are weakly dominated by all-subsidized support. Winner subsidies raise informed bids, but Theorems 4 and 5 and Proposition 4 show that their advantage over all-subsidized support depends on data cost, value distributions, ad-selection gains, and the number of advertisers. The first-price extension finds weakly lower platform net revenue than its second-price counterpart when endogenous acquisition breaks bidder symmetry.
- **Evidence:** Lemma 1 derives dominant truthful bidding conditional on the advertiser's acquired information under the all-subsidized framework, after which the paper characterizes equilibrium data acquisition and the platform's optimal subsidy.; Theorems 1 and 2 characterize when all-subsidized support is profitable and how induced acquisition redistributes advertiser payoffs.; Proposition 2 and Theorem 3 show that loser subsidies lower informed advertisers' bids and that all-subsidized net revenue weakly dominates loser-subsidized net revenue.; Theorems 4 and 5 and Proposition 4 compare winner-subsidized and all-subsidized mechanisms across data costs, ad-selection gains, value distributions, and market size.; The first-price-auction, heterogeneous targeting-ability, and noisy-data extensions test the robustness of the mechanism comparisons.
- **Caveat:** The main model holds the exchange's basic-data configuration fixed and studies only additional targeting data. It assumes that acquisition occurs before advertisers observe the platform's basic user data, whereas real-time acquisition after observing basic data is left for future research. The baseline also uses ex ante symmetric advertisers, independent binary targeting features, common acquisition cost and data quality, and a second-price auction, with selected departures handled only in extensions.

### Walrasian Pricing for Combinatorial Markets with Compact-Bidding Languages: An Application to Truckload Transportation

Mohsen Emadikhiav; Robert Day (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2023.0676](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0676). First published online: 2025-01-30.

- **Question:** Can a truckload procurement market use compact bids to allocate bundles efficiently while producing simple, anonymous, budget-balanced prices that carriers and shippers can interpret?
- **Players:** a shipper or shipper conglomerate procuring coverage for lanes; multiple carriers that submit package or compact network bids and may exchange lane obligations
- **Timing:** Carriers submit bids describing costs and feasible lane bundles. The auctioneer first solves the winner-determination problem. It then runs iterative dual pricing: a winner-aware dual proposes lane prices, carrier-specific separation problems identify preferred nonwinning packages, and violated Walrasian constraints are added until none remains. Final lane prices determine carrier and shipper payments.
- **Actions:** carriers report package costs or compact network and lane-cost information; under the exchange format, carriers may buy and sell existing lane obligations; the shipper procures the required lane coverage under the allocation and anonymous-pricing rules
- **Information:** Carriers privately know their networks, existing contracts, operational constraints, and lane-covering costs.; The baseline compact-bidding benchmark assumes disclosure of network information to a trusted auctioneer.; The experiments also vary partial disclosure and quantify the efficiency cost of withholding private network information.; The auctioneer observes submitted bids but does not require full enumeration of all possible packages.
- **Objective:** The enumerative reverse-auction winner-determination problem minimizes the submitted cost of winning carrier packages plus the cost of covering residual lane demand in the spot market.
- **Representative equation:** `$\min_{\chi,r}\;\sum_{s\in S} b_s\chi_s+\sum_{l\in L_0}\gamma_l r_l\quad\text{subject to lane coverage, XOR, and integrality constraints}$ (Problem (1a)-(1e), p. 1723 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Exact or epsilon-Walrasian equilibrium with anonymous linear lane prices
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 links a zero relaxation gap to individual rationality and Walrasian prices. Propositions 2-5 establish the relation between compact and enumerative formulations, polynomially solvable separation, finite termination, strong budget balance, and exact Walrasian implementation. Numerical experiments report average total-cost savings of 14.24% in procurement-only markets and 39.72% with full lane exchange. Relative to VCG, iterative dual pricing preserves positive shipper surplus while still giving carriers large gains; clique cuts eliminate or sharply reduce residual envy in nearly all instances.
- **Evidence:** An enumerative XOR winner-determination problem provides the theoretical allocation and pricing benchmark.; A polynomial compact-bidding formulation and dynamically generated equilibrium constraints make computation practical.; Propositions establish exact Walrasian equilibrium when the integer-program relaxation is tight and epsilon-Walrasian pricing otherwise.; Generated truckload instances compare procurement-only and lane-exchange markets under iterative dual pricing and VCG.
- **Caveat:** The mechanism relies on a trusted auctioneer or secure computation and assumes carriers are willing to reveal enough private network information. The proposed Walrasian pricing is not strategy-proof like VCG, exact equilibrium depends on the relaxation gap, and the numerical evidence uses generated instances. Stronger cuts, manipulability under different bid languages, and short-term time-space implementations remain open directions.

### Mergers Between On-Demand Service Platforms: The Impact on Consumer Surplus and Labor Welfare

Xiaogang Lin; Tao Lu; Xin Wang; Gang Kou (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2022.0553](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2022.0553). First published online: 2025-01-31.

- **Question:** When can a merger of on-demand platforms improve consumer surplus and independent-worker welfare despite reducing price and wage competition?
- **Players:** two competing on-demand service platforms before the merger; a merged firm controlling both platforms after the merger; a population of single-homing customers; a population of independent service agents
- **Timing:** In the premerger game, the two platforms simultaneously choose customer prices and agent wages. Customers and agents then choose a platform or the outside option, generating a two-sided participation fixed point. In the postmerger counterfactual, one firm jointly chooses a common price and wage for the two retained platforms and pools agents to serve demand from both.
- **Actions:** each premerger platform chooses its service price and agent wage; customers choose platform 1, platform 2, or the outside option; agents choose platform 1, platform 2, or nonparticipation; the postmerger firm jointly chooses price and wage while pooling agents
- **Information:** Prices and wages are observable across market sides in the baseline.; Customers and agents know market primitives and anticipate participation, congestion, utilization, and matching outcomes.; An extension makes wages unobservable to customers and prices unobservable to agents and imposes passive beliefs off equilibrium.; The merger and the postmerger pooling rule are common knowledge.
- **Objective:** Each premerger platform chooses its price and wage to maximize the margin per completed transaction times the number of matches, taking the rival's choices and two-sided participation into account.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p_i,w_i}\;\Pi_i(p_i,w_i\mid p_j,w_j)=(p_i-w_i)\min\{n_iN,k_iK\mu\}$ (Equation (3), p. 1617 (PDF p. 6))
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric Nash equilibrium of premerger price-wage competition and the postmerger joint optimum
- **Solution:** Proposition 1 shows that a merger increases the weight of cross-side supply and congestion in customers' price sensitivity. Theorem 1 gives necessary-and-sufficient service-value thresholds under which consumer surplus and labor welfare rise; low service value and an unsaturated premerger market can produce a win-win-win outcome. Proposition 2 shows that price and total platform profit always rise, whereas the wage can rise or fall. Propositions 3-4 show that congestion has a potentially nonmonotone effect on consumer gains, but stronger congestion favors labor gains, and greater differentiation makes both groups more likely to benefit. Extensions show that extensive agent multihoming weakens these benefits.
- **Evidence:** A simultaneous price-and-wage game models two competing premerger platforms.; A merged firm jointly sets both platforms' prices and wages and pools agents across demand streams.; Theorems compare consumer surplus, labor welfare, prices, wages, and profit across market-coverage regimes.; Extensions study multihoming agents, unobservable prices or wages, loyal users, nonlinear congestion, repositioning, and asymmetric equilibria.
- **Caveat:** The baseline omits explicit geography, uses linear congestion and freely chosen prices and wages, studies two platforms merging into a monopoly, assumes stationary demand and supply, transparent prices and wages, single-homing agents, and symmetric equilibria. The paper relaxes several assumptions, but does not quantify a particular merger with operational or geographic data.

### A Study of Ride-Hailing Platforms’ Business Models in the Presence of Surge Demand

Haiyang Feng; Nan Feng; Ling Zhang; Zhengrui Jiang; Minqiang Li (2025). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2022.0695](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2022.0695). First published online: 2025-03-13.

- **Question:** Should a ride-hailing platform serve riders only with owned vehicles or admit private drivers, and how should it adjust vehicle capacity and normal- versus surge-period prices under each business model?
- **Players:** one monopoly ride-hailing platform that chooses its business model, owned fleet, and prices; riders in the normal and surge periods that decide whether to request service; heterogeneous private drivers that decide whether to participate when the platform is open
