- **Evidence:** Lemma 1 derives symmetric equilibrium prices, demands, and profits under traditional online selling.; The local-selling analysis separates preference-dominates-location and location-dominates-preference regimes.; Proposition 1 characterizes when local selling raises equilibrium seller prices.; Proposition 2 identifies when higher commission revenue offsets the platform's forgone fulfillment profit.; Propositions 3 and 4 trace comparative statics and show that sellers always benefit whereas consumers need not benefit from local selling.; Extensions add offline consumers, endogenous seller participation, correlated consumer dimensions, and hybrid local/national structures.
- **Caveat:** The baseline uses two symmetric sellers, linear two-dimensional differentiation, full market coverage, and exogenous commission and fulfillment terms. It abstracts from inventory, service capacity, dynamic learning, endogenous platform fee design, and broader seller entry, although extensions relax participation, correlation, and channel-structure assumptions.

### Ecosystem Competition: Platforms, Subsidiary Markets and Multihoming in the Videogames Industry

Ramnath K. Chellappa; Rajiv Mukherjee (2026). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2024.1175](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2024.1175). First published online: 2026-07-01.

- **Question:** How should console platforms coordinate hardware prices, publisher licensing fees, and per-game royalties when game purchases feed back into platform adoption and publishers may multihome?
- **Players:** two competing videogame console platforms; videogame publishers choosing platform adoption and game prices; gamers choosing a console and how many games to purchase
- **Timing:** In stage 1, the two platforms simultaneously set console fees for gamers and licensing fees for publishers, anticipating royalty revenue. In stage 2, publishers choose platform affiliation and set game prices; gamers choose a console and then purchase games. The extension allows publishers to multihome.
- **Actions:** each platform chooses gamer-side console fee and publisher-side license fee; each publisher chooses one or both platforms and a game price; each gamer chooses a console and whether to purchase games
- **Information:** Platforms and publishers know the distributions of gamer locations and game valuations.; Platforms form fulfilled expectations over cross-side adoption and use a representative expected game valuation when setting fees.; Publishers observe console and licensing fees before setting game prices; gamers observe console fees, licensing fees, and game prices before adopting a platform.
- **Objective:** Each platform chooses its gamer and publisher fees to maximize console-fee revenue, licensing revenue, and royalty revenue from game sales induced by both sides' adoption.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{\{f(p^i),l(p^i)\}}\Pi^i=n_g^if(p^i)+n_d^il(p^i)+k\mu d(p^i)n_g^in_d^i$ (Equation (9), printed p. 7 (PDF p. 7), visually verified)
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric fulfilled-expectations ecosystem-pricing equilibrium
- **Solution:** Access to downstream game surplus intensifies competition for gamers, so platforms subsidize the gamer side more deeply. With singlehoming, royalty income can coexist with higher publisher license fees. With publisher multihoming, license fees remain above traditional-model levels but vary nonmonotonically with royalties, while the share of multihoming publishers falls as royalties rise. Platform profit also becomes nonmonotone, and at sufficiently high royalty rates multihoming can leave a platform worse off than singlehoming.
- **Evidence:** Lemma 1 gives the publisher's optimal game price and downstream surplus.; Equation (9) adds publisher licensing revenue and per-game royalty revenue to each platform's objective.; Lemma 2 and Propositions 1-3 compare royalty-based ecosystem fees with traditional two-sided licensing when publishers singlehome.; The multihoming analysis derives console and licensing fees, publisher adoption shares, and their dependence on the royalty.; Propositions 5-7 show higher multihoming-side license fees, nonmonotone royalty effects, and that publisher multihoming need not improve platform profit.
- **Caveat:** The framework uses two symmetric platforms, Hotelling differentiation, full console-market coverage, uniform game values, fulfilled expectations, and a representative expected gamer valuation in platform fee setting. It abstracts from dynamic console generations, heterogeneous publishers and games, endogenous royalty contracting, and empirical estimation.

### Response to Entry in Streaming Markets: A Game-Theoretic Model

Deepika Jain; Emre M. Demirezen; Sreelata Jonnalagedda; Subodha Kumar (2026). DOI: [10.1287/isre.2022.0577](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2022.0577). First published online: 2026-07-03.

- **Question:** How should an incumbent streaming service choose subscription or usage pricing and content investment after a rival threatens entry, and when can it deter entry or retain a positional advantage?
- **Players:** an incumbent streaming platform with exclusive and nonexclusive content; a prospective entrant with nonexclusive content; heterogeneous consumers who may singlehome or multihome
- **Timing:** Stage 1: the entrant decides whether to enter and chooses subscription or usage pricing. Stage 2: the incumbent observes that choice and selects its pricing model. Stage 3: the entrant selects its price and content attractiveness. Stage 4: the incumbent selects its price and content attractiveness. Stage 5: consumers choose the incumbent, entrant, both, or neither. An extension adds an incumbent strategic-exclusivity investment at stage 0.
- **Actions:** the entrant chooses entry and a pricing model; the incumbent chooses a pricing model in response; each firm sequentially chooses a price and content-attractiveness index; consumers choose singlehoming, multihoming, or nonadoption; the incumbent may invest in strategic exclusivity in an extension
- **Information:** Consumer valuation T is uniformly distributed on [0,V].; Both firms know valuation, content-cost, overlap, and exclusivity primitives when choosing strategies.; The incumbent observes the entrant's pricing-model choice before responding.; Consumers observe both prices, pricing models, and content appeal before adoption.
- **Objective:** Consumers maximize net utility across singlehoming, multihoming, and nonadoption; for example, an incumbent-only consumer under usage pricing receives exclusivity-adjusted content value net of usage payment. The firms then choose price and content appeal to maximize their induced profits.
- **Representative equation:** `$U_I^{u}(T)=k_IT(1+\beta)(1-p_Ix)$ (Table 1, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 6), visually verified; firm profit maximization is described in Sections 3.3.2-3.3.3)
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium for entry, pricing model, price, content, and adoption
- **Solution:** Conditional on content cost being low enough for two-platform participation, the incumbent does not always differentiate: both firms use usage pricing at low consumer valuation, both use subscription at high valuation, and differentiation is common in intermediate regions subject to content cost and exclusivity. Entry is governed by a content-cost threshold, and greater willingness to pay can sometimes strengthen deterrence rather than entry because it changes the incumbent's optimal response. The incumbent's positional profit advantage can disappear at low valuation and low content cost, and the entrant can invest more in content appeal when content is cheap and the exclusivity premium is weak. Endogenous strategic exclusivity is adopted only when its incremental benefit exceeds a fixed-cost-dependent threshold.
- **Evidence:** Table 1 derives consumer utilities for singlehoming and multihoming under all four combinations of subscription and usage pricing.; Lemmas EC.1-EC.3 solve the incumbent's and entrant's pricing-model choices and the complete equilibrium by backward induction.; Proposition 1 maps pricing-model matching versus differentiation across consumer-value regions when content costs permit entry.; Proposition 2 characterizes entry-deterrence thresholds and shows that higher valuation need not monotonically strengthen entry.; Propositions 3 and 4 characterize positional profit advantage and when the entrant invests more in content appeal than the incumbent.; Section 5 adds endogenous preentry strategic exclusivity and alternative move sequences.
- **Caveat:** The model is single-period, uses uniform valuations, reduced-form catalog appeal and overlap, quadratic content costs, and an exogenous baseline exclusivity premium. It omits advertising-supported tiers, versioning, dynamic content release and retention, and empirical estimation; these are identified as directions for extending the framework.

## Manufacturing & Service Operations Management

### Product Development in Crowdfunding: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis

Sıdıka Tunç Candoğan; Philipp B. Cornelius; Bilal Gokpinar; Ersin Körpeoğlu; Christopher S. Tang (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0344](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0344). First published online: 2024-01-17.

- **Question:** How does the number of features present at campaign launch affect customer pledging and comments, the creator's later product-improvement decision, and campaign success?
- **Players:** crowdfunding creator; early customer/backer 1; later customer/backer 2
- **Timing:** Stage 0: the creator launches with a given initial feature count q_i and pledge price p=G/2; the paper derives the continuation SPE conditional on (p,q_i). Stage 1: customer 1 pledges or not. Stage 2: customer 1 may comment. Stage 3: after comments the creator decides whether/how much to improve. Stage 4: customer 2 observes final features and decides whether to pledge; both pledges are needed for funding.
- **Actions:** creator chooses whether/how much to improve the product during the campaign; initial features are a conditioning parameter in the analyzed SPE; customer 1 chooses pledge and commenting; customer 2 chooses pledge
- **Information:** Each customer's valuation v_j is privately realized and independent uniform on [0,1].; The pledge price and feature counts are observed; customer 1 anticipates later improvement and customer 2 observes final features.; Comments inform/reduce the creator's improvement cost rather than directly revealing valuation.
- **Objective:** After customer 1 pledges/comments, the creator compares expected campaign profit with product improvement against no-improvement profit, incorporating customer 2's pledge probability and feature costs.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi^I=\frac{(q_i+q_u)-b(q_i+q_u)^2-p}{(q_i+q_u)-b(q_i+q_u)^2}\left[2p-2c(q_i+q_u)^2\right]-C_iq_i-\frac{C_uq_u}{N+1}$ (main PDF, Section 2.1, displayed Stage-3 creator profit immediately before condition (1), PDF p. 6 (printed p. 706))
- **Equilibrium:** subgame-perfect equilibrium of the four-stage crowdfunding game
- **Solution:** Customer 2 first pledges above a final-quality cutoff. That success probability enters the creator's improvement profit and condition (1). Anticipating improvement, customer 1's comment and pledge cutoffs are derived, closing the SPE. If condition (1) fails, customer 1 is indifferent between commenting and not commenting; the main text selects commenting, while the positive-comment-cost robustness extension selects no comment. The empirical section operationalizes initial development and comments in 21,380 Kickstarter campaigns and checks the directional predictions with multiple econometric specifications.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; Kickstarter observational data; probit and OLS regressions, control-function instrumental variables, and recursive bivariate probit
- **Caveat:** The theory fixes the initial feature count, uses two customers, independent uniform values, an all-or-nothing threshold, and quadratic feature complexity; it does not model delivery outcomes. Empirically, the sample is limited to Kickstarter Technology and Design campaigns, text/LDA variables proxy for product features, and comment text itself is not analyzed. The policy-shock/IV strategy strengthens identification but the paper does not structurally estimate the complete equilibrium model.

### Supply Chain Contracts in the Small Data Regime

Xuejun Zhao; William B. Haskell; Guodong Yu (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0325](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0325). First published online: 2024-02-16.

- **Question:** How can a supplier set wholesale prices with few observations by combining demand samples with the retailer's revealed best-response orders and guarding against distributional ambiguity?
- **Players:** supplier as upper-level decision maker; retailer as lower-level newsvendor decision maker
- **Timing:** The supplier observes historical wholesale prices, retailer orders and demands; it constructs an augmented empirical distribution/uncertainty set and chooses new wholesale prices; the retailer, assumed to know its demand model, chooses an optimal order.
- **Actions:** supplier estimates an ambiguity set and chooses a wholesale-price vector; retailer chooses newsvendor order quantities as best responses
- **Information:** the retailer knows the demand distribution/model; the supplier has only small historical demand and price–order data; historical optimal orders impose first-order-condition restrictions on candidate distributions
- **Objective:** The robust supplier chooses wholesale prices to maximize its worst-case margin times the retailer order induced by any demand distribution in the retailer-data-compatible Wasserstein uncertainty set.
- **Representative equation:** `$S(\mathcal D):\quad\max_{w\in W}\;\min_{P\in\mathcal D}(w-c)^\top q(w;P)$ (main PDF, Section 6, robust supplier problem S(D), PDF page 7)
- **Equilibrium:** supplier-led Stackelberg/bilevel solution under distributional ambiguity
- **Solution:** Demand-only sample-average and parametric pricing can be extremely fragile with few observations. The augmented empirical distribution uses the retailer's past optimal orders to restrict plausible demand, and the compatible Wasserstein DRO model further improves robustness. The paper proves finite-dimensional reformulations, consistency and an epsilon-optimal multiproduct algorithm.
- **Evidence:** optimization theory; synthetic numerical experiments
- **Caveat:** The method assumes the retailer knows its model and historically orders optimally; finite price menus, continuity, compact support, and ambiguity aversion are material to the robust Stackelberg solution.

### Fast or Slow? Competing on Publication Frequency

Lin Chen; Guillaume Roels (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0024](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0024). First published online: 2024-02-21.

- **Question:** Should competing publishers release content frequently or slowly when publication timing changes both readers' content mix and the intensity of price competition?
- **Players:** publisher 1; publisher 2
- **Timing:** The two publishers first choose publication-cycle lengths simultaneously. Conditional on those choices, they simultaneously choose subscription/content prices, potentially using mixed strategies. Homogeneous readers then solve a downstream consumption problem that determines demand; they are not strategic players in the publisher game. Cycle choices anticipate the price subgame.
- **Actions:** publishers simultaneously choose positive publication-cycle lengths u_i; publishers simultaneously choose prices r_i in the continuation subgame
- **Information:** Costs, content technology, publication cycles, and demand primitives are common knowledge.; Publishers observe frequency choices before the price subgame and may randomize over prices.
- **Objective:** Each publisher's operating profit is price times its equilibrium demand share minus its frequency cost; the outer publication-cycle choice maximizes the expected price-subgame profit.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_1=r_1\tilde d^*(r,u)-\frac{k_1}{u_1},\quad \Pi_2=r_2\tilde w^*(r,u)-\frac{k_2}{u_2};\qquad u_i^*\in\arg\max_{u_i\ge0}\pi_i(u_i;u_{-i}^*)$ (main PDF, Section 3.3.2, Equations (8) and (10), PDF p. 7)
- **Equilibrium:** subgame-perfect equilibrium with a pure or mixed-strategy price Nash subgame
- **Solution:** For each pair of positive cycle lengths, the authors characterize downstream reader demand and solve the pricing subgame, including support and indifference conditions for mixed prices. Expected pricing profit then becomes the payoff in the cycle game. The content-based model can sustain matched cycles/pure pricing, whereas cycle-based differentiation often yields different cycles and mixed pricing. Theorem 2 does not characterize the white parameter region, even numerically.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical equilibrium mapping
- **Caveat:** The white parameter region in Theorem 2 is not characterized even numerically; only intermediate bounds around it receive partial numerical treatment. The core model has two publishers and homogeneous readers, relaxes integer publication counts to continuous cycle lengths, excludes a zero-demand cycle region, and assumes a stationary fixed market with pay-per-content revenue and no advertising, network effects, or heterogeneous reader preferences.

### Anticipated Wait and Its Effects on Consumer Choice, Pricing, and Assortment Management

Ruxian Wang; Chenxu Ke; Zifeng Zhao (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2020.0346](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2020.0346). First published online: 2024-02-26.

- **Question:** How does customers' anticipation of congestion reshape demand, assortment and prices for a multiproduct service firm and for competing firms sharing a service system?
- **Players:** customers choosing among products and the outside option; a multiproduct monopolist or competing firms
- **Timing:** Firms choose an assortment and/or prices or market shares; customers anticipate the waiting time generated by aggregate demand and choose products; realized congestion must equal the waiting time used in their choices.
- **Actions:** firms choose products, prices, or served quantities/shares; customers choose a product or opt out based on price, quality and anticipated wait
- **Information:** customers know primitives and form rational expectations of aggregate waiting; idiosyncratic tastes are private Gumbel shocks; firms understand the fixed-point demand response
- **Objective:** The monopolist chooses product prices to maximize total margin evaluated at the rational-expectations demand fixed point.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p} R(p)=\sum_i (p_i-c_i)q_i(p)$ (main PDF, Section 3.1, Equation (6), PDF page 9)
- **Equilibrium:** Rational-expectations equilibrium for customer choice; Nash equilibrium in price competition; Cournot equilibrium in the quantity/share game
- **Solution:** A unique scalar customer fixed point maps a candidate action profile into demand and waiting. For price competition, log-supermodularity yields a nonempty complete lattice of Nash equilibria and monotone tatonnement under the paper's conditions; for the quantity game, convex waiting guarantees existence and common workload can deliver uniqueness. These results show when ignoring anticipated wait reverses product and price prescriptions.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; simulation-based estimation demonstration
- **Caveat:** Price-equilibrium lattice and uniqueness statements require the paper's common-workload/log-wait conditions, and the logit tastes/shared-congestion structure is stylized.

### Frontiers in Operations: Battery as a Service: Flexible Electric Vehicle Battery Leasing

Lingling Shi; Bin Hu (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0587](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0587). First published online: 2024-02-27.

- **Question:** Can temporary battery upgrades and downgrades raise a manufacturer's profit while lowering customer cost and the total battery capacity required?
- **Players:** EV manufacturer/BaaS provider; continuum of heterogeneous BaaS customers
- **Timing:** The manufacturer sets the primary high-capacity lease rate; customers choose a primary battery based on known regular range need and anticipated peak options; the manufacturer sets upgrade/downgrade rates; customers observe peak range need and keep or switch batteries; the manufacturer acquires any extra battery capacity required.
- **Actions:** manufacturer chooses primary lease and peak upgrade/downgrade rates and implied battery acquisition; customers choose primary capacity and later keep, upgrade or downgrade
- **Information:** customers know their regular range need at the primary lease stage; peak need is random then privately realized before switching; the manufacturer knows demand distributions but not each future realization
- **Objective:** After solving peak switching and customer primary-lease responses, the manufacturer chooses the primary lease rate to maximize total leasing/switching revenue net of high-capacity battery acquisition.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p_h}(1-\tau)(p_h-c_h)+(1-\rho)\left[c_h^2/(a(1-\rho)^2)+a\tau-2\tau c_h/(1-\rho)\right]/4$ (main PDF, Section 4, Equation (2), PDF page 8)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the sequential manufacturer–customer flexible-leasing game
- **Solution:** The optimal peak rates either induce extra high-capacity acquisition when batteries are cheap or balance upgrades and downgrades when they are costly. For sufficiently large high-capacity range and moderate battery cost, flexible leasing can simultaneously raise manufacturer profit, lower total customer cost and reduce total battery capacity; the NIO-based calibration falls in this region.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; EV-industry calibration
- **Caveat:** The two-capacity, uniform-demand and linear-inconvenience model omits customer acquisition, operating inventories and platform competition; the calibration is illustrative rather than an estimated likelihood/moment fit.

### No Panic in Pandemic: The Impact of Individual Choice on Public Health Policy

Miao Bai; Ying Cui; Guangwen Kong; Anthony Zhenhuan Zhang (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0514](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0514). First published online: 2024-03-21.

- **Question:** How should a policymaker time and size activity restrictions when individuals endogenously reduce activity in response to infection risk, and what error results from treating behavior as fixed?
- **Players:** public-health policymaker/central planner; a population of strategic individuals
- **Timing:** In each day/state, the policymaker sets an intervention/activity environment and individuals choose whether to go out or stay home; those choices determine contact and the next SIR state. The policymaker solves the sequence over a finite horizon by backward induction/dynamic programming.
- **Actions:** policymaker chooses activity restrictions and lockdown starts; individuals choose outside activity versus staying home
- **Information:** The public epidemic state and announced policy are common knowledge.; Individuals form rational expectations about infection risk and other individuals' symmetric activity choices.; Idiosyncratic utility shocks generate a smooth aggregate-choice rule.
- **Objective:** The central planner minimizes total lockdown-policy burden and cumulative infections over the horizon, subject to SIR dynamics, behavioral equilibrium, and lockdown-count constraints.
- **Representative equation:** `$\min_{A,z}\ f(A)=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}d_1A(t)+d_3\left[S(1)-S(T)\right]$ (main PDF, Section 4.1.3.1, Equation (6), with constraints in Equations (7)-(12), printed p. 1628 (PDF page 7))
- **Equilibrium:** unique symmetric individual-choice equilibrium embedded in a finite-horizon Stackelberg policy solution
- **Solution:** For any epidemic state and policy, the authors solve a unique symmetric activity fixed point. This equilibrium contact rate updates the SIR state, allowing the planner's finite-horizon problem to be solved backward. Comparing endogenous-choice and fixed-behavior policies shows that voluntary distancing changes both the optimal timing and measured benefit of restrictions.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; dynamic optimization; Minnesota case calibration; numerical counterfactuals
- **Caveat:** The representative-population SIR/logit structure studies average activity and omits targeted responses across population groups, heterogeneous health risk and contact networks, learning, and imperfect compliance. It assumes a constant infection rate and does not capture reinfections, imported cases, latency, or disease-severity compartments. Minnesota inputs are a public-data/validated-model parameterization rather than a structurally estimated game, so quantitative policy conclusions remain sensitive to epidemiological inputs, activity-cost parameters, and planner welfare weights.

### Allocating Inventory Risk in Retail Supply Chains: Risk Aversion, Information Asymmetry, and Outside Opportunity

Chengfan Hou; Mengshi Lu (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0624](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0624). First published online: 2024-04-17.

- **Question:** How should a manufacturer allocate inventory risk through preorder or consignment when a retailer's degree of risk aversion is private and an uncertain outside opportunity affects participation?
- **Players:** risk-neutral manufacturer/principal; privately risk-averse retailer/agent
- **Timing:** The manufacturer offers a type-contingent menu and may shut down trade for some reports; the retailer observes its risk type and outside opportunity, selects/rejects a contract, orders or receives consigned inventory, and random demand realizes.
- **Actions:** manufacturer selects contract form, quantities/transfers and shutdown thresholds; retailer reports/selects a menu item and accepts or rejects; inventory is held under push/preorder or pull/consignment
- **Information:** retailer privately knows a binary CVaR risk type; outside opportunity is stochastic; demand distribution and contract primitives are common knowledge
- **Objective:** The manufacturer chooses type-contingent quantities and promised utilities to maximize expected profit subject to both types' participation and truth-telling constraints.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{q_1,q_2,U_1,U_2}\;\nu[sS_{\beta_1}(q_1)-cq_1-U_1]+(1-\nu)[sS_{\beta_2}(q_2)-cq_2-U_2]\quad\text{s.t. IR and IC}$ (main PDF, Section 3, Equation (1), PDF page 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Optimal incentive-compatible screening contract; separating equilibrium under preorder and pooling equilibrium under consignment
- **Solution:** Preorder can screen the retailer's private risk type and deliberately distort inventory to economize on information rent; consignment shifts inventory risk upstream but only supports pooling. Depending on outside-option risk, the manufacturer may recover first-best behavior, exclude a type, or distort the type that earns rent.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** The tractability and sharp pooling/separation result rely on two risk types, CVaR preferences, fixed retail terms and simple preorder/consignment forms.

### The Effects of Selling Formats and Upstream Competition on Product Pricing and Quality Design

Lu Hsiao; Xin Ma; Ying-Ju Chen (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0470](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0470). First published online: 2024-05-14.

- **Question:** How do agency versus reselling formats and the distribution of consumer valuations change endogenous product quality, prices, fees and the effects of upstream competition?
- **Players:** one or two manufacturers; retail intermediary/platform
- **Timing:** In agency selling the manufacturer chooses quality, the intermediary sets agency fee, then the manufacturer sets retail price. In reselling the manufacturer chooses quality and wholesale price, then the intermediary sets retail price. Competition extensions add simultaneous manufacturer choices at the specified stages.
- **Actions:** manufacturer chooses product quality and wholesale or retail price; intermediary chooses agency fee or resale price; competing manufacturers choose qualities/prices simultaneously within stages
- **Information:** quality, prices and contract terms are fully observed; consumer marginal valuations are private draws from the F_K family; cost and valuation-distribution parameters are common knowledge
- **Objective:** Under reselling, the manufacturer chooses wholesale price and quality to maximize wholesale margin net of quality-dependent unit cost, anticipating the intermediary's optimal retail-price response.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{w,q>0}\;\Pi_M^{RS}(w,q\mid p^*)=\left(w-\frac{1}{2}cq^2\right)\left(1-\frac{p^*}{q}\right)^K$ (main PDF, Section 4.3, Equation (6), PDF page 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Stackelberg equilibrium under bilateral agency/reselling; stage-game equilibrium under upstream competition and hybrid selling
- **Solution:** Agency selling yields premium quality and the highest channel profit under the paper's comparable baseline, while the endogenous agency fee is approximately U-shaped in the consumer-distribution parameter. Reselling can dominate quality comparisons when channel-specific consumer mixes differ. With two manufacturers, agency accentuates quality differentiation; a hybrid equilibrium has the low-quality firm use agency and the high-quality firm resell, improving consumer surplus.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** Predictions depend on the F_K valuation family, public quality, convex per-unit quality cost and the imposed move order; competition extensions specialize to uniform valuations.

### Workforce Scheduling with Heterogeneous Time Preferences: Effective Wages and Workers’ Supply

Omar Besbes; Vineet Goyal; Garud Iyengar; Raghav Singal (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0414](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0414). First published online: 2024-08-01.

- **Question:** How should a platform schedule heterogeneous workers when fixed pay and assignment rules create different effective hourly wages and workers strategically choose when to be available?
- **Players:** platform committing a scheduling/allocation policy; heterogeneous strategic workers
- **Timing:** Under DC, workers choose availability and the platform randomly allocates up to its myopic period cap; Equation (3) describes the resulting day-over-day availability equilibrium. Under FCFS, slots are released in advance and workers reserve them sequentially before becoming available. Under PFCFS, workers report temporal types and the mechanism bundles and prioritizes advance allocations before availability is realized.
- **Actions:** the platform commits to the DC, FCFS, or PFCFS allocation mechanism being evaluated; under DC, workers choose time-block availability; under FCFS, workers sequentially reserve advance slots; under PFCFS, workers report temporal types and the mechanism assigns prioritized, bundled slots
- **Information:** Each worker's temporal type is private information known only to that worker; the compensation, platform policy, demand/capacity primitives, and all other model primitives are common knowledge. Under PFCFS, workers report temporal types to the mechanism.
- **Objective:** A worker receives compensation for allocated periods, pays a reservation cost for every period made available, and receives utility minus infinity if availability is declared outside her type-compatible set.
- **Representative equation:** `$u(x_d,y_d,T_d)=\begin{cases}-\infty,&\exists t\notin T_d\text{ such that }y_{dt}=1,\\\sum_{b=1}^{B_d}\left[c\sum_{t\in T_d^{(b)}}x_{dt}y_{dt}-a\sum_{t\in T_d^{(b)}}y_{dt}\right],&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$ (main PDF, Section 2.3, Equation (1), PDF p. 6 (printed p. 1773))
- **Equilibrium:** Day-over-day worker-availability Nash equilibrium under DC; mechanism outcomes under FCFS and PFCFS
- **Solution:** For DC, the authors map aggregate availability into random allocation probabilities and study a day-over-day Nash equilibrium, whose existence is not guaranteed in every market. FCFS lets workers reserve slots sequentially in advance and can still have poor worst-case supply or wage performance. PFCFS is a direct, type-aware priority mechanism: Theorem 1 on PDF p. 11 (printed p. 1778) guarantees a supply ratio of at least 1-r/2, hence at least one half, and a wage ratio of one, both with probability one. Corollaries 1-2 on PDF p. 12 establish optimality in unimodal and nonoverlapping bimodal markets. Truthful type reporting is weakly optimal but not necessarily unique.
- **Evidence:** analytical equilibrium, mechanism, and worst-case guarantees; numerical policy comparisons; public New York City ride-hailing data used for illustrative demand and temporal-preference inputs
- **Caveat:** The analysis uses a one-day finite horizon, fixed price and compensation, homogeneous reservation wages, and a separation of scheduling from pricing. DC equilibrium existence is not universal; PFCFS truth telling is weak rather than uniquely optimal, and global mechanism optimality is proved only for unimodal or nonoverlapping bimodal markets. The New York City exercise is illustrative rather than structural and does not model within-day repositioning or richer labor-supply frictions.

### Can a Supplier’s Yield Risk Be Truthfully Communicated via Cheap Talk?

Tao Lu (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0089](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0089). First published online: 2024-08-05.

- **Question:** Can a supplier credibly reveal private yield quality through costless nonbinding communication when the buyer also has private market information and controls the order response?
- **Players:** privately informed supplier; privately informed buyer/OEM
- **Timing:** Supplier and buyer privately observe yield type t and market state m; the supplier sends a type message; the buyer updates beliefs and chooses order quantity; random yield realizes and payment follows the exogenous order/delivery-based contract.
- **Actions:** supplier reports a high or low yield type; buyer chooses an order quantity conditional on message and its market state
- **Information:** supplier privately observes binary yield type; buyer privately observes binary market potential; types may be correlated under a common joint prior; messages are costless and unverifiable and beliefs follow Bayes' rule on path
- **Objective:** After a message, the buyer chooses an order to maximize expected sales revenue net of order- and delivery-based payments under its posterior over supplier yield.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_B(Q\mid t',m)=\sum_{t\in T}\beta(t\mid t',m)\,\mathbb{E}_{\xi_t}[\xi_t QP(\xi_tQ\mid m)-\eta wQ-(1-\eta)w\xi_tQ]$ (main PDF, Section 3.3, Equation (1), PDF page 4)
- **Equilibrium:** Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium: truth-revealing equilibrium or babbling equilibrium; refined by no incentive to separate (NITS)
- **Solution:** The buyer may inflate orders when expected yield falls, but only over a range; this nonmonotonic response and correlation with market potential create the operational and informational drivers of truth telling. Proposition 2 gives the exact existence condition. Babbling remains available, but when market potentials are sufficiently large it fails NITS and truthful revelation is the sole refined outcome; communication can raise channel profit while redistributing surplus.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** Babbling cannot generally be ruled out without NITS; truth telling depends on binary correlated information, the exogenous simple contract and the baseline common-CV/order-equals-input assumptions.

### Advising Entrepreneurs: Optimal Recommendation of Alternatives

Zeya Wang; Morvarid Rahmani; Karthik Ramachandran (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0361](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0361). First published online: 2024-08-26.

- **Question:** In what order should an advisor reveal alternative solutions to an entrepreneur who controls which option to test, learns from failures, and has a finite runway?
- **Players:** advisor; entrepreneur
- **Timing:** Across N rounds, the advisor first recommends a new option, multiple options, or none; the entrepreneur then trials any previously recommended option or takes an outside option. Success ends the game; failure updates beliefs and the next round begins.
- **Actions:** advisor chooses which unrevealed alternative(s) to recommend each round; entrepreneur chooses which available alternative to try or exits to the outside option
- **Information:** Advisor and entrepreneur share priors over each alternative's viability in the main model.; Trial success also depends on entrepreneur execution capability gamma, and failure updates viability beliefs by Bayes' rule.; The entrepreneur cannot access an alternative before the advisor reveals it.
- **Objective:** Each round, the advisor chooses a recommendation anticipating the entrepreneur's best response and continuation payoffs; the entrepreneur chooses the trial maximizing own expected continuation payoff.
- **Representative equation:** `$o_t^*\in\arg\max_{o_t}\pi_t^A(n_t,m_t\mid o_t,\mu_t^*(o_t)),\qquad \mu_t^*(o_t)\in\arg\max_{\mu_t}\pi_t^E(n_t,m_t\mid o_t,\mu_t)$ (main PDF, Section 3.6, Equations (2)–(3); payoff recursions are Equations (4)–(7), PDF page 6)
- **Equilibrium:** finite-horizon sequential/subgame-perfect equilibrium
- **Solution:** Backward induction compares recommending one alternative, revealing both, withholding, and exiting at every failure-count state. After the first failure, recommending a new alternative is optimal when execution capability is very high or very low, while an intermediate-capability entrepreneur should retry the same alternative. Unequal trial costs or learning can make the initially inferior alternative optimal to reveal first, and correlated alternatives can make simultaneous revelation optimal; the finite runway shifts these recommendation thresholds.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical comparative statics
- **Caveat:** The shared-prior, finite-option model gives the advisor control over awareness and abstracts from endogenous fees/contracting, strategic misreporting of trial outcomes, and repeated reputation across ventures.

### Pride or Guilt? Impacts of Consumers’ Socially Influenced Recycling Behaviors on Closed-Loop Supply Chains

Wenjie Huang; Jason Nguyen; Chung-Li Tseng; Wenlin Chen; Samuel N. Kirshner (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0721](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0721). First published online: 2024-09-06.

- **Question:** How should a manufacturer price a product and reward recycling when consumers' pride and guilt depend on the recycling behavior of their community?
- **Players:** manufacturer; population of socially influenced consumers
- **Timing:** The manufacturer selects retail price and recycling reward; consumers buy and choose whether to recycle; the population share evolves under the paper's behavioral dynamics until an evolutionarily stable recycling state is reached.
- **Actions:** the manufacturer chooses product price; the manufacturer chooses recycling incentive; consumers choose whether to recycle
- **Information:** The manufacturer knows the behavioral primitives and anticipates the stable recycling fraction; consumers observe or respond to the community recycling rate through pride and guilt payoffs.
- **Objective:** The manufacturer chooses price and recycling reward to maximize product margin plus expected recovery savings, taking the evolutionarily stable recycling fraction as induced by the reward.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi^*=\max_{p,f}(1-b_0p+b_1U(f))[p-c_n+\tau^*(f)(\Delta c-f)]$ (main PDF, Section 4, Equation (5), PDF page 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Evolutionarily stable recycling equilibrium nested in the manufacturer's Stackelberg problem
- **Solution:** The authors partition the problem into four regions determined by the product's difficulty of remanufacturing and the relative strengths of socially influenced pride and guilt. A stable interior recycling rate arises when remanufacturing is moderately difficult and pride is stronger than guilt. In that region, pride-focused intervention is a win-win for profit and recycling while the recycling rate is below one half; once recycling is higher, guilt becomes the more effective lever, although it can reduce manufacturer profit when consumers place substantial weight on recyclability.
- **Evidence:** Analytical theory; Numerical / simulation
- **Caveat:** The ESS results rely on homogeneous mixing, a binary recycling choice, and stylized social payoffs; real communities may have network structure, persistent heterogeneity, and nonequilibrium behavior.

### Demand Equilibria in Spatial Service Systems

John Gunnar Carlsson; Xiaoshan Peng; Ilya O. Ryzhov (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0434](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0434). First published online: 2024-09-12.

- **Question:** How does strategic customer choice partition spatial demand among congested service facilities, and how should a provider allocate service capacity to decentralize efficient demand?
- **Players:** nonatomic spatial customers
- **Timing:** For a fixed vector of facility service rates supplied by the centralized design layer, customers observe locations and anticipated congestion and simultaneously choose a facility; the resulting arrival masses and waiting costs must be consistent with those choices. The paper separately optimizes service rates and compares equilibrium with the social partition.
- **Actions:** each customer chooses a service facility
- **Information:** Facility locations and service rates are public; each customer knows her location and anticipates equilibrium waiting cost as a function of the mass assigned to each facility.
- **Objective:** At equilibrium, every customer assigned to facility k weakly minimizes travel plus waiting cost over all facilities.
- **Representative equation:** `$d_k(x)+f_k(A_k)\le\min_{j\ne k}\{d_j(x)+f_j(A_j)\},\qquad x\in A_k,\ k=1,\ldots,K$ (main PDF, Section 3.1, Equation (1), PDF p. 4 (printed p. 2308))
- **Equilibrium:** Unique nonatomic spatial demand (Wardrop) equilibrium
- **Solution:** The authors encode queueing delays as facility weights, so a candidate demand vector induces a weighted Voronoi partition and that partition induces a new demand vector. Theorem 1 gives existence and Theorem 2 uniqueness; Theorem 3 establishes service-rate comparative statics. Theorem 4 characterizes the social partition, Theorem 5 optimizes rates, and Theorem 6 shows that the decentralized partition equals the social optimum when those rates are used. Capacity allocation is a centralized design problem around the nonatomic equilibrium, not a strategic second player.
- **Evidence:** Analytical theory; Optimization / algorithm; Numerical / simulation
- **Caveat:** Existence, uniqueness, and decentralization rely on exogenous nonatomic Poisson arrivals, independent stationary M/M/1 queues, fixed facility locations, homogeneous distance-plus-waiting preferences, and sufficient aggregate capacity. The model does not endogenize whether or how often customers seek service and omits interdependent or self-exciting arrivals and facility-location choice. The Los Angeles hospital exercise uses bed-count proxies and normalized rates rather than structural estimation.

### Optimal Salesforce Compensation with General Demand and Operational Considerations

Haotian Song; Guoming Lai; Wenqiang Xiao (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0400](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0400). First published online: 2024-09-12.

- **Question:** How should a firm compensate a sales division that privately knows local market conditions and chooses hidden sales effort, especially when inventory may be controlled by the firm or delegated and compensation can be based only on censored sales?
- **Players:** risk-neutral firm/principal; risk-neutral sales division or retail-store agent
- **Timing:** The firm offers a direct mechanism/menu specifying payment and, under control, inventory as a function of the agent's report. The agent observes market condition theta, reports a type, chooses output/effort and, under delegation, inventory; demand realizes, sales may be censored by stock, and payment is made.
- **Actions:** firm chooses a payment schedule/menu and possibly inventory Q(theta); agent reports private market condition; agent chooses output/sales effort r and, under delegation, inventory Q
- **Information:** The agent privately observes market condition Theta; the firm knows its distribution F.; Effort/output is hidden action.; Under demand-based contracts demand is contractible; under sales-based contracts the firm sees only sales censored by inventory.
- **Objective:** In the demand-based control setting, the firm maximizes expected sales revenue net of production cost and the type-contingent transfer, subject to incentive compatibility and individual rationality.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{T,Q}\ \Pi(T,Q)=\mathbb E_{\Theta,\epsilon}\!\left[pS(r(\Theta),Q(\Theta))-cQ(\Theta)-T(d(r(\Theta),\epsilon),\Theta)\right]\quad\text{s.t. IC, IR}$ (main PDF, Section 3, problem (P_CD) immediately following the displayed definition of Pi(T,Q), PDF page 5)
- **Equilibrium:** truthful IC/IR second-best direct mechanism, implementable by a menu of linear commissions under monotonicity conditions
- **Solution:** Across the four demand- versus sales-based and inventory-control versus delegation settings, the authors derive a common second-best upper bound. Under monotonicity condition (D) or (S), a menu of linear commissions implements that bound, so neither censored sales information nor delegating inventory necessarily creates an efficiency loss. Under demand-based delegation the inventory term can be separated from the selling incentive; under sales-based delegation the inventory choice is instead induced through the commission rate.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; mechanism-design characterization; numerical illustration
- **Caveat:** Linear menus attain the second best only under the stated monotonicity/regularity conditions; the agent is risk neutral, and the base lost-sales/zero-salvage operations model is stylized.

### Information Dependency in Mitigating Disruption Cascades

Nitin Bakshi; Shyam Mohan (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0408](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0408). First published online: 2024-09-13.

- **Question:** How much should each firm in a multitier supply network invest before a severe disruption, and how much upstream operational information is actually needed to compute decentralized mitigation when disruptions can cascade?
- **Players:** risk-neutral firms located at nodes of an arborescent supply network
- **Timing:** Stable links, prices, operating parameters, and contingent losses are fixed first. Before any trigger shock, all firms simultaneously choose total mitigation and allocate it between their own node and incoming supplier links; a shock can then disrupt a node and cascade downstream.
- **Actions:** choose ex ante node-level mitigation investment; choose link-specific mitigation investment for direct suppliers
- **Information:** The complete-information benchmark makes all network operational attributes visible.; The paper then asks which local attributes are sufficient: under nonconcurrent trigger shocks, information through the firm's tier-2 upstream neighborhood is enough for its equilibrium decision.; Concurrent shocks enlarge the information requirement for partners typically lying within two downstream tiers of jointly shocked firms.
- **Objective:** Firm i chooses mitigation to maximize the negative of expected downstream-contingent loss and investment cost (equivalently, to minimize their sum).
- **Representative equation:** `$U_i^*=\max_{y_i\ge 0} U_i(y_i)=\max_{y_i\ge 0}\{-l_i w_i^d(y_i)-y_i\}=-\min_{y_i\ge 0}\{l_i w_i^d(y_i)+y_i\}$ (main PDF, printed p. 2055/PDF p. 6, Section 4.1, formulation (D))
- **Equilibrium:** simultaneous-move network Nash equilibrium
- **Solution:** The authors express each node's disruption probability recursively, solve the convex firm-level best response, and combine those responses into a unique Nash profile. The recursion shows why distant upstream primitives cancel from a firm's own first-order condition under nonconcurrent shocks: only the extended local neighborhood through tier 2 is required. Concurrent triggers restore selected nonlocal dependencies.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; limited functional-form illustrations and a numerical counterexample outside the maintained curvature condition
- **Caveat:** The sharp tier-2 visibility result is derived from a risk-neutral model with an exogenous arborescent network and prices, rare nonconcurrent trigger shocks in the benchmark, specified mitigation/disruption technology, and initially downstream propagation. Extensions treat multisourcing, concurrency, zero investment, other curvature, directed acyclic topologies, and bidirectional cascades, but the paper still assumes the network map and required operational primitives are available. It does not estimate the network game or compare decentralized efficiency with a centralized/cooperative benchmark.

### Innovative Business Models in Ocean-Bound Plastic Recycling

Opher Baron; Gonzalo Romero; Zhuoluo Zhang; Sean X. Zhou (2024). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0643](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0643). First published online: 2024-09-24.

- **Question:** Which contracting and organizational model best motivates processors and informal collectors to recover ocean-bound plastic while balancing firm profit, social benefit, and environmental impact?
- **Players:** focal company; local processing organization; multiple informal collectors
- **Timing:** In Case O (plastic offsets only), the focal firm first sets the offset price and per-unit bonuses to the processor and collectors; the processor then sets its acquisition price; collectors finally choose collection quantities. Cases S and OS replace or augment those first-stage terms with segregated-plastic sales and purchasing-contract decisions. Outcomes are compared across plastic-offset-only (O), segregated-plastic-only (S), and combined (OS) business models.
- **Actions:** the focal firm sets transfer, bonus, wholesale, or volume terms; the processor sets the collection/acquisition price and processing decision; collectors choose collection effort or quantity
- **Information:** Model parameters and contractual terms are common knowledge in the analytical game; case data are used to instantiate costs and impact measures.
- **Objective:** In the plastic-offset-only case, the firm chooses offset sales d_o and total per-unit bonus r to maximize its weighted triple-bottom-line objective subject to additionality, offset-market-potential, and nonnegativity constraints.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{d_o,r}\;\{\rho_1\Pi_F^O(r,d_o)+\rho_2S^O(r)+\rho_3E^O(r)\}\quad\text{s.t. }V^O(r)-V^B\ge d_o,\;0\le d_o\le Q_o,\;r\ge0$ (main PDF, printed pp. 2165-2166/PDF pp. 6-7, definition of T^O immediately before and Equation (4))
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium of the focal-firm-processor-collector supply-chain game
- **Solution:** The paper solves collector quantities and the processor's acquisition/processing response and substitutes them into the focal firm's triple-bottom-line problem. It performs this analysis for plastic offsets only (O), segregated plastic only (S), and the combined business model (OS), and then compares profits, social and environmental impacts, synergies, and additionality. The results distinguish interventions that generate additional collection from those that primarily redistribute surplus.
- **Evidence:** closed-form backward-induction analysis; numerical experiments; parameter calibration using confidential Plastic Bank operating data and public sources
- **Caveat:** The business-model ranking depends on the triple-bottom-line weights, symmetric collector technology, linear and separate customer demand systems, one-period timing, exogenous local recycled-plastic price, and case-specific costs. The main model omits supply-side and product-market competition and dynamic market/capacity/community evolution; buyers of segregated plastic are represented only through demand. The Plastic Bank exercise calibrates parameters and runs numerical experiments but is neither structural estimation nor a causal field evaluation.

### Information Provision from a Platform to Competing Sellers: The Role of Strategic Ambiguity

Tal Avinadav; Tatyana Chernonog; Noam Shamir (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0262](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0262). First published online: 2024-11-01.

- **Question:** Can a platform profitably communicate demand information to competing sellers by reporting a region rather than a point forecast, even though its message is nonbinding and its commission rises with seller revenue?
- **Players:** privately informed platform; n competing sellers
- **Timing:** Demand state theta is observed by the platform; the platform sends a common, costless, unverifiable message; sellers update beliefs and simultaneously choose prices; demand and commission revenue then realize.
- **Actions:** platform chooses a message/partition of demand states; each seller simultaneously chooses a price after the message
- **Information:** the platform privately observes the common demand shock; sellers observe the same message and form Bayesian posterior beliefs; messages are cheap talk and cannot be contractually verified
- **Objective:** For any message-induced posterior and seller price profile, the platform maximizes its commission share of total seller revenue.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_P=\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i q_i$ (main PDF, Section 3, Equation (2), printed p. 273 (PDF page 5))
- **Equilibrium:** Region-forecast information-sharing equilibrium (partition cheap-talk equilibrium); no meaningful point-forecast equilibrium when products are substitutes
- **Solution:** A precise point report cannot credibly align incentives for substitute products. Coarser interval reports can: the authors solve the sellers' posterior-dependent prices, then choose interval boundaries that make boundary states indifferent. Among multiple partitions, the maximal-interval equilibrium is preferred by the platform and Pareto dominates less informative feasible partitions under the stated conditions.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** The conclusion depends on a one-period interaction, risk-neutral symmetric sellers, linear demand with zero marginal cost, a bounded uniform common-demand shock, the same nonverifiable message being sent to every seller, and sender-preferred/Pareto equilibrium selection. The main extensions only partially relax symmetric substitution. Repeated interaction and seller-specific partitions for heterogeneous sellers are explicitly left for future work, and the paper provides no empirical calibration of forecast communication.

### Telehealth in Acute Care: Pay Parity and Patient Access

Özden Engin Çakıcı; Alex F. Mills (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0345](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0345). First published online: 2024-11-28.

- **Question:** How does a payer's telehealth reimbursement rate affect a provider's division of capacity between office and virtual care, strategic patients' channel choices, duplicate visits, and overall acute-care access?
- **Players:** payer; capacity-constrained healthcare provider; strategic acute-care patients
- **Timing:** The payer selects the telehealth reimbursement first; the provider then commits a share of capacity to telehealth; patients subsequently choose telehealth, office care, or balking in the induced queueing network.
- **Actions:** payer chooses reimbursement r, including whether to impose pay parity; provider chooses telehealth capacity commitment theta; patients choose telehealth, office care, or balking
- **Information:** The reimbursement, capacity allocation, service rates, rewards, and expected delays are common knowledge.; Patients make symmetric choices using equilibrium waiting-time expectations.; A telehealth visit may generate a duplicate office visit with publicly known probability q.
- **Objective:** Given reimbursement r and the patient equilibrium induced by capacity share theta, the provider maximizes revenue from office encounters, telehealth encounters, and duplicate follow-up office visits.
- **Representative equation:** `$F(r,\theta)=\lambda\left[R\pi_O(\theta)+(r+Rq)\pi_T(\theta)\right]$ (main PDF, Section 5.1, Equation (23), printed p. 48 (PDF page 9))
- **Equilibrium:** subgame-perfect Stackelberg equilibrium with a symmetric patient queueing Nash equilibrium
- **Solution:** The authors first derive expected waits and the patient channel-choice equilibria for each capacity allocation. Substituting equilibrium channel shares into F(r,theta) yields the provider's optimal allocation by regime; comparing the resulting access levels across r identifies when parity aligns with or distorts access. Duplicate visits are the key wedge between revenue maximization and access maximization.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; queueing analysis; numerical sensitivity analysis
- **Caveat:** The homogeneous-patient, stationary single-provider benchmark uses exponential service and a symmetric Nash equilibrium in expected waiting times, so it may overestimate sojourn times and assumes patients know expected delays. The model abstracts from detailed appointment-booking behavior, channel-specific variable costs and physician preferences, office location, and provider entry/exit. Extensions add heterogeneous episodes, endogenous duplicate-visit effort, overtime, and two-provider specialization, but the results remain analytical rather than an empirical estimate of a particular pay-parity policy.

### Learning in Repeated Multiunit Pay-as-Bid Auctions

Rigel Galgana; Negin Golrezaei (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0403](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0403). First published online: 2024-12-12.

- **Question:** What equilibrium and welfare properties arise in multiunit pay-as-bid auctions, and how can a bidder learn near-optimal bids when opponents' repeated bids are unknown or adversarial?
- **Players:** N strategic bidders
- **Timing:** In each round bidders simultaneously submit nonincreasing bid vectors; the auction allocates M units to the highest marginal bids and charges winning bids. Across rounds a focal bidder updates from observed or bandit feedback.
- **Actions:** each bidder submits a vector of marginal-unit bids; a learning bidder updates its bid vector after full or bandit feedback
- **Information:** baseline valuations are fixed and private to each bidder; the bid grid and tie-breaking rule are common knowledge; repeated-game algorithms allow adversarial rival bid sequences and either full or bandit feedback
- **Objective:** A bidder's one-shot payoff is total value of units won minus its winning bids; the repeated learner minimizes regret relative to the best fixed feasible bid vector.
- **Representative equation:** `$\mu_n(b_n,b_{-n})=\sum_{m=1}^{x_n(b)}(v_{n,m}-b_{n,m})$ (main PDF, Section 2, Equation (1), PDF page 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Pure Nash equilibrium (PNE), coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE), and correlated equilibrium (CE); no-regret play converges in empirical distribution to CCE
- **Solution:** A PNE need not exist, but the paper gives sufficient conditions and a grid-dependent welfare bound when it does. CCE and CE can be nonuniform, yet every CCE achieves a constant welfare fraction. Dynamic programs make best fixed bids tractable, and the proposed algorithms obtain sublinear regret, linking repeated learning to CCE without claiming that the algorithm itself is a Nash equilibrium.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; simulation experiments
- **Caveat:** PNE can fail to exist, CCE characterization is incomplete, and the welfare/learning guarantees rely on discrete bids, fixed values and the specified tie-breaking/feedback model.

### Laissez-Faire vs. Government Intervention: Implications of Regulation Preventing Nonauthorized Remanufacturing

Gökçe Esenduran; Minyue Jin; Yu Zhou (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0128](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0128). First published online: 2024-12-26.

- **Question:** Does forcing all remanufacturing to be authorized improve economic and environmental outcomes relative to laissez-faire, once an OEM, an independent remanufacturer, and an upstream supplier respond strategically?
- **Players:** component supplier; original equipment manufacturer (OEM); independent remanufacturer
- **Timing:** The supplier chooses its component wholesale price; the OEM chooses new-product quantity and an authorization fee; the independent remanufacturer then chooses remanufactured quantity and, under laissez-faire, the authorized fraction. Market prices clear from quantities.
- **Actions:** supplier sets component wholesale price w; OEM chooses new-product quantity q_n and authorization fee f; remanufacturer chooses q_r and the authorized fraction eta when regulation permits
- **Information:** Costs, product valuations, demand functions, and the regulatory regime are common knowledge.; Authorization status is a deliberate and observable channel choice, not hidden information.
- **Objective:** Anticipating the remanufacturer's response, the OEM chooses new-product quantity and its per-unit authorization fee to maximize new-product margin plus authorization revenue.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{q_n,f\ge0}\ \pi_{OEM}=\left[p_n(q_n,q_r^*,\eta^*)-w-c_n\right]q_n+f\eta^*q_r^*$ (main PDF, Section 3.4, Equation (7), PDF page 7)
- **Equilibrium:** subgame-perfect Stackelberg equilibrium
- **Solution:** At low remanufacturing cost, mandatory authorization can raise remanufacturing and benefit the supplier, OEM, and independent remanufacturer simultaneously, but it can also raise environmental impact. At moderately high remanufacturing cost, laissez-faire can instead be a win–win–win because the remanufacturer enters, the OEM expands new production, and the supplier lowers its wholesale price. Mandatory authorization can outperform laissez-faire in both total economic performance and environmental impact only in a distinct moderately low-cost region, at the expense of remanufacturer profit.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical comparative statics
- **Caveat:** Policy conclusions depend on vertical differentiation, the core-supply relation, the assumed environmental accounting, and an OEM that cannot remanufacture directly.

### Buying Cheap: Brand Switching During Economic Distress and Its Disparate Impact on Consumers

Shantanu Dutta; Divya Singhvi; Somya Singhvi (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0380](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0380). First published online: 2025-02-26.

- **Question:** How does economic distress change brand switching between national and private labels, retailer/manufacturer pricing, and welfare across income groups, and what do subsidy or price-control policies do?
- **Players:** national-brand manufacturer; retailer that also supplies a private label; high- and low-income consumers
- **Timing:** The national-brand manufacturer sets its wholesale price; the retailer then chooses national-brand and private-label retail prices subject to shelf capacity; heterogeneous consumers choose a product or outside option. Distress changes high-income consumers' private-label risk response.
- **Actions:** the manufacturer chooses the national-brand wholesale price; the retailer chooses both retail prices; consumers choose national brand, private label, or no purchase
- **Information:** Firms know the demand primitives and income-group distribution; consumers know their own valuations but perceive private-label quality risk with income-specific sensitivity.
- **Objective:** Given the national-brand wholesale price, the retailer jointly prices both brands to maximize channel margin subject to shelf capacity.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{p_N,p_R}(p_N-w_N)d_N(p_N,p_R,\lambda_H)+p_Rd_R(p_N,p_R,\lambda_H)\quad\text{s.t. }d_N+d_R\le s$ (main PDF, Section 3 model formulation immediately before Section 3.1, PDF page 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect Stackelberg channel-pricing equilibrium
- **Solution:** The authors derive income-specific brand demands from consumer utility, solve the retailer's price problem separately for slack and binding shelf capacity, and substitute the best response into the manufacturer's wholesale-price problem. The resulting equilibrium predicts how distress-induced changes in private-label risk alter prices and switching. NielsenIQ evidence disciplines the behavioral channel, after which cash-subsidy and price-control counterfactuals reveal heterogeneous consumer impacts rather than a uniform gain from cheaper brands.
- **Evidence:** Analytical theory; Empirical / structural
- **Caveat:** Distributional conclusions depend on the two-income-group demand specification, the modeled link from distress to private-label risk perception, and the shelf-capacity representation.

### Incorporating Income Disparity and Utility Heterogeneity in Resource Allocation

Siddharth Prakash Singh; Owen Q. Wu (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2024.1163](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.1163). First published online: 2025-03-19.

- **Question:** How can a planner allocate a scarce divisible resource and its associated cost or subsidy across income groups when households privately differ in resource utility and money is not quasilinear?
- **Players:** social planner/resource authority; consumer households grouped by observable income and private resource-utility type
- **Timing:** The planner observes/verifies income and commits to one menu of resource–money bundles for each income class. A household privately knows utility type g and selects a menu item; aggregate resource and monetary balance must hold.
- **Actions:** planner designs income-dependent menus (s_ij,m_ij); households report utility type indirectly by choosing a menu item
- **Information:** Income f_i is observable/verifiable to the planner.; Resource-utility type g_j is private information.; The planner knows the population shares theta_ij and utility functions/distributions.
- **Objective:** The income-dependent mechanism maximizes aggregate household welfare over resource and money allocations subject to balance, nonnegativity, IR, and IC.
- **Representative equation:** `$W^M=\max_{\{s_{ij},m_{ij}\}}N\sum_{i\in I,j\in J}\left[G(s_{ij},g_j)+F(f_i+m_{ij})\right]\theta_{ij}$ (main PDF, Section 3.3, Equation (9), with feasibility/IR/IC constraints (4)–(6) and (10)–(11), PDF page 6)
- **Equilibrium:** dominant-strategy truthful IC/IR menu outcome
- **Solution:** The incentive-compatible income-dependent menus allocate weakly more resource—and generally more cost—to higher private-utility types within each income group while tailoring financial burden across observable incomes. In the Chennai water calibration, an income-agnostic utility menu closes 7.46% of the baseline-to-first-best welfare gap and an income-dependent fixed allocation closes 65.10%, whereas the full two-dimensional menu closes about 86%, showing that both heterogeneity dimensions matter.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; convex optimization; Chennai case calibration
- **Caveat:** The mechanism requires verifiable income, known group shares and utility functions, and enforceable monetary transfers; the Chennai welfare figures are calibrated simulations rather than causal estimates.

### Flexibility Value of Reshoring Capacity Under Policy Uncertainty and Domestic Competition

Panos Kouvelis; Xiao Tan; Sammi Y. Tang (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0387](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0387). First published online: 2025-05-08.

- **Question:** How much reshoring capacity should a global firm build when future demand and trade policy are uncertain and a domestic rival competes in the destination market?
- **Players:** global firm with offshore and potential onshore production; domestic competing firm
- **Timing:** In the tariff model the global firm first invests in reshoring capacity; demand is realized and firms choose market quantities simultaneously; the tariff then realizes and the global firm allocates output across offshore, legacy onshore and new reshored capacity. The tax model uses the paper's corresponding two-stage policy timing.
- **Actions:** global firm invests in irreversible reshoring capacity; global and domestic firms choose Cournot quantities; global firm allocates realized production across locations
- **Information:** demand and policy are random with known distributions; installed reshoring capacity is public; realized states are observed at the stages specified by each policy model
- **Objective:** The global firm chooses reshoring capacity to maximize expected operating profit from the ensuing Cournot and location-allocation game net of capacity investment.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{K_U\ge 0}\;R(K_U)-C_UK_U,\qquad R(K_U)=\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[\pi(\varepsilon,K_U)]$ (main PDF, Section 3 (Tariff Policy Model), Stage 1 unnumbered capacity problem, journal p. 1168 / PDF p. 5)
- **Equilibrium:** Cournot equilibrium in the quantity subgame embedded in a backward-induction capacity/location game
- **Solution:** Finished-goods tariffs create opposing forces: higher expected serving cost suppresses reshoring, while the option to cover overflow demand encourages it; raw-material tariffs lack the overflow effect and therefore reduce reshoring. When tax credits are observed before output, the output-reduction force disappears and demand stimulation plus overflow value increase reshoring. Tariffs reduce the global firm's profit, whereas credits can help it; either policy can hurt the domestic rival when added reshoring intensifies competition.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** The tariff and tax models use different timing; closed-form concavity/results require stated parameter conditions and rely on a linear-demand duopoly.

### Product Return Policies: The Impacts of Vertical Bargaining and Contracting with Retail Competition

Chengzhang Li; Tingliang Huang; Yufei Huang (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0717](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0717). First published online: 2025-05-16.

- **Question:** How do manufacturer return acceptance and retailer money-back guarantees interact with retail competition and contract form, and when will channel members voluntarily offer consumer returns?
- **Players:** manufacturer; two competing retailers
- **Timing:** Manufacturer and retailers choose return/MBG policies; the manufacturer then negotiates bilateral wholesale or two-part-tariff contracts in parallel with both retailers; retailers choose Cournot quantities; consumers purchase and returns/misfit realize.
- **Actions:** manufacturer accepts or rejects retailer returns; each retailer offers or withholds a money-back guarantee; manufacturer and each retailer bargain over contract terms; retailers choose competing quantities
- **Information:** policies and contract terms are observed by channel members; consumer fit/return realization is uncertain; parallel bilateral negotiations create endogenous disagreement payoffs
- **Objective:** Each manufacturer–retailer dyad selects contract terms to maximize its generalized Nash product relative to endogenous disagreement payoffs.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{C_i}(\Pi-D_i)^{1-\theta}(\pi_i-d_i)^{\theta}$ (main PDF, bargaining problem, Equation (6), PDF page 9)
- **Equilibrium:** Cournot quantity equilibrium; Nash–Nash solution for parallel bilateral bargaining; first-stage return-policy equilibrium
- **Solution:** Under a wholesale-price contract, both retailers offering MBGs with manufacturer return acceptance is the unique policy equilibrium. With two-part tariffs, low bargaining weight yields the symmetric return profile, intermediate values can support asymmetric profiles, and high values again favor the Pareto-dominant symmetric return profile. Contracting changes return incentives through disagreement payoffs and competitive spillovers.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** The policy ranking relies on symmetric retailers, Cournot competition, exogenous return probability and the imposed contract/bargaining structures; some sequential-negotiation extensions are numerical.

### User-Generated Content Platforms: Managing the Relationship Triangle

Ruize Ma; Yunke Mai; Bin Hu (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2024.0917](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.0917). First published online: 2025-05-26.

- **Question:** How should a UGC platform dynamically set creator wages, ad load, and promotions to grow interdependent creator and viewer populations while monetizing content?
- **Players:** UGC platform as the sole strategic controller; a continuum/aggregate base of creators; a continuum/aggregate base of viewers
- **Timing:** At every time t over a finite horizon, the platform chooses wage w, advertising share rho, and promotions alpha_m and alpha_n. Creator quality/output and viewer consumption take static optimal-response values, which feed Bass/replicator-style state equations for the two population bases.
- **Actions:** platform chooses creator wage, advertising load, and creator/viewer promotion effort; representative creators choose content quality/effort; representative viewers choose consumption quantity
- **Information:** The platform observes aggregate creator and viewer states and all model primitives.; Individual heterogeneity and strategic beliefs are not modeled; creator/viewer responses enter as aggregate static optimizers.
- **Objective:** The platform maximizes discounted advertising margin net of creator compensation and promotion costs, subject to endogenous creator/viewer response and state dynamics.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{w,\rho,\alpha_m,\alpha_n}\int_0^T\!\left[(\rho(t)-w(t))n(t)v^*(t)-C_m(\alpha_m(t))-C_n(\alpha_n(t))\right]e^{-rt}dt$ (main PDF, Section 3.3, Problem (2), PDF page 5)
- **Equilibrium:** static creator/viewer optimal responses embedded in a central optimal-control solution
- **Solution:** The optimal advertising and creator-wage paths mirror one another across the platform life cycle: the platform initially monetizes to fund promotion, later reduces advertising and raises creator pay to stimulate word-of-mouth growth, and returns to myopic monetization when mature. It should share advertising revenue generously and may optimally loss-lead shortly after—not exactly at—launch. The celebrity, liquidity, ad-removal, sponsored-content, and tipping extensions preserve or qualify these lifecycle policies.
- **Evidence:** analytical optimal control; numerical simulation; aggregate behavioral response model
- **Caveat:** The game-theory content is evolutionary: aggregate creator/viewer payoffs drive replicator-style population dynamics inside a single platform's optimal-control problem. The paper studies an isolated platform rather than finite strategic users or competing platforms.

### R&D Data Sharing in New Product Development

Zhi Chen; Jussi Keppo (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0463](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0463). First published online: 2025-06-04.

- **Question:** When will competing firms voluntarily share proprietary R&D data, and when do their sharing incentives under- or overshoot the innovation-maximizing government policy?
- **Players:** n competing innovating firms
- **Timing:** In the voluntary game, firms simultaneously choose unobservable data-collection effort and a verifiable fraction of technical data to share; performance shocks then realize and market shares are awarded by rank. The paper separately uses a government-mandated sharing rate as a centralized policy benchmark, not as another player in the voluntary game.
- **Actions:** each firm simultaneously chooses data-collection effort and a voluntary sharing percentage
- **Information:** effort is unobservable; sharing quantities are verifiable, and model primitives are common knowledge; normally distributed performance shocks realize after effort/sharing; data sets may be complementary or redundant through the CES parameter
- **Objective:** Each firm maximizes its expected rank-contingent share of the endogenous market size minus its data-collection cost.
- **Representative equation:** `$\pi_i=\sum_{j=1}^{m}A_j-c(e_i),\qquad A_j=\mathbb{E}\left[\gamma_j\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}v_\ell\right)\mathbf{1}_{\{i\text{ ranks }j\}}\right]$ (main PDF, Section 3.2, Equation (3), PDF page 8)
- **Equilibrium:** Symmetric pure-strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium under voluntary data sharing
- **Solution:** Firms share when data are complementary or uncertainty is high because market expansion dominates free riding; they withhold data when uncertainty is moderate and data are redundant. Relative to the government, firms can undershare complementary data at moderate uncertainty but overshare redundant data at high uncertainty, so intervention is not uniformly pro-sharing.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical robustness illustrations
- **Caveat:** The main characterization uses symmetric firms, i.i.d. normal shocks, CES data aggregation, exogenous rank shares, and an endogenous-market-size proxy equal to total realized performance. Sharing is free, nonrival, and verifiable, whereas effort is hidden; Assumption 1 supplies sufficient uncertainty for an interior response, and equilibrium need not be unique. Sequential sharing, privacy, data quality versus quantity, and empirical estimation are outside the model.

### Balancing Supply with Demand on Ride-Hailing Platforms in Markets with Price Regulations: An Operational Approach

Qin Zhou; Jingqi Wang; Yifan Jiao; Jinzhao Du (2025). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2022.0216](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0216). First published online: 2025-06-09.

- **Question:** How can a ride-hailing platform balance peak and off-peak driver supply when fares are regulated and drivers strategically choose when to work?
- **Players:** ride-hailing platform; strategic full-time drivers
- **Timing:** Regulated trip prices are fixed; the platform chooses a work/qualification target or prioritization rule; drivers then choose peak versus off-peak work and whether to qualify/participate; trips and platform matching outcomes follow.
- **Actions:** the platform selects a qualification target or prioritization policy; full-time drivers choose their peak-work share and whether to qualify under the policy
- **Information:** The platform knows the driver-utility and demand primitives and anticipates driver responses; drivers observe the policy and compare utilities from qualifying and not qualifying.
