- **Timing:** First, the platform sets customer price p, provider wage w_o, and booking-agent wage w_b. Second, each provider decides whether to participate. Third, each booking agent chooses how many customers x to visit. Finally, visited customers decide whether to buy. The one-period game is solved backward, and the platform anticipates all downstream responses.
- **Actions:** the platform chooses customer price, provider wage, and booking-agent wage; providers decide whether to participate; booking agents choose customer-visiting effort and submit aggregated demand; customers decide whether to purchase based on valuation and price
- **Information:** Platform price and wages are observed before provider, agent, and customer decisions.; Customers privately know valuations v distributed uniformly on [0,1].; Providers privately know reservation earnings κ distributed uniformly on [0,K].; The base model treats aggregate demand implied by the valuation distribution as known; demand uncertainty is an extension.
- **Objective:** The platform maximizes its commission margin per served unit times equilibrium served demand, subject to customer coverage and provider-capacity feasibility.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi^p=(p-w_o-w_b)n\lambda$ (main PDF, Equation (4), PDF page 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Backward-induction equilibrium of the platform-led sequential game
- **Solution:** Lemma 1 separates high- and low-aggregation-cost regimes. Proposition 1 shows that a larger provider pool lowers price and provider wage but raises the booking-agent wage exactly in the high-cost regime; later propositions compare demand, price, stakeholder surplus, and platform profit with the no-agent benchmark and identify win–win–win regions.
- **Evidence:** Closed-form backward-induction analysis of the sequential pricing, participation, effort, and purchase game; Calibration to Hello Tractor's farm-mechanization platform operations in Nigeria
- **Caveat:** The base model is a one-period known-demand environment with uniform customer values, uniform provider reservation earnings, nonoverlapping agent territories, and sufficient coordination to serve all collected demand. Demand uncertainty, overlapping/direct demand, heterogeneous agents, and additional provider types are extensions.

### Reducing Traffic Incidents in Meal Deliveries: Penalize the Platform or Its Independent Drivers?

Wenchang Zhang; Christopher S. Tang; Liu Ming; Yue Cheng (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0259](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0259). First published online: 2026-04-29.

- **Question:** Should traffic-safety penalties target delivery drivers or the platform, given that platform delivery promises and fees affect driver speeding and customer demand?
- **Players:** government regulator; delivery platform; drivers; customers
- **Timing:** The government sets driver and platform penalties; the platform chooses the per-distance driver commission b and therefore the customer fee rate k=alpha b, then quotes the driver-induced delivery time; customers order; drivers decide acceptance and delivery time/speed; incidents and penalties realize.
- **Actions:** government chooses penalties A and R; platform chooses the per-distance driver commission b; the customer delivery-fee rate is linked by k=alpha b; restaurant service revenue gamma is exogenous; customers choose whether to order; drivers accept and choose delivery behavior/speed
- **Information:** baseline platform observes customer distance and value; penalties and platform terms are public; incident probability depends on excess speed under the specified technology
- **Objective:** The government chooses driver and platform penalties to maximize expected social surplus over participating orders after the platform–driver continuation equilibrium.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{A,R}\;\bar S(A,R)=\int_{D(A)}S(x,v;A,R)\mathbf{1}_{\{\pi^*(x,v;A,R)\ge0\}}F_C(dx,dv)$ (main PDF, Section 5.2, Equation (15), PDF page 10)
- **Equilibrium:** Stackelberg equilibrium of the government–platform–driver/customer game
- **Solution:** Under the paper's condition, the optimal driver penalty is zero; any nonzero penalty is assigned to the platform, and the optimal platform penalty is bounded above and may itself be zero depending on primitives. Penalizing the platform changes delivery promises and prices at the system-design level, whereas direct driver penalties can inefficiently suppress participation. The calibrated counterfactuals quantify the safety–service trade-off.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; calibration using Shenzhen delivery-order data
- **Caveat:** The single-platform/single-restaurant model omits platform competition and labor/throughput dynamics; counterfactuals inherit the chosen speeding and incident-risk functional forms.

### Probabilistic Selling for Vertically Differentiated Products in a Decentralized Channel

Zhechao Yang; Hongseok Jang; Xiajun Amy Pan (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2024.1036](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.1036). First published online: 2026-04-30.

- **Question:** Who should administer probabilistic selling in a vertically differentiated channel, and how do capacity limits and wholesale incentives change the optimal mixture, assortment, prices, and channel profit?
- **Players:** upstream supplier; downstream retailer; high- and low-valuation consumers
- **Timing:** The supplier is the channel leader. Under retailer administration, the supplier sets wholesale terms and the retailer chooses the assortment, posted prices, and random product mix; under supplier administration, the supplier also chooses the mix and the retailer subsequently chooses retail prices.
- **Actions:** supplier chooses wholesale prices for high- and low-quality products; supplier or retailer selects the probabilistic-selling mix and quantity; retailer chooses assortment quantities and retail prices; consumers choose among deterministic products, the probabilistic product, and no purchase
- **Information:** Product qualities, market-segment sizes, capacities, contract terms, and demand primitives are common knowledge.; Consumers know their own valuation segment and the disclosed distribution of the probabilistic product.
- **Objective:** Under retailer administration, the retailer chooses deterministic and probabilistic quantities/prices to maximize total retail margin net of probabilistic-selling cost.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{r>0,\ 0\le X\le N,\ 0\le Y\le M}\ \pi_{R,RA}=D_h(r_h-w_h)+D_p(r_p-w_p-c)+D_l(r_l-w_l)$ (main PDF, Section 3.1, Equation (1), PDF page 7)
- **Equilibrium:** supplier-led backward-induction equilibrium (reported in the paper as a Nash equilibrium)
- **Solution:** The authors derive demand for each deterministic and lottery product, solve the retailer's price/assortment response, and then optimize supplier wholesale terms. Capacity scarcity changes which cannibalization and segmentation constraints bind, so shifting control of the lottery can redistribute profit and sometimes improve total channel performance.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** The equilibrium label should be read with the paper's supplier-leadership timing in mind; the results depend on linear wholesale contracting, disclosed lotteries, and a stylized two-quality/two-segment demand structure.

### Startup Contracting and Entrepreneur-Investor Bargaining

Evgeny Kagan; Kyle Hyndman; Anyan Qi (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2024.1228](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.1228). First published online: 2026-05-15.

- **Question:** How do common versus preferred stock and the presence of one versus multiple investors shape investment, equity allocation, risk sharing, and the entrepreneur's bargaining outcome?
- **Players:** entrepreneur; one or two outside investors
- **Timing:** The entrepreneur and investor bargain over investment and equity in the one-investor benchmark; with two investors, bilateral bargains are formed simultaneously while each agreement's surplus depends on the other. Venture payoff is then realized.
- **Actions:** investors choose investment amounts as part of the bargain; the entrepreneur and investors negotiate equity shares
- **Information:** The baseline has common knowledge of the binary venture technology, outside options, and bargaining weights; extensions and experiments examine beliefs and risk attitudes that can select among predicted outcomes.
- **Objective:** In the one-investor common-stock benchmark, the negotiated contract maximizes the Nash product of investor and entrepreneur gains over disagreement.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{I_0\in[0,e],\,s_0\in[0,1]}[\pi_0(I_0,s_0)-d_0][\pi_e(I_0,s_0)-d_e]\quad\text{s.t. }\pi_0(I_0,s_0)\ge d_0,\;\pi_e(I_0,s_0)\ge d_e$ (main PDF, Section 3.1.1.1, Equation (3), PDF page 7)
- **Equilibrium:** Bilateral Nash-bargaining solution and two-investor Nash-in-Nash equilibrium
- **Solution:** The Nash/Nash-in-Nash benchmark predicts that two investors improve the entrepreneur's equity share and that preferred stock's downside protection lets the entrepreneur retain more equity. In 24 laboratory sessions with 290 subjects, two investors instead reduce the entrepreneur's conditional equity share; they raise the chance of at least partial agreement, leaving unconditional profit indistinguishable without an outside option but strictly worse with one. Preferred stock raises the entrepreneur's share only with a strong outside option. Revised off-path beliefs and a risk-exposure framework reconcile these departures from the benchmark.
- **Evidence:** Analytical theory; Lab experiment; Empirical / structural
- **Caveat:** The two-investor predictions are sensitive to disagreement beliefs and equilibrium selection; the risk-neutral symmetric-bargaining benchmark does not by itself fit all laboratory behavior.

### Greenwashing Under Competition

Liqun Wei; Soraya Fatehi; Anyan Qi; Jianxiong Zhang (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2025.0420](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2025.0420). First published online: 2026-05-18.

- **Question:** How does transparency determine whether a socially responsible firm can separate from a profit-maximizing greenwasher, and which visible CSR instruments are used in equilibrium?
- **Players:** one socially responsible firm; one profit-maximizing firm; consumers who infer firm type
- **Timing:** Nature assigns the two firm types; firms choose prices and visible/unobservable CSR and advertising decisions; consumers observe the permitted signals, update beliefs and choose between the differentiated firms.
- **Actions:** firms choose price, observable CSR, unobservable CSR and advertising; consumers update type beliefs and choose a seller
- **Information:** each firm knows both firms' types; consumers know that exactly one firm is socially responsible but not its identity; transparency controls how accurately visible CSR reflects real activity; price is not a signal in the baseline
- **Objective:** The profit-maximizing type maximizes operating profit net of CSR and advertising cost; the responsible type additionally values the social benefit of its CSR.
- **Representative equation:** `$U_L=n_Lp_L-[\alpha kx_L^2+(1-\alpha)ky_L^2]-\hat{k}z_L^2;\quad U_H=n_Hp_H+\beta[\alpha x_H+(1-\alpha)y_H]-[\alpha kx_H^2+(1-\alpha)ky_H^2]-\hat{k}z_H^2$ (main PDF, model payoffs, Equations (3)–(4), PDF page 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium refined by the undefeated equilibrium / lexicographically maximum sequential equilibrium
- **Solution:** Low transparency supports pooling greenwashing, intermediate transparency induces costly separation in which the responsible firm overinvests in observable CSR and advertising, and high transparency yields natural separation. The same regimes can be read through advertising influence: high influence favors pooling, moderate influence costly separation, and low influence natural separation. With low transparency, stronger product-market competition changes pooling into costly separation; with high transparency, separation is unaffected by competition. Greenwashing always reduces consumer surplus but can raise total CSR and welfare, and at high transparency those two outcomes can first rise and then fall with advertising influence.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical illustrations
- **Caveat:** The result relies on exactly one responsible firm, covered Hotelling demand, no price signaling and the selected undefeated-equilibrium refinement. Message-based greenwashing appears only in the extension where consumers directly value advertising; the baseline pooling outcome is action-based greenwashing.

### The Value of Time and Location Commitment for Decentralized Emergency Medical Services

Pieter L. van den Berg; Andre P. Calmon; Andreas K. Gernert; Stef Lemmens; Maria Rabinovich; Gonzalo Romero (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2025.0324](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2025.0324). First published online: 2026-05-21.

- **Question:** How much service coverage is lost when decentralized ambulances do not commit to time or location, and where should a planner add flexible ambulances to recover the most coverage?
- **Players:** independent roaming ambulance providers (time-committed and location-uncommitted) in the stylized game; independent stationed ambulance providers (time-uncommitted and location-committed) in the stylized game
- **Timing:** The paper first evaluates the incumbent fleet and solves a nonstrategic planner placement problem, then stress-tests it by simulation. In the separate stylized game, providers enter as roaming or stationed ambulances while expected profit is nonnegative; pure-type markets reach a symmetric free-entry fleet size at zero profit, and a mixed-type equilibrium is explored numerically.
- **Actions:** enter or exit the stylized market as a roaming or stationed ambulance provider; stationed providers choose locations, represented by the symmetric equidistant-location equilibrium; roaming providers search for demand without committing to a fixed location
- **Information:** The stylized game's circular-city demand, spatial reach d, time availability q, revenue normalization, and cost a are common knowledge.; The nonstrategic planner analysis uses historical fleet, incident, travel-time, availability, and demand-location data.
- **Objective:** A representative strategic payoff is the expected profit per roaming ambulance: its equal share of total covered demand minus operating cost. Free entry drives this payoff to zero at the symmetric equilibrium fleet size.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_r(k_r)=\frac{TC_r(k_r)}{k_r}-a=\frac{1-(1-d)^{k_r}}{k_r}-a$ (main PDF, printed/PDF p. 16, Appendix B.3, Remark B.1(ii))
- **Equilibrium:** symmetric free-entry zero-profit equilibria for roaming and stationed ambulance providers
- **Solution:** The authors estimate availability/location distributions for six fleet types, compute demand-node coverage, and optimize where incremental flexible units should be placed; out-of-sample simulation stress-tests the comparison. In the stylized game, they derive unique symmetric zero-profit fleet sizes for pure roaming and pure stationed markets. Theorem B.2 gives the entry condition a<d and a unique time-commitment threshold above which stationed providers generate higher equilibrium coverage; mixed entry is examined numerically.
- **Evidence:** coverage and location optimization; Nairobi operational case study using Flare incident and fleet records; out-of-sample trace-driven stochastic simulation; stylized analytical free-entry game
- **Caveat:** The paper is multi-method rather than solely an equilibrium contribution. Its tactical coverage model uses independent and static availability/location probabilities, binary threshold coverage, and initially low congestion; the authors use simulation to relax several of these assumptions but not to establish causality. The free-entry game is deliberately stylized: circular uniform demand, two extreme commitment archetypes, uniform random dispatch, no congestion, symmetric/equidistant stationed locations, and a continuous fleet-size relaxation. Quantitative conclusions are Nairobi/Flare-specific, and the authors identify dynamic real-time relocation, richer provider behavior, incentive contracts, equity, and external-context validation as future work.

### Endogenous Commitments: Implications for Supply Chains

Narendra Singh (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2024.1270](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.1270). First published online: 2026-06-01.

- **Question:** When will a manufacturer and retailer voluntarily commit to second-period wholesale and retail prices, and can one party induce the other's commitment in a durable-goods channel?
- **Players:** manufacturer; retailer; forward-looking consumers
- **Timing:** The manufacturer chooses whether to commit and sets first-period wholesale price (and w2 if committed); the retailer chooses whether to commit and sets first-period retail price (and p2 if committed); consumers decide whether to buy in period 1; remaining prices and purchases occur in period 2.
- **Actions:** manufacturer chooses commitment status and wholesale prices; retailer chooses commitment status and retail prices; consumers choose buy now, wait, or not buy
- **Information:** commitment choices and announced prices are public; consumer valuations are privately realized but distributed uniformly; consumers form rational expectations about uncommitted period-2 prices
- **Objective:** Manufacturer and retailer maximize discounted two-period channel profits over first- and second-period sales induced by strategic consumers.
- **Representative equation:** `$\Pi_M=q_1w_1+\rho_f q_2w_2;\qquad \Pi_R=q_1(p_1-w_1)+\rho_f q_2(p_2-w_2)$ (main PDF, Section 3.1, firm payoff equations, PDF pages 4–5)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium
- **Solution:** Only no commitment (NN) and mutual commitment (CC) can be SPNE; the mixed profiles NC and CN are not equilibria. When consumers are less strategic, NN is voluntary, whereas at moderate or high strategic behavior the manufacturer can induce NN by deterring the retailer's commitment. CC arises when consumers are sufficiently patient and the firms are not too patient. Endogenizing commitment can hurt the retailer and the whole supply chain, make commitment harmful to both firms, and cause coordination to improve and then deteriorate as consumers become more strategic.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; numerical comparative statics
- **Caveat:** The equilibrium regions depend on two periods, uniform valuations, zero cost, common discounting and fully credible price commitments; inventory and richer price paths are extensions.

### Increasing mHealth Usage Through Strategic Payer Incentives for Providers and Patients

Saligrama Agnihothri; Arvind Sainathan; Balaraman Rajan (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2025.0182](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2025.0182). First published online: 2026-06-04.

- **Question:** How should a payer reward a provider and patients to increase mHealth uploads and reminders while reducing costly severe health states?
- **Players:** payer; healthcare provider; patient population
- **Timing:** The payer sets capitation/reward terms; the provider chooses panel size and reminder intensity while patients choose upload intensity in the continuation game; health states evolve as a continuous-time Markov chain and payments/costs accrue.
- **Actions:** payer chooses provider capitation and engagement rewards; provider chooses reminder intensity and patient panel; patients choose app-upload intensity
- **Information:** contract terms and health-transition primitives are common knowledge; provider and patients anticipate the steady-state health distribution; the paper applies an explicit selection rule if the continuation game has multiple Nash equilibria
- **Objective:** The payer chooses payments to maximize expected per-provider surplus, net of rewards, capitation and expected severe-state cost, subject to provider participation and the provider–patient equilibrium.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{r_d,r_p}\;N^*\left[p-(\mu^e+\alpha^e)r_p-r_d-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+(\mu^e+\alpha^e)q}\frac{c_{si}}{\tau(\alpha^e,\mu^e)}\right]$ (main PDF, payer problem, Equations (7)–(9), PDF page 9)
- **Equilibrium:** Provider–patient Nash equilibrium embedded in a payer Stackelberg game
- **Solution:** The continuation game can support reminder-intensive or patient-reward-intensive engagement. The payer's optimum uses a pure reminder-based or pure reward-based policy rather than mixing both, with the better instrument governed by the marginal health-treatment productivity of engagement and participation constraints.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; literature-grounded numerical parameterization
- **Caveat:** Predictions come from a steady-state model with one payer and one capacity-constrained provider, a homogeneous-patient baseline, three Markov health states with exponential transitions, independent Poisson uploads and reminders, a reminder that triggers an upload, and instantaneous effective intervention. The provider-patient game may have multiple equilibria, so the Pareto/provider-revenue selection rule is consequential. The online supplement allows patient heterogeneity, but the paper does not estimate or behaviorally validate the strategic model on its own patient-level data.

### Scope Contracts to Coordinate Assortment Planning in Omnichannel Retail Supply Chains

Amin Aslani; Osman Alp (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2023.0539](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2023.0539). First published online: 2026-06-08.

- **Question:** How can a manufacturer coordinate an independent retailer's capacity-constrained physical-store assortment when the manufacturer also operates an online channel?
- **Players:** omnichannel manufacturer; independent physical-store retailer
- **Timing:** In the decentralized benchmark, the manufacturer announces product-level wholesale prices and the retailer then selects a capacity-constrained store assortment; consumers subsequently choose products and channels and may return purchases. For coordination, the manufacturer instead commits to a scope contract with attribute-level wholesale discounts and, when needed, a lump-sum transfer, after which the retailer chooses the assortment.
- **Actions:** the manufacturer sets product-level wholesale prices or a scope contract; the retailer chooses the physical-store assortment; consumers choose product/channel and keep or return outcomes
- **Information:** Demand primitives, product attributes, costs, and channel ownership are common knowledge; consumer tastes are integrated through a nested-logit choice model.
- **Objective:** Given wholesale prices, the retailer chooses the feasible store assortment that maximizes expected physical-channel margin.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{M\subset X,\,|M|\le C}\;\Pi_D^r(M\mid\mathbf w)=\sum_{x\in M}P^r_{x\mid M}(\mathcal{P}_x^r-w_x)$ (main PDF, Section 4, Equation (5), PDF page 6)
- **Equilibrium:** Subgame-perfect Stackelberg wholesale-pricing and assortment equilibrium
- **Solution:** The authors first solve the retailer's assortment response under arbitrary wholesale prices and embed it in the manufacturer's bilevel problem. They solve the centralized assortment benchmark and identify why simple wholesale pricing generally misaligns attribute coverage. A scope contract discounts products that cover selected attribute levels and adds a transfer/single coordinating parameter, allowing the decentralized equilibrium to reproduce the centralized assortment while satisfying participation.
- **Evidence:** Analytical theory; Numerical / simulation
- **Caveat:** Coordination relies on observable and contractible product attributes, enforceable wholesale discounts and lump-sum transfers, a showcase-capacity constraint, and the assumed nested-logit demand, utility-inaccuracy, and return structure. Customer inaccuracy parameters are treated as primitives rather than estimated in the paper. The numerical study is illustrative, and the model omits inventory costs and fulfillment constraints. The authors also leave the long-run sustainability of profit coordination that lowers customer welfare for future analytical or empirical work.

### Incentive Design and Pricing Under Limited Inventory

Ruiting Zuo; Tinglong Dai; Jussi Keppo (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2026.0118](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2026.0118). First published online: 2026-06-15.

- **Question:** How should a capacity-constrained service firm jointly design sales incentives and prices when demand unfolds continuously, inventory perishes, and a sales agent's effort is hidden?
- **Players:** service firm/principal; sales agent
- **Timing:** At time zero the firm offers a terminal demand-contingent contract; the agent accepts if participation is met. During the horizon the firm observes cumulative demand/inventory and chooses incentives and, in the pricing model, prices, while the agent continuously chooses hidden effort; inventory expires at T.
- **Actions:** firm chooses terminal contract and incentive-intensity process Z_t; firm chooses static or dynamic price p_t; agent chooses adapted hidden effort A_t
- **Information:** The firm observes cumulative demand/sales and inventory but not effort.; Both parties know the Brownian demand law and contract; compensation is measurable with respect to the demand history.; The agent's continuation value is the state variable that enforces incentive compatibility.
- **Objective:** Anticipating the agent's optimal effort, the firm chooses an acceptable terminal contract to maximize discounted demand revenue net of compensation and terminal overbooking penalty.
- **Representative equation:** `$V^p=\sup_{\xi_T\in\Xi_a}\mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^T e^{-rt}dD_t-e^{-rT}\xi_T-e^{-rT}\pi(D_T-I_0)^+\right]$ (main PDF, Section 3, Equation (4), PDF page 5)
- **Equilibrium:** optimal continuous-time incentive-compatible contracting equilibrium
- **Solution:** Any acceptable terminal contract is represented by initial promised utility and an adapted incentive sensitivity Z. That converts hidden action into the explicit response A=eta Z and reduces the principal's problem to stochastic control in time, inventory/demand, and promised value. HJB analysis identifies optimal incentives and prices; the numerical scheme solves the finite-inventory boundary problem.
- **Evidence:** analytical theory; HJB/dynamic programming; numerical algorithm; airline parameterization
- **Caveat:** Brownian demand can decline through cancellations and is an approximation; the model has one product, one risk-neutral agent, exogenous starting inventory, and strong contract commitment/observability assumptions.

### Crowdsourcing Electric Vehicles for Omni-Sharing Distributed Energy Storage

Wenqing Ai; Tianhu Deng; Wei Qi; Wei Gu (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2021.0610](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2021.0610). First published online: 2026-07-02.

- **Question:** How should a community price crowdsourced electricity from electric vehicles and allocate storage and energy costs so that all consumers prefer stable omni-sharing cooperation?
- **Players:** energy consumers i in N, who are the formal cooperative-game players; coalitions S of those consumers, including the grand coalition N; ride-sharing and private-use electric-vehicle drivers whose aggregate supply responds to the community's posted uniform price
- **Timing:** During off-peak hours, consumers and EV drivers charge storage from the grid. During the peak period, consumers first share stationary storage; the community then purchases residual energy from willing EV drivers under a uniform-price scheme and finally buys any remaining shortfall from the grid. For the cooperative-game layer, consumers either enter with installed capacities or jointly choose community capacity, then allocate realized daily cost in the storage-present game or optimized expected cost in the joint-planning game across the grand coalition.
- **Actions:** the community chooses a uniform crowdsourcing price and quantity for EV energy; EV drivers decide whether the offered payment covers charging, spatial-mismatch, degradation, and outside-option costs; consumers choose whether to cooperate in the grand coalition or deviate as a subcoalition; in joint planning, the coalition selects stationary-storage capacity; the grand coalition assigns total cost to individual consumers
- **Information:** Time-of-use grid prices and the payment rule are common knowledge.; Peak-period demand is stochastic, while consumer storage capacities are known in the storage-present case.; EV availability, energy, location, and type are represented by aggregate distributions; the community uses the induced energy-supply function.; Every coalition can evaluate its characteristic cost V(S), including the optimal coalition structure outside S.
- **Objective:** The operating layer minimizes the cost of satisfying residual energy demand using EVs and the grid; the cooperative layer minimizes expected total daily storage-and-energy cost and allocates it efficiently and coalition-rationally.
- **Representative equation:** `$\min_{0\le h\le b} W(h,b)=\lambda(h)h+\lambda^H(b-h); \quad V_S(c_S,q_S)=(\lambda^C+\lambda^L)c_S-\lambda^L(c_S-q_S/\eta)^+ + \tilde{\lambda}(b_S(c_S))(q_S-\eta c_S)^+$ (Equations (6) and (8); pp. 8 and 10 of the main PDF)
- **Equilibrium:** Core-stable grand coalition with an optimal uniform-price crowdsourcing scheme
- **Solution:** The optimal EV purchase is min{b, h-bar}, where h-bar equates the marginal crowdsourcing payment with the grid peak price. The induced average energy price is below the peak grid tariff and rises with residual demand. The storage-present allocation is always core-stable; the joint-planning game has a generalized critical-fractile capacity and a dual allocation that is core-stable under a mild expected-price condition. Omni-sharing weakly lowers required capacity and total cost relative to stationary-only P2P sharing.
- **Evidence:** A stochastic cooperative cost game for both storage-present and joint storage-planning settings; Constructive core allocations using fractional allocation and stochastic-programming duality; Quantification with residential energy-consumption and ride-sharing-market data
- **Caveat:** The analysis concerns one community, aggregate EV heterogeneity, time-of-use tariffs, and sufficient conditions for the joint-planning core allocation. It does not model competition among neighboring communities for EV energy, and log-concavity of the aggregate crowdsourcing function is an assumed regularity supported numerically.

### Tip Your Farmer? Implications of Tipping on Smallholder Welfare in Agricultural Supply Chains

Saed Alizamir; Basak Kalkanci (2026). DOI: [10.1287/msom.2021.0059](https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2021.0059). First published online: 2026-07-20.

- **Question:** When does direct consumer tipping improve smallholder welfare, consumer surplus, and intermediary profit, and when can the intermediary strategically absorb tips through a lower wholesale price?
- **Players:** agricultural intermediary firm; a unit mass of heterogeneous smallholder farmers; a stochastic population of heterogeneous socially conscious consumers
- **Timing:** The firm commits to a wholesale price. Each farmer then chooses whether to meet the firm's farming standard or take an outside option, which determines supply. Consumer market size is realized; consumers choose whether to buy and, when enabled, how much to tip their matched farmer. The firm randomly allocates available supply to consumers and sells excess output to an industry buyer. In equilibrium, beliefs about the wholesale price and expected tips equal actual outcomes.
- **Actions:** the firm chooses the wholesale price paid to participating farmers; each farmer chooses whether to adopt the required farming practices and supply the firm; each consumer chooses whether to buy; each sufficiently socially conscious consumer chooses a nonnegative tip; the firm matches supply to stochastic consumer demand and salvages excess supply
- **Information:** Farmers observe the firm's committed wholesale price before their production decision.; Consumers do not directly observe the sourcing relationship at purchase time and form beliefs about the wholesale price.; The firm and farmers form beliefs about the average tip a farmer will receive.; Equilibrium imposes rational expectations: price and tip beliefs are consistent with the firm's optimum and consumers' realized behavior.; Farmers and consumers have privately heterogeneous types represented by continuous populations.
- **Objective:** The firm selects wholesale price w to maximize expected retail and salvage revenue net of procurement cost, taking the induced farmer supply, consumer demand, and equilibrium expected tips as given.
- **Representative equation:** `$\max_{w\ge r} \Pi_\tau(w;\tilde w,\tilde t)=p\,E[\min\{q_\tau(w,\tilde t),D_\tau(\tilde w)\}]+s\,E[(q_\tau(w,\tilde t)-D_\tau(\tilde w))^+]-wq_\tau(w,\tilde t)$ (Equation (8), p. 7 of the main PDF)
- **Equilibrium:** Rational-expectations equilibrium with full or partial market coverage and pure, mixed, or inactive tipping
- **Solution:** Active tipping occurs only for intermediate farmer outside options. A triple win is possible when the outside option lies in a moderate interval and consumer social consciousness is sufficiently high. Elsewhere, the firm may reduce its wholesale price enough to lower farmers' expected income or leave some untipped farmers worse off ex post. A commitment not to change the wholesale price weakly benefits farmers and consumers but can hurt the firm; jointly fixing the price and farmer base guarantees weak gains for all three groups.
- **Evidence:** Rational-expectations equilibrium with endogenous sourcing price, farmer entry, customer purchase, and tipping decisions; Closed-form threshold characterization of full- and partial-market-coverage regimes; Numerical extension with an endogenous retail price
- **Caveat:** The base model has continuum, price-taking farmers and consumers, uniform type distributions, random matching, an exogenous retail price, and no strategic industrial buyer. The equilibrium selection rule and fairness specification matter, and the authors explicitly call for experimental or empirical validation of the assumed fairness utility. The model also assumes farm-level traceability survives the full supply chain; product mixing could instead require pooled tips and alter consumer and farmer incentives. The endogenous-retail-price analysis is numerical rather than a full closed-form replacement of the base model.
